clues.description: This East Asian archipelago sits off the continental mainland, an island nation famous for blending deep tradition with cutting-edge technology.
Stretching from the snowy north of Hokkaido to the subtropical Okinawa, its terrain is rugged and volcanic, with a temperate climate.
A long imperial history, ancient temples, and a writing system mixing several scripts define a culture revered around the globe for its refinement.
Its sprawling capital ranks among the planet's largest cities, while a sacred snow-capped cone and springtime cherry blossoms draw countless visitors.
High-speed bullet trains glide past Kyoto's shrines in a place nicknamed the Land of the Rising Sun, home to sushi, samurai, and Mount Fuji.
The largest nation on its South American continent occupies nearly half of that landmass and faces the Atlantic along an enormous coastline.
It stands apart from its Spanish-speaking neighbors as the only major country in the region whose primary language is Portuguese.
An immense rainforest covers much of its interior, drained by a river that carries more water than any other on Earth.
Its purpose-built inland capital rose in the mid-twentieth century, while a giant mountaintop statue of Christ overlooks a famous beach city.
Samba, a wildly celebrated Carnival, football legends like Pelé, and the cities of Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo make this place unmistakable.
Lying entirely in the Southern Hemisphere, this vast landmass is unique in being both an entire continent and a single nation.
Surrounded by ocean, it is famous for a sun-baked interior known as the outback and densely populated cities clinging to the coast.
Indigenous peoples lived here for tens of thousands of years before British colonization shaped a now diverse, multicultural society.
Marsupials like kangaroos and koalas roam its bush, while a massive sandstone monolith called Uluru rises from the red center.
A shimmering coral reef off its northeast and the sail-shaped opera house in Sydney mark the planet's sixth-largest country by area.
Occupying the northern reaches of North America above its larger neighbor, this is the second-largest country on Earth by area.
Famously cold winters blanket a vast wilderness of forests, lakes, and tundra stretching all the way into the Arctic.
Two official languages, English and French, reflect a heritage tied to both the Pacific and the Atlantic shores.
Its capital straddles the boundary between two provinces, home to the Parliament buildings and the historic Rideau Canal.
Maple syrup, ice hockey, the towering Rockies, thundering Niagara Falls, and multicultural Toronto and Vancouver all belong to this northern realm.
This South Asian giant is among the most populous nations on Earth, with a civilization stretching back thousands of years.
Bordered by towering Himalayan peaks to the north and warm seas to the south, it embraces astonishing linguistic and cultural diversity.
Independence from Britain came in 1947, and today it is celebrated as the world's largest democracy with a booming technology sector.
A white marble mausoleum built for an emperor's beloved wife stands near Agra, while the sacred Ganges flows through the northern plains.
Spicy curries, the prolific Mumbai film industry, vibrant festivals, and a capital city in the north make this subcontinent unmistakable.
This Western European nation reaches from Alpine peaks to Mediterranean shores and a long Atlantic coast, anchoring the continent's heart.
Renowned worldwide for art, haute fashion, and celebrated vineyards, its capital is fondly nicknamed the City of Light.
A revolution born here in the late eighteenth century reshaped European politics, while its language spread across former colonies.
The Seine bisects its capital, where the Arc de Triomphe, Notre-Dame cathedral, and the Louvre's glass pyramid draw millions.
An iron lattice tower built for an 1889 fair towers over a founding EU member that holds a permanent UN Security Council seat.
This Central European powerhouse stretches from the North Sea down to the Alps, with a federal structure of sixteen states.
It is the most populous member of the European Union and a leading global force in engineering, automobiles, and manufacturing.
Its history runs from the Reformation through a twentieth-century division and eventual reunification after a famous wall fell.
Its capital, once split by that very wall, is now defined by the columned Brandenburg Gate and a renowned museum island.
Beer halls during Oktoberfest, the dark pine of the Black Forest, and luxury car brands all point to this Mitteleuropa nation.
Shaped like a boot kicking a ball across the Mediterranean, this Southern European peninsula juts toward the African coast.
It was the cradle of a mighty ancient empire and later the birthplace of the Renaissance, with art and cuisine that conquered the world.
An enormous oval amphitheater for gladiators still stands in its capital, where pasta and pizza were perfected over centuries.
Within that capital sits an independent walled enclave, the spiritual seat of the Catholic Church, home to the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
Venice's canals, Florence's Renaissance masterpieces, and a famously tilting bell tower at Pisa mark this Mediterranean nation.
This southwestern European nation occupies most of the Iberian Peninsula, with coasts on both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
Once the launching point for explorers who built a global empire, it is famed for passionate flamenco and historic bullfighting.
Its sun-soaked culture gave the world the midday siesta and the saffron rice dish paella shared from a wide pan.
The capital sits high on a central plateau, celebrated for the Prado Museum, the Royal Palace, and famously late nightlife.
Gaudí's unfinished basilica in Barcelona, the Basque Country, Catalonia, and the Canary Islands all belong to this Iberian land.
This island realm lies off the northwestern coast of mainland Europe, separated from the continent by a narrow channel.
It unites four constituent nations and is famous for its monarchy, afternoon tea, and an outsized literary and political legacy.
Once the seat of a globe-spanning empire, it still hosts a major financial center and departed the European Union in 2020.
The River Thames winds through its capital, past Buckingham Palace, the clock tower nicknamed Big Ben, and the British Museum.
The Beatles, the BBC, Shakespeare, and a union of England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland define this sovereign island state.
Bridging North and Central America just south of its powerful northern neighbor, this nation touches both the Pacific and the Atlantic.
Ancient Maya and Aztec civilizations flourished here long before Spanish conquest, leaving pyramids and a rich indigenous heritage.
A vibrant culture of festivals, mariachi, tequila, and the colorful Day of the Dead defines life across its varied regions.
Its sprawling capital, one of the planet's largest, rose atop a drained Aztec lake and centers on a grand plaza called the Zócalo.
Tacos, the beaches of Cancún, the Yucatán Peninsula, and the painter Frida Kahlo all mark this leading Latin American economy.
Occupying the southern half of an East Asian peninsula, this nation rose from the ashes of war into a global powerhouse.
Tech conglomerates like Samsung and Hyundai dominate its economy, while a pop-music wave has swept across the world.
A tense, heavily fortified frontier separates it from a reclusive neighbor to the north along a demilitarized zone.
Its megacity capital is split by the Han River, mixing ancient royal palaces with gleaming ultra-modern skyscraper districts.
Spicy fermented kimchi, addictive dramas, and the bustling port of Busan all belong to this republic on the peninsula.
Stretching down the southern cone of South America, this elongated nation reaches from subtropical north to icy Tierra del Fuego.
Towering Andean peaks line its western border while vast grassy plains called the Pampas spread across its fertile heartland.
Famous for sizzling beef, the sultry tango, and roaring football passion, it holds the title of eighth-largest country on Earth.
Its European-flavored capital, dubbed the Paris of the south, sits on the Río de la Plata with broad avenues and an iconic obelisk.
Thundering Iguazú Falls, the Recoleta Cemetery, and footballing icons Maradona and Messi all belong to this southern land.
Straddling North Africa and the Middle East, this desert nation is split by a mighty river flowing north to the Mediterranean.
It cradled one of humanity's oldest civilizations, ruled for millennia by god-kings whose monuments still astonish travelers.
Colossal stone tombs and a riddle-posing lion-bodied statue rise from the sands near Giza, just outside its sprawling capital.
That capital is the largest city in both Africa and the Arab world, perched along the banks of the life-giving Nile.
Ancient temples at Luxor and Aswan, hieroglyphics, pharaohs, and Red Sea diving resorts all mark this cradle of antiquity.
Anchoring the southern tip of its continent, this nation faces two oceans meeting near a famously stormy cape.
It carries the unusual distinction of three capital cities and recognizes eleven official languages across its diverse population.
A painful history of racial segregation gave way to reconciliation led by an iconic prisoner-turned-president, Nelson Mandela.
A flat-topped mountain looms over Cape Town, while Kruger National Park draws safari-goers hoping to spot the Big Five.
Dubbed the Rainbow Nation, this safari, wine, and history destination is among the strongest economies on the African continent.
This Southeast Asian kingdom occupies the heart of the region, uniquely never having fallen under European colonial rule.
Glittering Buddhist temples, a revered monarchy, and bustling street food culture lie at the core of its national identity.
Its tropical climate nurtures jungles and beaches that draw millions of backpackers and beachgoers each year.
The capital sits on the Chao Phraya River, where the ornate Grand Palace, floating markets, and a famous backpacker road thrive.
Nicknamed the Land of Smiles, it gave the world pad thai noodles, full-moon beach parties, and the megacity of Bangkok.
This low-lying northwestern European nation has much of its land reclaimed from the sea and sitting below sea level.
Spinning windmills, fields of tulips, and an obsession with cycling characterize a flat landscape laced with canals.
A seventeenth-century golden age produced masters like Rembrandt and, later, Van Gogh, under a constitutional monarchy.
Its government sits in a historic city, while its largest city, ringed by canals, houses the Royal Palace and Anne Frank's hiding place.
Often loosely called Holland, this liberal, tolerant nation of Amsterdam draws visitors with its art, canals, and famously open culture.
This Northern European kingdom forms the larger eastern part of the Scandinavian Peninsula, fronting the Baltic Sea.
Endless forests and thousands of lakes cover a land famed for sleek design and a generous welfare state.
It is among the world's most prosperous and egalitarian societies, ruled by a long-standing royal family.
Its island-spread capital is built across fourteen islets, home to the salvaged Vasa warship and a charming medieval Old Town.
Flat-pack furniture giant IKEA, the pop quartet ABBA, and the annual Nobel Prizes all originate from this northern realm.
This Central European nation stretches from the Baltic Sea in the north to the Tatra Mountains along its southern frontier.
Its history brims with resistance and resilience, from partitions and wartime devastation to a famous Solidarity movement.
A key member of the EU and NATO, it gave the world the composer Chopin and the dumpling delicacy pierogi.
Its capital, painstakingly rebuilt after wartime destruction, features a reconstructed Royal Castle beside the Vistula River.
Medieval Kraków, the port of Gdańsk, and a deep Catholic and Jewish heritage all belong to this resilient Central European state.
This small Western European nation is wedged between France and the Netherlands, with a short coast on the North Sea.
Famed for artisanal chocolate, crisp waffles, and hundreds of distinctive beers, it punches well above its modest size.
Split between Dutch-speaking Flemish and French-speaking regions, it cherishes a wealth of well-preserved medieval towns.
Its capital is often called the de facto capital of Europe, hosting EU institutions, a grand central square, and a cluster-shaped Atomium.
A cheeky little statue of a urinating boy, the Battle of Waterloo, and the forested Ardennes hills all lie within this compact kingdom.
This landlocked, mountainous Central European nation sits atop the continent, threaded by the soaring peaks of the Alps.
Long famous for political neutrality, discreet banking, fine chocolate, and precision watchmaking, it ranks among the wealthiest places on Earth.
Four national languages coexist here, and a federal capital that is notably not its largest city seats the government.
That capital hosts the medieval Zytglogge clock tower, while Zurich serves as the country's bustling financial hub.
A jagged pyramid-shaped peak called the Matterhorn, melted cheese fondue, and a white cross on a red flag all mark this Alpine confederation.
This southwestern European nation occupies the western edge of the Iberian Peninsula, with a long Atlantic coastline.
Among the continent's oldest nations, it once commanded a sprawling maritime empire forged by daring seafaring explorers.
Soulful fado music, fortified wine from the Douro Valley, and creamy custard tarts express its distinctive culture.
Its capital rises across seven hills beside the Tagus River, marked by the riverside Belém Tower and the Jerónimos Monastery.
Rattling vintage trams climbing Lisbon's slopes and the golden beaches of the Algarve make this sun-soaked country unmistakable.
This southeastern European nation juts into the Mediterranean, scattered across a peninsula and thousands of sun-drenched islands.
It is hailed as the birthplace of democracy, Western philosophy, theater, and the ancient Olympic Games.
Its capital ranks among the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, crowned by a sacred citadel of marble temples.
A columned temple to the goddess Athena dominates that hilltop Acropolis, overlooking the old Plaka quarter and skewers of souvlaki.
Whitewashed villages on Santorini, a legacy that shaped Western civilization, and endless azure islands define this Aegean land.
This Northern European nation forms the western spine of the Scandinavian Peninsula, with an immensely long, jagged coastline.
Deep glacier-carved inlets called fjords cut into its mountains, and its people enjoy one of the planet's highest living standards.
Seafaring raiders sailed from these shores in the medieval era, and today shimmering aurora lights dance across its northern skies.
Its capital lies at the head of a fjord, hosting the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony, a striking opera house, and a sculpture-filled park.
A petroleum-funded sovereign wealth fund, the dramatic North Cape, and Viking longships all belong to this prosperous coastal kingdom.
Lying in the South Pacific southeast of its larger continental neighbor, this remote nation comprises two main islands.
Dramatic scenery of mountains, fjords, and rolling pastures supports famously large flocks of sheep and a fervent rugby culture.
It served as the cinematic backdrop for Middle-earth, while a strong indigenous Māori and Pacific heritage shapes its identity.
Its windy capital sits at the southern tip of the northern island, home to the beehive-shaped parliament building.
The flightless kiwi bird, the black-jerseyed All Blacks performing the haka, and Queenstown's adventure sports all mark this island nation.
This rugged, mountainous nation sits in South-Central Asia, completely landlocked and bordered by several countries that touch the historic Silk Road.
Its terrain is dominated by the Hindu Kush, and it shares frontiers with Pakistan to the east and south and Iran to the west.
Long a crossroads of empires, it blends Persian and Central Asian culture, with Pashtun and Tajik peoples and a turbulent modern history of conflict.
Its capital lies in a high valley ringed by peaks, and the giant Bamiyan Buddhas once carved into its cliffs were destroyed in 2001.
The Taliban returned to power here in 2021 after foreign forces withdrew, and the Wakhan Corridor stretches east toward China from its territory.
This small, mountainous country sits in Southeastern Europe on the Balkan Peninsula, with a coastline facing the Adriatic and Ionian seas.
It borders Greece to the south and Montenegro to the north, and a scenic Riviera runs along its rocky Mediterranean shoreline.
Once isolated under a hardline communist regime, it is dotted with thousands of old concrete bunkers and blends Ottoman and European influences.
Its capital, Tirana, is famed for brightly painted buildings, while the stone town of Gjirokaster is a celebrated UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Locals call their land the realm of eagles, speak a unique Indo-European language with no close relatives, and gesture nods and shakes in reverse.
This vast North African nation borders the Mediterranean Sea, with most of its enormous territory swallowed by the Sahara Desert.
It is the largest country on its continent by area, sharing southern desert borders with Mali and Niger and an eastern frontier with Libya.
Ancient Roman ruins, Berber heritage, and a long French colonial past shape its identity, alongside major oil and natural gas reserves.
Its whitewashed capital climbs hillsides above a Mediterranean bay, and the Tassili rock art and Hoggar Mountains lie deep in its desert interior.
It won bloody independence from France in 1962, speaks Arabic and Tamazight, and counts Chott Melrhir, a vast salt lake, among its lowest points.
This tiny European microstate is tucked high in a mountain range that forms a natural border between two larger neighbors.
Landlocked in the Pyrenees, it sits between Spain and France and ranks among the smallest sovereign states on the continent.
Catalan is its official tongue, and it is famous as a duty-free shopping haven and ski destination drawing millions of visitors yearly.
Its capital is the highest in Europe, and the country is unusually ruled by two co-princes: a French president and a Spanish bishop.
This co-principality uses the euro despite not joining the EU, has no airport, and is one of the world's only remaining feudal-style states.
This large southern African nation has a long Atlantic coastline and a separate northern province split off by a neighboring country's territory.
It borders Namibia to the south and the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the north, with the Cabinda exclave rich in offshore oil.
A former Portuguese colony, it endured a long civil war after 1975 and is a major producer of diamonds and petroleum.
Its seaside capital, Luanda, is one of the world's most expensive cities, and Benguela is a key Atlantic port to its south.
Portuguese is the official language here, semba and kizomba music thrive, and oil revenues dominate one of Africa's largest economies.
This small, mountainous landlocked nation sits in the Caucasus region where Europe meets Asia, near the Black and Caspian seas.
It is bordered by Turkey, Georgia, Iran, and Azerbaijan, and the snow-capped Mount Ararat dominates the view from its capital.
It was the first state to adopt Christianity, and ancient monasteries carved into cliffs and stone khachkar crosses dot its highlands.
Its capital, Yerevan, is famed for pink tuff-stone buildings, brandy distilleries, and the sacred shores of high-altitude Lake Sevan.
Its unique 36-letter alphabet was devised by a single monk, Mesrop Mashtots, and a vast worldwide diaspora keeps its ancient culture alive.
This landlocked Central European nation is dominated by towering Alpine peaks and lies at the heart of the continent.
It shares borders with Germany, Italy, Switzerland, and Hungary, with the Danube River flowing through its capital.
Once the seat of the powerful Habsburg dynasty, it boasts imperial palaces, classical music traditions, and famous coffeehouse culture.
Its grand capital on the Danube is renowned for waltzes and opera, while Salzburg was the birthplace of composer Mozart.
Home to the Schonbrunn Palace and the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's concert, German is its language and skiing is a national passion.
This Western Asian nation lies in the Caucasus, with a long eastern coastline along the world's largest inland body of water.
Bordered by Russia, Georgia, Armenia, and Iran, it sits where Europe and Asia blur and includes the separated Nakhchivan exclave.
Often called the Land of Fire for its natural burning gas vents, it has ancient Silk Road heritage and immense oil wealth.
Its windswept capital on the Caspian shore is crowned by three curving skyscrapers shaped like flames overlooking a medieval walled old town.
Petroleum from this Caspian coast fueled early 20th-century industry, and its people speak a Turkic language while mostly practicing Shia Islam.
This tiny island nation in Western Asia sits in the Persian Gulf, an archipelago connected to the mainland by a long causeway.
A 25-kilometer causeway links it to Saudi Arabia, while Qatar lies just across the gulf waters to its east.
Famous for centuries of pearl diving, it blends Arab and Persian heritage and was the Gulf's first state to strike oil in 1932.
Its capital, Manama, mixes traditional souks with gleaming towers, and the country hosts a Formula One Grand Prix on a desert circuit.
This small kingdom is a regional banking hub, hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, and its name means 'two seas' in Arabic.
This densely populated South Asian nation sits in a low-lying monsoon zone, nearly surrounded by one giant neighbor.
Almost entirely encircled by India, it touches Myanmar in its southeast and opens onto the Bay of Bengal to the south.
Built on the world's largest river delta, it endures frequent flooding and is a leading exporter of ready-made garments and jute.
Its capital, Dhaka, teems with cycle rickshaws, while the Sundarbans mangroves shelter the famed Royal Bengal tiger near the coast.
Born in 1971 after a war of independence from Pakistan, it speaks Bengali and is one of the most crowded nations on Earth.
This flat, forested, landlocked nation lies in Eastern Europe, threaded with rivers, lakes, and vast marshlands.
It borders Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia, with the Pripyat marshes spreading across its southern lowlands.
A former Soviet republic with a Slavic Orthodox heritage, it retains a state-run economy and Soviet-era monuments and symbols.
Its tidy capital, Minsk, rebuilt after wartime devastation, anchors a country sharing the ancient Bialowieza forest and its bison with Poland.
Ruled for decades by a single strongman often dubbed Europe's last dictator, it remains a close military ally of Moscow.
This small Central American nation faces the Caribbean Sea and is the only country on that isthmus where English is the official language.
It borders Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south, with a tropical coastline fringed by cays and reefs.
Once known as British Honduras, it blends Creole, Garifuna, and Maya cultures and protects ancient pyramids like Caracol and Xunantunich.
Its offshore barrier reef is the second largest on Earth, featuring the famous deep-blue sinkhole known as the Great Blue Hole.
Tiny in population, it shelters the world's only jaguar preserve at Cockscomb Basin and gained full independence from Britain in 1981.
This narrow West African nation stretches from a short Gulf of Guinea coastline northward into tropical savanna.
It is wedged between Togo to the west and Nigeria to the east, with Burkina Faso and Niger lying to its north.
Widely regarded as the birthplace of the Vodun religion, it was once home to the mighty Kingdom of Dahomey and its female warriors.
Its largest city, Cotonou, bustles on the coast, while Porto-Novo serves as the official capital and Ganvie sits on stilts above a lagoon.
The historic port of Ouidah was a major departure point of the transatlantic slave trade, and French is the country's official language.
This small landlocked kingdom is perched in the eastern Himalayas, a remote nation of deep valleys and towering snow peaks.
It is sandwiched between India to the south and the Tibetan region of China to the north, near the eastern end of the great range.
It measures progress through Gross National Happiness, is the world's only carbon-negative country, and bans cigarette sales.
Its capital is Thimphu, and the cliffside Tiger's Nest monastery near Paro clings dramatically to a sheer rock face above a valley.
The last great Buddhist Himalayan kingdom, it calls itself the Land of the Thunder Dragon and limits tourism with a daily visitor fee.
This landlocked South American nation spans high Andean plateaus and stretches down into Amazon lowlands and tropical forest.
Bordered by Brazil, Peru, Chile, Argentina, and Paraguay, it shares the high navigable Lake Titicaca with one of those neighbors.
Rich in indigenous Aymara and Quechua heritage, it lost its Pacific coastline in a 19th-century war and prizes silver from Potosi.
Its seat of government, La Paz, sprawls across thin-aired heights, while the dazzling Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat.
It has two capitals, Sucre and La Paz, an indigenous-majority population, and a wiphala rainbow flag flown beside its national colors.
This mountainous country lies in Southeastern Europe on the Balkan Peninsula, with only a tiny sliver of Adriatic coastline.
It is nearly enclosed by Croatia, with Serbia and Montenegro along its eastern edge, and the Dinaric Alps crossing its interior.
A crossroads of Ottoman and European cultures, it emerged from the breakup of Yugoslavia after a devastating 1990s war.
Its capital, where the spark that ignited World War One was struck in 1914, hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics among forested hills.
The famous arched Stari Most bridge spans the Neretva at Mostar, and the nation is governed under a rotating three-member presidency.
This landlocked Southern African nation is largely covered by the Kalahari Desert and renowned for abundant wildlife.
It borders South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe, and Zambia, the latter meeting it at one of the world's shortest international borders.
A stable diamond-rich democracy, it hosts the vast inland Okavango Delta where seasonal floods create a wildlife oasis.
Its capital is Gaborone, and the mighty Victoria Falls thunders just beyond its northeastern corner along the Zambezi River.
Home to the largest elephant population on Earth in Chobe, its people are called Batswana and the currency is the pula.
This Southeastern European nation lies on the Balkan Peninsula, with a Black Sea coastline along its entire eastern edge.
It borders Romania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece, and Turkey, with the Danube River marking much of its northern frontier.
Once part of the Ottoman Empire, it has Orthodox Christian traditions, Thracian gold treasures, and rose fields prized for fragrant oil.
Its capital, Sofia, sits beneath Vitosha Mountain, while Plovdiv ranks among Europe's oldest continuously inhabited cities.
Birthplace of the Cyrillic script's spread and home to yogurt-making traditions, its people nod the head to mean no and shake it for yes.
This landlocked West African nation lies in the semi-arid Sahel, a land of flat savanna and seasonal rains south of the Sahara.
It is surrounded by six neighbors including Mali, Niger, Ghana, and Ivory Coast, with no access to the sea.
Formerly called Upper Volta, it is a major cotton and gold producer and a center of traditional bronze and textile craftsmanship.
Its capital, Ouagadougou, hosts FESPACO, Africa's largest film festival, and the country celebrates a revered revolutionary leader, Thomas Sankara.
Its name means 'land of upright people,' it speaks French alongside Mooré, and it faces growing instability from Sahel insurgencies.
This tiny landlocked nation lies in East Africa's Great Lakes region, a country of steep green hills and high plateaus.
It borders Rwanda to the north, Tanzania to the east, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo across a vast lake to its west.
One of the world's poorest nations, its economy leans on coffee and tea, and its culture is famed for thunderous royal drumming.
Its largest city sits on the shores of deep Lake Tanganyika, while Gitega serves as the political capital in the interior highlands.
Sharing Hutu and Tutsi heritage with neighboring Rwanda, it endured a long civil war and speaks Kirundi and French.
This Southeast Asian nation sits on the Indochinese Peninsula with a coastline along the Gulf of Thailand.
It borders Thailand, Laos, and Vietnam, with the Mekong River and the great Tonle Sap lake at its watery heart.
Heir to the Khmer civilization, it is famed for vast medieval temple complexes and scarred by the brutal Khmer Rouge era of the 1970s.
Its capital, Phnom Penh, sits at a river confluence, while the sprawling temple city of Angkor near Siem Reap draws millions of visitors.
The towers of its most famous temple appear on the national flag, the only flag in the world to feature a building.
This Central African nation stretches from a Gulf of Guinea coastline through rainforest up to dry northern savanna.
It borders Nigeria, Chad, the Central African Republic, and the Congo, often called Africa in miniature for its varied landscapes.
Once a German colony later split between Britain and France, it is officially bilingual and famed for vibrant makossa music.
Its largest port city is Douala, its capital is Yaounde, and an active volcano towering over the coast shares the country's name.
Its football team, the Indomitable Lions, dazzled the 1990 World Cup, and English- and French-speaking regions fuel internal tensions.
This island nation is an Atlantic archipelago off the western bulge of Africa, made up of ten volcanic isles.
Lying west of Senegal, it was uninhabited until Portuguese settlers arrived, and a tall active volcano rises on the island of Fogo.
Its Creole culture blends African and Portuguese roots, and the soulful morna music genre was made famous worldwide by Cesaria Evora.
Its capital, Praia, sits on the largest island, Santiago, while wind-swept Sal and Boa Vista draw beachgoers and kitesurfers.
Once a hub of the Atlantic slave trade, this Portuguese-speaking nation now thrives on tourism, remittances, and a barefoot diva's legacy.
This landlocked nation sits almost exactly in the middle of the continent, blanketed by savanna and dense equatorial rainforest.
It borders Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, the two Congos, and Cameroon, with no coastline anywhere along its frontiers.
Rich in diamonds, gold, and uranium yet deeply impoverished, it has endured repeated coups and chronic political instability.
Its capital, Bangui, sits on the Ubangi River, and a notorious self-proclaimed emperor, Bokassa, once crowned himself here in 1977.
Sango and French are spoken across this conflict-torn nation, whose Dzanga-Sangha reserve shelters forest elephants and lowland gorillas.
This vast landlocked nation lies in north-central Africa, with the Sahara Desert covering its arid northern reaches.
It borders Libya, Sudan, the Central African Republic, Cameroon, Nigeria, and Niger, far from any ocean.
Nomadic herding shapes its culture, oil drives its economy, and the volcanic Tibesti and Ennedi massifs rise from its northern sands.
Its capital, N'Djamena, sits beside a shrinking namesake lake once among Africa's largest, now threatened by desertification.
Often called the Dead Heart of Africa, this French- and Arabic-speaking nation straddles the Sahel and the desert and the savanna.
This South American nation in the southern hemisphere is famously long and thin, stretching thousands of kilometres down the continent's western edge.
Squeezed between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes, its territory ranges from arid northern deserts to icy fjords and glaciers in the far south.
It holds the driest non-polar desert on Earth, the Atacama, and produces more copper than any other country on the planet.
Its capital Santiago sits in a central valley, while distant Easter Island, with its giant stone moai statues, also falls under this flag.
Reaching toward Cape Horn at the continent's tip, this wine-exporting republic narrowly skirted earthquakes and boasts the towering Torres del Paine peaks.
This vast East Asian nation spans deserts, high plateaus and fertile river valleys across one of the largest territories on the continent.
Its lands are crossed by the Yangtze and Yellow rivers, and ancient traditions of calligraphy, tea ceremonies and martial arts run deep here.
A monumental defensive wall snakes across its northern hills for thousands of miles, built and rebuilt over many centuries against invaders.
The capital Beijing pairs a glittering modern skyline with the Forbidden City and Tiananmen Square, near the buried terracotta army of Xi'an.
Home to more people than any other land for most of history, it invented paper, gunpowder and the compass and remains a manufacturing powerhouse.
This South American country is the only one on the continent touching both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.
Its landscapes leap from steamy Amazon rainforest to snow-capped Andean ranges that split into three branches running through the interior.
Famous for smooth coffee and the rhythms of salsa and cumbia, it is also the world's leading source of fine emeralds.
The city of Medellin, once notorious, reinvented itself with cable cars and libraries, while Cartagena guards its walled colonial old town.
Its yellow, blue and red flag flies over Bogota, the high-altitude capital, in a nation that inspired the magical realism of Gabriel Garcia Marquez.
This tiny African island nation sits in the Indian Ocean between the mainland coast of Mozambique and the large island of Madagascar.
Made up of three main volcanic islands and scattered islets, it blends African, Arab and French influences in language and custom.
Its people speak Comorian, French and Arabic, and the active volcano Mount Karthala looms over the largest island, Grande Comore.
The modest capital Moroni anchors a small republic that has weathered many coups, with the island of Mayotte still administered by France nearby.
Nicknamed the 'Perfumed Islands', it grows much of the world's fragrant ylang-ylang, the flower distilled into oil for luxury perfumes.
This small Central American nation forms part of the narrow isthmus linking the two continents of the Americas.
It boasts coastlines on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, with rainforests, cloud forests and volcanoes packed into the interior.
A pioneer of ecotourism and conservation, it abolished its army in 1948 and runs largely on renewable energy.
The capital San Jose sits in the central highlands, ringed by volcanoes like Arenal and Poas in a country bordered by Nicaragua and Panama.
Its people, called Ticos, greet life with the cheerful motto 'pura vida' and share their forests with sloths, toucans and resplendent quetzals.
This European country curls along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, with a famously long and crinkled coastline.
Once part of Yugoslavia, it borders Slovenia, Hungary, Serbia and Bosnia, and its territory bends in a distinctive crescent or boomerang shape.
Roman ruins like Diocletian's Palace in Split and the medieval walls of Dubrovnik reflect a long, layered Mediterranean history.
Its sunny islands such as Hvar and Brac draw sailors, while the capital Zagreb sits inland and the Plitvice Lakes cascade through the forests.
Game of Thrones filmed King's Landing along its honey-coloured ramparts, and its national team reached the 2018 World Cup final in checkerboard jerseys.
This is the largest island in the Caribbean Sea, lying just south of Florida and west of Hispaniola in the Americas.
Vintage 1950s American cars still cruise its streets, and its culture fuses Spanish and African roots into music, dance and rhythm.
World-renowned for hand-rolled cigars and aged rum, it became a socialist state after a 20th-century revolution.
Its capital, with crumbling pastel colonial facades and a seafront promenade called the Malecon, anchors a single-party republic.
Bearded revolutionaries Fidel Castro and Che Guevara led its uprising, and a 1962 missile crisis here brought the world near nuclear war.
This island nation sits in the eastern Mediterranean Sea, closer to the coasts of Turkey, Syria and Lebanon than to mainland Europe.
An EU member with deep Greek roots, it remains split between a Greek-speaking south and a Turkish-controlled north since 1974.
Ancient ruins, Byzantine churches and mosaics fill the landscape, and copper mined here in antiquity gave the metal its very name.
A UN buffer zone slices through its divided capital Nicosia, while resort towns like Limassol and Paphos line the sunny coast.
Greek myth names it the birthplace of Aphrodite, goddess of love, said to have risen from the sea foam off its rocky southern shore.
This landlocked Central European nation of rolling hills and historic castles sits at the very heart of the continent.
It borders Germany, Austria, Poland and Slovakia, the latter once joined to it before a peaceful split in 1993.
Folk puppetry, beer gardens and Bohemian glassmaking are cherished here, and locals drink more beer per head than anyone on Earth.
Its capital straddles the Vltava River, famed for the medieval Charles Bridge, a hilltop castle and an astronomical clock that chimes hourly.
The birthplace of pilsner lager and the city long called Bohemia's crown, it uses the koruna and inspired writers from Kafka to Kundera.
This enormous central African nation, the second largest on the continent, is cloaked in dense equatorial rainforest.
A mighty river of the same regional basin loops through it, and the country holds vast deposits of cobalt, copper and diamonds.
Its vibrant musical heritage gave the world soukous and rumba, while a brutal era of Belgian colonial rule under King Leopold scarred its past.
The sprawling capital Kinshasa faces Brazzaville across the river, and the country sits within the Great Lakes region beside Rwanda and Uganda.
Once known as Zaire, it hosted the 1974 'Rumble in the Jungle' boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in Kinshasa.
This small Scandinavian kingdom in northern Europe occupies a peninsula and hundreds of islands jutting up from the German border.
Flat and windswept, it pioneered offshore wind power and is famous for minimalist design, cycling and the cosy concept of hygge.
Its Viking seafarers once raided across Europe, and the interlocking plastic brick toy beloved worldwide was invented here.
The harbourside capital, with its Nyhavn canal and a small bronze mermaid statue, is linked to Sweden by the long Oresund Bridge.
A constitutional monarchy ruling Greenland and the Faroe Islands, it inspired Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales and Shakespeare's Hamlet at Elsinore castle.
This small, hot African nation guards a strategic strait where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden in the Horn of Africa.
Bordered by Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia, it sits on a vital shipping lane and hosts foreign military bases from several world powers.
Its scorched volcanic terrain includes salt flats, lava fields and one of the saltiest, lowest lakes anywhere on the planet.
The bustling port capital, sharing the country's name, serves as the main maritime gateway for landlocked Ethiopia's imports and exports.
Hypersaline Lake Assal lies more than 150 metres below sea level, while the Afar people herd livestock across this French-speaking former colony.
This Caribbean nation occupies the eastern two-thirds of the island of Hispaniola, sharing it with Haiti to the west.
Lush mountains and white-sand beaches define it, and the upbeat merengue and bachata genres of music were born on its soil.
Its colonial capital, Santo Domingo, founded by Columbus's brother, holds the oldest European cathedral and fortress in the Americas.
Resort coastlines like Punta Cana draw millions of tourists, while Pico Duarte rises as the highest peak in the entire Caribbean.
It exports a remarkable number of Major League Baseball stars, and its flag is the only national one to display an open Bible.
This South American nation straddles the line of zero latitude, bordering Colombia and Peru on the continent's Pacific side.
The Andes Mountains run down its spine, dividing coastal lowlands from Amazon jungle, and it uses the US dollar as currency.
Indigenous and colonial cultures mingle here, and snow-capped volcanoes like Cotopaxi and Chimborazo tower over the highlands.
Its high-altitude capital Quito boasts a superbly preserved colonial old town, and a famous volcanic archipelago lies far offshore.
The Galapagos Islands, where Charles Darwin studied finches and giant tortoises, belong to this exporter of bananas and fine cacao.
This relatively small country is located on the mainland of the Americas, sitting within the narrow isthmus that links two larger continents.
It is a densely populated and compact nation situated in the central region of the Americas, bordered by neighbors on two sides.
Volcanic landscapes and vibrant coffee plantations define much of its terrain, and its culture is deeply rooted in Mayan heritage.
The capital shares its name with the country, and the nation borders Guatemala and Honduras while boasting beautiful Pacific coastlines.
Known for its surfing beaches and a beloved stuffed corn flatbread, this nation declared independence from Spain in 1821.
This small country is located in the central part of Africa, with territory lying very close to the line dividing the hemispheres.
It is a compact nation made up of both a mainland portion and several islands, with one island hosting the seat of government.
This country boasts a diverse landscape including rainforests and volcanic mountains, and is known for its oil reserves.
Its capital city, Malabo, is situated on the island of Bioko, and it is a former Spanish colony.
It is the only sovereign African state where Spanish is an official language, and its economy is heavily reliant on offshore oil production.
This northeast African nation hugs a long stretch of Red Sea coastline in the region known as the Horn of Africa.
It borders Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, with arid coastal lowlands rising to cooler central highlands inland.
After decades of armed struggle, it won independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and is often called one of the world's most closed states.
Its highland capital, Asmara, is a UNESCO-listed showcase of 1930s Italian colonial Art Deco architecture, once dubbed 'Little Rome'.
The volcanic Dahlak Archipelago dots its waters, and its lengthy national service has driven many young citizens to flee abroad.
This northern European country, the smallest and most northerly of the three Baltic states, faces Finland across a narrow gulf.
Bordered by Latvia to the south and Russia to the east, it sits on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea amid forests and bogs.
Its language is closely related to Finnish, and after Soviet rule it became famous as one of the world's most advanced digital societies.
The capital, Tallinn, preserves a fairy-tale medieval old town of cobbled lanes, spires and turreted city walls beside the sea.
Birthplace of the internet calling service Skype, it offers e-residency and online voting, and singing helped power its peaceful break from Moscow.
This large, landlocked African nation in the Horn of Africa is dominated by dramatic highlands and deep rift valleys.
Bordered by Eritrea, Sudan, Kenya and Somalia, it gives rise to the Blue Nile and was never formally colonised by a European power.
Often credited as the birthplace of coffee, it keeps its own calendar and a 13-month year, with ancient Christian kingdoms in its past.
Its capital Addis Ababa hosts the African Union headquarters, and rock-hewn churches were carved into the cliffs at Lalibela centuries ago.
The ancient fossil skeleton 'Lucy' was unearthed in its Afar region, and runners from here regularly dominate the world's long-distance races.
This South Pacific island nation lies in the southern hemisphere, scattered across hundreds of volcanic islands and coral atolls in Melanesia.
A former British colony, its culture mixes Indigenous Pacific traditions with the descendants of Indian laborers brought to cut sugarcane.
Its two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, hold most of the population, and the kava drink features in welcoming ceremonies.
The international airport sits at Nadi, while the capital Suva governs an archipelago famed for diving among vivid soft corals and reefs.
Its rugby sevens team are Olympic champions, and tourists soak in luxury resorts on white beaches once dubbed the 'Soft Coral Capital of the World'.
This Nordic country in northern Europe stretches well into the Arctic Circle, bordering Sweden, Norway and a long frontier with Russia.
Nicknamed the land of a thousand lakes, it is blanketed in vast forests dotted with tens of thousands of glittering waterways.
Steamy saunas are a national institution, and its language, unrelated to its neighbors', belongs to the Finno-Ugric family.
Its seaside capital, Helsinki, faces the Baltic, while Rovaniemi in the north markets itself as the official hometown of Santa Claus.
Repeatedly ranked the world's happiest nation, it gave us the Moomins, Nokia phones and the dazzling northern lights of Lapland.
This central African nation straddles the line of zero latitude, fronting the Atlantic Ocean within the equatorial rainforest belt.
Bordered by Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and the Republic of the Congo, it is largely covered by dense, sparsely populated jungle.
Roughly a tenth of its land is protected national parks teeming with forest elephants, gorillas and even surfing hippos at Loango.
Its coastal capital, Libreville, sits near the Equator, and oil and timber exports underpin a relatively small population's economy.
Once ruled for decades by the Bongo family, this former French colony is famed for beaches where hippopotamuses are filmed swimming in the surf.
This is the smallest country on the African mainland, a thin sliver of West Africa wrapped almost entirely around a single river.
Apart from a short Atlantic coast, it is completely surrounded by Senegal, following the meandering waterway deep inland.
Long a hub for the peanut and groundnut trade, it draws birdwatchers and beach tourists to its short stretch of coastline.
Its compact capital, Banjul, sits at the river's mouth, and English remains the official language from its British colonial era.
Marketed as the 'Smiling Coast of Africa', it featured in Alex Haley's 'Roots', which traced his ancestry to the village of Juffureh here.
This nation straddles the boundary of Europe and Asia, perched in the Caucasus on the eastern shore of the Black Sea.
Bordered by Russia, Turkey, Armenia and Azerbaijan, it is crossed by snow-capped Caucasus peaks and was once part of the Soviet Union.
Renowned for ancient hilltop churches and haunting polyphonic singing, it claims an 8,000-year wine-making tradition using buried clay vessels called qvevri.
Its capital, Tbilisi, tumbles down hillsides above a river gorge, dotted with sulphur bathhouses and a hilltop fortress.
It uses a unique curling alphabet found nowhere else, breeds the fierce Khachapuri cheese bread, and fought a brief 2008 war with Russia over breakaway regions.
This West African nation sits just north of the Equator, fronting the Gulf of Guinea between Ivory Coast and Togo.
Its landscapes shift from coastal lagoons to inland savanna, and it is one of the world's leading producers of cocoa and gold.
Colourful kente cloth and adinkra symbols mark its culture, and whitewashed coastal forts like Cape Coast Castle recall the transatlantic slave trade.
Its capital, Accra, hugs the coast, while the Ashanti kingdom around Kumasi reveres a sacred Golden Stool as a symbol of unity.
The first sub-Saharan colony to win independence, it raised a black star on its flag and produced UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan and statesman Kwame Nkrumah.
This Central American nation sits between two oceans, a tropical land studded with smoking volcanoes and dense highland cloud forests.
Bordered by Mexico to the north and Belize to the east, it features a Pacific coastline and rugged mountains where coffee thrives.
An ancient Maya civilization flourished here, raising towering stone pyramids and carving intricate hieroglyphic monuments deep in the jungle.
Near the colonial city of Antigua looms Volcan de Agua, while the vast ruins of Tikal rise above the northern rainforest canopy.
Famous for its colorful handwoven textiles and the beautiful Lake Atitlan, it is home to the largest Maya population in the region.
This West African nation faces the Atlantic Ocean, with a tropical climate and a misty interior plateau feeding several great rivers.
Bordered by Sierra Leone, Liberia, and Mali, it holds the highland source where the mighty Niger River first begins its journey.
Renowned for griot storytellers and the rippling melodies of the kora, it also possesses enormous reserves of bauxite ore.
Its coastal capital, Conakry, sits on a narrow peninsula, while inland the green Fouta Djallon highlands earn the title 'water tower of Africa'.
Once led by independence hero Sekou Toure, this former French colony was the first in its region to break free from colonial rule.
This small nation lies on the western coast of Africa, facing the Atlantic Ocean along a low-lying, swampy stretch of shoreline.
It is a small nation situated along the Atlantic coast, a region known for its mangroves and dense tropical vegetation.
The population relies heavily on cashew nut production and fishing, and traditional music plays a significant role in its culture.
Its coastal capital and the inland town of Bafata are its two principal cities, and the Bijagos Archipelago, a unique network of islands, lies within its borders.
Once a Portuguese colony, this nation shares strong cultural ties with its neighbors and belongs to the West African Economic and Monetary Union.
Tucked into the northeastern shoulder of South America, this nation faces the Atlantic with vast, sparsely populated rainforest interiors.
Bordered by Venezuela, Brazil, and Suriname, it is the only English-speaking country on the continent and a member of CARICOM.
Its towering Kaieteur Falls plunges far higher than Niagara, and recent offshore oil discoveries have transformed its tiny economy.
The coastal capital, Georgetown, with its colonial wooden architecture, sits below sea level behind protective sea walls and canals.
Once British colonial territory, its diverse population descends from African, Indian, and indigenous peoples, exporting bauxite, gold, and rum.
This Caribbean nation occupies the western third of a large mountainous island, surrounded by turquoise tropical seas.
Sharing its island, Hispaniola, with the Dominican Republic, it is the only French and Creole-speaking country in the region.
Enslaved people here staged history's only successful slave revolution, founding the first independent Black republic in the Americas.
Its capital, Port-au-Prince, devastated by a catastrophic 2010 earthquake, sits beneath rugged peaks once crowned by the Citadelle Laferriere fortress.
Vodou rituals, vibrant naive paintings, and compas music define a culture forged by African heritage and revolutionary defiance.
This Central American nation stretches between the Caribbean Sea and a short Pacific outlet, with mountainous interiors and tropical lowlands.
Bordered by Guatemala, El Salvador, and Nicaragua, it is famed for banana plantations that gave rise to the term 'banana republic'.
The ancient Maya carved the elaborate stone stelae of Copan here, while the Bay Islands offer world-class coral reef diving.
Its inland capital, Tegucigalpa, sits in a mountain valley, while the Caribbean port of La Ceiba serves as a gateway to the reefs.
Exporting coffee and bananas, this nation suffered devastating Hurricane Mitch in 1998 and shares the Gulf of Fonseca with neighbors.
This landlocked Central European nation lies within the Carpathian Basin, a fertile plain ringed by distant mountains and bisected by a great river.
Bordered by Austria, Slovakia, Romania, and Serbia, it speaks a unique Finno-Ugric language unrelated to its Slavic and Germanic neighbors.
Famed for thermal spa baths, paprika-laced goulash, and a 1956 uprising against Soviet domination that shook the Eastern Bloc.
The Danube divides its capital, where a vast neo-Gothic parliament building lines the river beside the Chain Bridge and Buda Castle.
Home to Lake Balaton, the largest in Central Europe, this nation traces its founding to the Magyar tribes of King Stephen.
This Nordic island sits in the North Atlantic just below the Arctic Circle, where fire and ice collide in dramatic fashion.
Straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, it bristles with active volcanoes, vast glaciers, geysers, and steaming geothermal fields.
Settled by Norse Vikings, its people preserved medieval sagas and founded one of the world's oldest parliaments at Thingvellir.
Its capital, Reykjavik, claims to be the world's northernmost, near the milky-blue waters of the famed Blue Lagoon spa.
Powered almost entirely by renewable geothermal and hydro energy, this volcanic land lures travelers chasing the dancing aurora borealis.
This sprawling Southeast Asian nation straddles the equator across the world's largest archipelago, packed with active volcanoes and coral seas.
Comprising over seventeen thousand islands, it holds the planet's largest Muslim population and a dizzying array of languages and cultures.
The eruption of Krakatoa shook the world, and its rainforests shelter orangutans, Komodo dragons, and the towering Borobudur Buddhist temple.
Its crowded capital, Jakarta, sits on Java, while the islands of Bali and Sumatra draw surfers, divers, and temple pilgrims.
Famed for nutmeg and clove 'Spice Islands' and shadow-puppet theater, this nation spreads across more than five thousand kilometers of ocean.
This large Western Asian nation spans high deserts and mountain ranges between the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf.
Bordered by Turkey, Iraq, Afghanistan, and Pakistan, it forms the modern heart of the ancient Persian world.
The mighty empire of Cyrus and Darius rose here, leaving the carved ceremonial palaces of Persepolis among its desert plains.
Its sprawling capital, Tehran, sits beneath the snowy Alborz peaks, while Isfahan dazzles with turquoise-tiled mosques and grand bridges.
A 1979 revolution established a Shia Islamic republic here, a nation famed for saffron, pistachios, and intricate hand-knotted carpets.
This Middle Eastern nation occupies a hot, arid land between two great rivers flowing toward the Persian Gulf.
Bordered by Iran, Turkey, Syria, and Kuwait, it sits atop the fertile floodplain historians call Mesopotamia, cradle of civilization.
The ancient Sumerians invented writing here and built the world's earliest cities, leaving stepped ziggurats rising from the plains.
Its capital, on the Tigris River, once shone as the Abbasid Caliphate's center of learning, near the legendary ruins of Babylon.
Holding the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala, this oil-rich nation endured wars and the long rule of Saddam Hussein.
This island nation lies off Europe's northwestern edge, a famously green land of rolling pastures, bogs, and rugged Atlantic cliffs.
Sharing its island with British-governed Ulster to the north, it gained independence in the twentieth century and joined the European Union.
Celtic heritage runs deep, from prehistoric Newgrange tombs to a Gaelic language, lively fiddle music, and a worldwide pub culture.
Its capital, Dublin, birthplace of Joyce and Wilde, sits on the Liffey, while the Cliffs of Moher dominate the western seaboard.
Symbolized by the shamrock and harp, this land of leprechaun lore celebrates a globally famous March feast of Saint Patrick.
This small Western Asian nation stretches along the eastern Mediterranean, reaching south to a narrow outlet on the Red Sea.
Bordered by Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, and Egypt, it is the world's only Jewish-majority state, founded in 1948.
Ancient sacred sites coexist with a booming high-tech economy that has earned this innovative land the nickname 'Start-Up Nation'.
Its coastal hub Tel Aviv buzzes with modernity, while the contested holy city of Jerusalem holds the Western Wall and Old City.
Bathers float effortlessly in the salty Dead Sea, the lowest point on Earth, near the desert fortress of Masada.
This West African nation faces the Gulf of Guinea, a tropical land of lagoons, rainforests, and savanna stretching inland.
Bordered by Liberia, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Ghana, it ranks as the world's leading producer of cocoa beans.
A former French colony, it built the world's largest church, a vast basilica modeled on Rome's Saint Peter's.
Its bustling port city of Abidjan drives the economy, while the inland town of Yamoussoukro serves as the official capital.
Named for a historic trade in elephant tusks, this French-speaking nation boasts a celebrated football team called the Elephants.
This Caribbean island nation lies in the tropics south of Cuba, with white beaches and a lush, mountainous interior.
An English-speaking former British colony, its Blue Mountains produce some of the world's most prized and expensive coffee.
The birthplace of reggae and Rastafarian culture, it gave the world Bob Marley and a globally beloved laid-back rhythm.
Its capital, Kingston, anchors the southern coast, while sprinters like Usain Bolt have made its black, green, and gold flag famous.
Nicknamed 'the land of wood and water', this island spawned jerk cooking and an unlikely Olympic bobsled team.
This relatively small country is located in western Asia, occupying an arid corner of the region where several historic cultures have long overlapped.
It is a relatively small nation situated in the Middle East, with very limited access to the sea through a single short southern gulf.
Ancient ruins and desert landscapes define much of its terrain, and hospitality is a deeply valued cultural trait.
The country shares borders with Israel, Syria, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia, and boasts a significant portion of the Dead Sea coastline.
Its capital city is known for its Roman amphitheater and its proximity to the rose-red biblical city of Petra.
This enormous Central Asian nation, the world's largest landlocked country, rolls across vast steppes, deserts, and distant mountains.
Bordering Russia, China, and three smaller -stan neighbors, it touches the Caspian Sea and sprawls over an area larger than Western Europe.
A former Soviet republic with deep nomadic and equestrian roots, it celebrates yurt dwellings, eagle hunting, and horseback traditions.
From the Baikonur Cosmodrome on its steppe, the first human, Yuri Gagarin, rocketed into orbit, launching the space age.
Its futuristic capital, Astana, rose from the plains with bold architecture, while oil and minerals fuel its booming economy.
This East African nation straddles the equator, sweeping from Indian Ocean beaches up through the Great Rift Valley to highland plateaus.
Bordered by Tanzania, Uganda, Ethiopia, and Somalia, it is celebrated for world-beating long-distance runners and tea exports.
The Maasai Mara teems with lions and elephants, hosting the spectacular annual wildebeest migration across its golden savanna.
Its capital, Nairobi, anchors the highlands, while the snowcapped peak that lends the country its name rises as Africa's second highest.
Coastal Mombasa carries Swahili and Arab heritage, while red-robed Maasai warriors symbolize this nation's vibrant safari culture.
This small, scorching nation sits at the head of the Persian Gulf, a flat desert land with searing summer temperatures.
Wedged between Iraq and Saudi Arabia, this oil-rich emirate is ruled by an emir and holds vast petroleum reserves.
Iraq's 1990 invasion triggered the Gulf War, after which retreating forces set hundreds of its oil wells ablaze.
Its capital city's waterfront features iconic blue-and-green spherical Towers overlooking the Gulf, a symbol of the nation's wealth.
Once a pearl-diving and dhow-trading port, this 'Land of Black Gold' gained independence from Britain in 1961.
This landlocked Central Asian nation is almost entirely mountainous, a high-altitude land of alpine meadows, glaciers, and snowy peaks.
Bordered by Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and China, this former Soviet republic sits along the ancient Silk Road trade routes.
Nomadic herders still raise horses and yurts here, preserving epic oral poetry and the ancient art of hunting with golden eagles.
The vast Issyk-Kul, one of the world's largest mountain lakes, never freezes despite the towering Tian Shan range around it.
Its capital, Bishkek, lies beneath snowy summits, in a republic famed for traditional games of horseback wrestling and goat-carcass polo.
This landlocked Southeast Asian nation is rugged and mountainous, blanketed in tropical forest and threaded by a mighty river.
Bordered by Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, and China, it is a one-party communist state and the region's most sparsely populated country.
Saffron-robed Buddhist monks fill ancient temples, and the mysterious Plain of Jars scatters giant stone vessels across a highland plateau.
The Mekong River runs along its border past the gilded temples of UNESCO-listed Luang Prabang and the capital, Vientiane.
Nicknamed the 'Land of a Million Elephants', this nation was the most heavily bombed country per capita in history.
This small northern European nation lines the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea, a flat land of dense forests and sandy beaches.
Sandwiched between Estonia and Lithuania, this Baltic state regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991 and joined the EU.
Long prized for amber washed up on its coast, it boasts Europe's finest concentration of ornate Art Nouveau architecture.
Its capital, Riga, a UNESCO-listed old town on the Daugava River, anchors a culture famed for vast singing festivals.
Citizens celebrate the Midsummer Jani festival with bonfires and oak-leaf crowns, under a flag of dark red bands framing white.
This small Middle Eastern nation hugs the eastern Mediterranean coast, where snowy mountains rise dramatically just behind the beaches.
Bordered only by Syria and Israel, it has a uniquely diverse society split among Christian, Sunni, Shia, and Druze communities.
The seafaring Phoenicians launched their alphabet from ancient ports here, and a famous cedar tree adorns the national flag.
Its coastal capital, Beirut, once dubbed 'Paris of the East', endured a long civil war and a devastating 2020 port explosion.
Famed for hummus, tabbouleh, and mezze, this banking hub earned the nickname 'Switzerland of the Middle East'.
This tiny southern African nation is a mountainous highland kingdom, the only country entirely above one thousand meters in elevation.
Completely encircled by South Africa, it is one of only three independent states surrounded by a single other country.
Its Sesotho-speaking people are renowned for distinctive woven blankets, conical straw hats, and skilled mountain pony riders.
Snow dusts its Drakensberg peaks in winter, and its highlands gather rainfall channeled by dams toward the Orange River.
Ruled by a king and known as the 'Kingdom in the Sky', it sells water and hydroelectric power to its giant neighbor.
This West African nation faces the Atlantic Ocean, a small tropical land of rainforests, rubber plantations, and humid coastal lowlands.
Bordered by Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Ivory Coast, it was founded in the 1800s as a homeland for freed American slaves.
Its flag echoes the stars and stripes, and English is the official language, reflecting deep ties to the United States.
Its Atlantic capital, Monrovia, was named for a US president, sitting near the Mesurado River along the rainforest coast.
Africa's oldest republic endured brutal civil wars before electing the continent's first female head of state, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.
This vast North African territory stretches from a Mediterranean shoreline deep into the burning sands of the Sahara, where rain rarely falls.
Sandwiched between Egypt to the east and Algeria to the west, this nation holds some of the continent's largest proven petroleum reserves.
Berber, Arab, and Ottoman influences blend in its culture, while Roman engineers once built thriving coastal cities across this desert land.
Its largest city and port, Tripoli, anchors a narrow inhabited strip, and the spectacular ruins of Leptis Magna draw archaeologists worldwide.
Once ruled for decades by a flamboyant colonel before a 2011 uprising, this oil-rich state remains one of Africa's most sparsely populated by area.
Tucked into the heart of the Alps in Central Europe, this is one of the smallest sovereign states on the entire continent.
A doubly landlocked microstate, it sits wedged between Switzerland and Austria along the upper reaches of the Rhine River.
Ruled as a principality by a hereditary prince, it values traditional craftsmanship in textiles and ceramics despite its highly industrialized economy.
Its tiny capital, Vaduz, is overlooked by a hilltop castle that remains the royal family's private residence above the valley.
Famous for favorable tax laws and false-teeth manufacturing, this dwarf nation has no army and shares no border with any sea.
This northern European nation faces the Baltic Sea, where golden amber washes ashore and pine forests meet sandy coastal dunes.
The southernmost of three Baltic republics, it borders Poland and Belarus and once formed a vast medieval grand duchy.
Amber jewelry and intricate wooden carvings define its heritage, and a strange hilltop covered in thousands of crosses draws pilgrims.
Its capital, Vilnius, boasts a UNESCO-listed Old Town of baroque churches and a self-declared bohemian artists' republic called Uzupis.
The first Soviet republic to break free, declaring independence in 1990, it claims a monument marking the geographic center of Europe.
This small landlocked country sits in Western Europe, wedged among three larger neighbors amid forested hills and deep river valleys.
Bordering France, Belgium, and Germany, it produces fine Moselle wines and blends French and German cultural traditions effortlessly.
A grand duchy ruled by a hereditary grand duke, it grew rich from steel and now thrives as a global banking hub.
Its fortified capital, a UNESCO World Heritage site perched on dramatic cliffs, hosts several institutions of the European Union.
A founding member of the EU with one of the world's highest GDPs per capita, its citizens commonly speak three official languages.
This landlocked Balkan nation in southeastern Europe is crisscrossed by rugged mountains and ancient trade routes between empires.
Bordering Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia, Kosovo, and Albania, it changed its official name in 2019 to resolve a long dispute with a southern neighbor.
Orthodox monasteries and ancient ruins dot its hills, reflecting layered Slavic, Greek, and Ottoman influences across many centuries.
Lake Ohrid, among Europe's oldest and deepest, lies on its border, while its capital Skopje sprawls beneath a hilltop fortress.
Birthplace of Mother Teresa and once part of Yugoslavia, this republic declared independence in 1991 with a sun-emblazoned flag.
This enormous island nation floats in the Indian Ocean off Africa's southeastern coast, separated from the mainland by a wide channel.
The world's fourth-largest island, it broke from other landmasses millions of years ago, evolving in striking biological isolation.
Lemurs leap through its forests and towering baobab trees line famous avenues, found nowhere else on the planet in such variety.
Its highland capital, Antananarivo, rises across hills once ruled by the powerful Merina kingdom that unified the island.
Dubbed the 'Eighth Continent' for its endemic wildlife, it inspired a hit animated film franchise and grows much of the world's vanilla.
This landlocked nation in southeastern Africa is dominated by an enormous freshwater lake stretching along its entire eastern edge.
Bordered by Zambia, Mozambique, and Tanzania, it earned a reputation for friendliness, often called the 'Warm Heart of Africa'.
Its great rift lake teems with hundreds of colorful cichlid fish species, while vibrant music and dance animate village life.
The capital, Lilongwe, lies inland, and a Scottish missionary explorer named the lake here during his nineteenth-century journeys.
Once a British protectorate called Nyasaland, this Christian-majority republic depends heavily on tobacco, tea, and lakeside fishing.
This Southeast Asian nation is split into two main land regions divided by a sea, blending tropical rainforests with bustling modern cities.
One half shares a peninsula with Thailand and Singapore, while the other occupies part of the island of Borneo alongside Indonesia and Brunei.
Twin steel-and-glass towers soar above its capital, once the tallest buildings on Earth, symbolizing rapid economic transformation.
Kuala Lumpur anchors a constitutional monarchy whose Malay, Chinese, and Indian communities celebrate Hari Raya and Deepavali together.
A leading palm-oil exporter and home to wild orangutans, it rotates its king among nine traditional sultans every five years.
This South Asian nation scatters across the Indian Ocean as hundreds of tiny coral islands grouped into ring-shaped atolls.
Lying southwest of India and Sri Lanka, its people have long depended on the sea for fishing and tuna exports.
Overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and vibrant reefs make it a dream honeymoon destination for divers and luxury travelers.
Its dense capital island, Male, packs a national population into one of the most crowded cities anywhere on the globe.
With its highest natural point only a couple of meters above the waves, it is the planet's lowest-lying and flattest country.
This large landlocked nation in West Africa spans expansive savanna in the south and vast Saharan dunes across its arid north.
The mighty Niger River curves through its territory, sustaining farming and famed mud-brick cities along its banks.
Renowned for griot storytellers and the kora harp, it nurtured a desert music tradition celebrated at festivals worldwide.
Its capital Bamako thrives while the legendary trading city of Timbuktu once stood as a great center of Islamic scholarship.
Its name honors a powerful medieval empire whose ruler, Mansa Musa, is often called the richest person in history.
This tiny island nation sits in the central Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily, blessed with sunshine and turquoise diving waters.
An archipelago of just a few inhabited islands, it ranks among the smallest and most densely populated members of the European Union.
Megalithic temples older than the pyramids stand here, and a famous warrior order of knights once defended it against Ottoman siege.
Its fortified capital, Valletta, a UNESCO World Heritage site, guards a strategic deep-water harbor coveted by past naval empires.
Its distinctive eight-pointed cross became a worldwide symbol, and English shares official status with a unique Semitic-rooted language.
This vast West African nation faces the Atlantic Ocean yet lies mostly beneath the endless sand seas of the western Sahara.
Bordering Western Sahara, Algeria, Mali, and Senegal, it bridges the Arab Maghreb and Black Africa across shifting dunes.
Berber and Arab traditions shape its culture, while caravans once crossed its sands along ancient trans-Saharan trade routes.
Its coastal capital, Nouakchott, anchors an economy built on rich iron-ore deposits hauled by one of the world's longest trains.
Home to the bird-rich Banc d'Arguin park and the eye-shaped Richat structure, it was among the last countries to abolish slavery.
This volcanic island nation lies in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, ringed by coral reefs and powdery white beaches.
Politically grouped with Africa, it blends Creole, Indian, Chinese, and European cultures into one remarkably diverse society.
Rugged green peaks rise above sugarcane fields, and the Black River Gorges park shelters rare birds across the island's interior.
Its bustling capital, Port Louis, preserves French and British colonial architecture around a busy historic harbor.
Once the only home of the flightless dodo, now extinct, this prosperous island exports sugar and vanilla while drawing reef divers.
This small landlocked nation in Eastern Europe sits among rolling hills and fertile farmland between two larger neighbors.
Wedged between Romania and Ukraine, it shares a language and history with the former and a breakaway region called Transnistria.
Vineyards blanket its countryside, and lively folk dances accompany a culture deeply tied to centuries of winemaking tradition.
Its capital, Chisinau, mixes Soviet-era and medieval architecture, while nearby cellars stretch for kilometers beneath the ground.
Boasting Cricova and Milestii Mici, among the world's largest underground wine collections, it ranks among Europe's least-visited states.
This glittering microstate clings to the Mediterranean coast of the French Riviera, packed onto an impossibly small sliver of land.
Sharing its only land border with France near the Italian frontier, it ranks as the second-smallest sovereign country on Earth.
A principality ruled by the Grimaldi dynasty, it lures the wealthy with glamorous casinos, yacht-filled harbors, and zero income tax.
Its Monte Carlo district hosts a legendary Formula One street race and an opulent belle-epoque casino overlooking the sea.
Once home to Hollywood star turned princess Grace Kelly, this sovereign city-state has the densest population of any nation.
This vast landlocked nation in Central and East Asia rolls across endless grassy steppes, rugged mountains, and arid plateaus.
Sandwiched between Russia and China, it ranks as the most sparsely populated sovereign country in the entire world.
Nomadic herders still roam its plains on horseback, raising livestock and living in portable round felt tents called gers.
Its capital, Ulaanbaatar, sits near vast cold steppe, while the Gobi Desert sprawls across the country's southern reaches.
Birthplace of the conqueror who built history's largest contiguous empire, it celebrates wrestling, archery, and horse racing at Naadam.
This small Balkan nation in southeastern Europe drops dramatically from rugged peaks straight down to the sparkling Adriatic Sea.
Bordering Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, Kosovo, and Albania, its name translates roughly to 'black mountain' from a Venetian phrase.
A deep, fjord-like bay shelters medieval walled towns whose history weaves through Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian rule.
Its capital, Podgorica, sits inland, while the UNESCO-listed Bay of Kotor draws visitors to its cliffside fortifications.
Sometimes called the 'Pearl of the Adriatic,' it adopted the euro despite not joining the EU and split from Serbia in 2006.
This North African kingdom boasts both Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines and sits just across a narrow strait from Europe.
The snowcapped Atlas Mountains slice through its interior, separating fertile plains from the vast dunes of the Sahara beyond.
Bustling souks, intricate tilework, and Berber music fill its ancient walled medinas, blending Arab and African traditions.
Its imperial cities include Marrakech with its famous square, Fez, and the white port of Casablanca, while Rabat serves as capital.
Famous for producing argan oil and mint tea, this constitutional monarchy hosted a Hollywood classic that shares Casablanca's name.
This long coastal nation in southeastern Africa stretches along the Indian Ocean, facing the island of Madagascar across a wide channel.
Bordered by Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa, and Eswatini, it boasts palm-fringed beaches and coral-rich archipelagos.
Its people speak many Bantu languages alongside Portuguese, and lively music and dance traditions thrive in coastal communities.
Its capital, Maputo, anchors the south, while the offshore Bazaruto archipelago dazzles divers with pristine marine life.
The only nation whose flag features an assault rifle, it won independence from Portugal in 1975 after a long liberation struggle.
This Southeast Asian nation curves along the Bay of Bengal, bordered by India, Bangladesh, China, Laos, and Thailand.
Once known by a colonial name beginning with B, it stretches from snowy northern peaks to a long tropical coastline.
Thousands of ancient temples crowd the plains of Bagan, and shimmering gold pagodas dominate its devoutly Buddhist landscape.
The Irrawaddy River threads through its heart, while the towering Shwedagon Pagoda crowns its largest city, Yangon.
Famous for saffron-robed monks and a Nobel-winning democracy icon, it endured long military rule and a 2021 army coup.
This sparsely populated nation in southwestern Africa fronts the Atlantic Ocean, dominated by ancient deserts and dramatic dunes.
Bordering South Africa, Angola, Botswana, and Zambia, its fog-shrouded shore earned the eerie name 'Skeleton Coast'.
Towering rust-red dunes ripple inland, while desert-adapted elephants and black rhinos survive in its harsh, arid wilderness.
Its capital, Windhoek, retains German colonial architecture, and the salt pan of Etosha draws wildlife to its shimmering edges.
Home to what may be the world's oldest desert, it won independence from South African rule in 1990 and pioneered communal conservancies.
This landlocked South Asian nation climbs from steamy lowland plains into the towering snowbound peaks of the Himalayas.
Wedged between India and Tibetan China, it claims eight of the world's ten highest mountains within its rugged borders.
Fluttering prayer flags, hillside monasteries, and intricate temples reflect deep Hindu and Buddhist roots intertwined over centuries.
Its capital, Kathmandu, fills a temple-rich valley, and Sherpa guides lead climbers toward the base camp of Earth's tallest summit.
Birthplace of the Buddha at Lumbini, it flies the only national flag that is not a rectangle but two stacked triangles.
This Central American nation lies between two oceans, dotted with smoking volcanoes and steaming tropical lowlands.
Bordering Honduras and Costa Rica, it ranks as the largest country on its isthmus, with both Pacific and Caribbean coasts.
Marimba melodies and colonial churches enliven cities like Granada and Leon, where Spanish-era architecture lines cobbled streets.
Its capital, Managua, sits beside a lake, while a vast freshwater body nearby holds rare sharks and twin-volcano Ometepe island.
Famous for surf breaks and a long-debated interoceanic canal scheme, it endured a Sandinista revolution that toppled the Somoza dynasty.
This large nation is located on the African continent, with most of its vast interior lying within the southern reaches of the Sahara.
It is a large, landlocked nation situated in the western part of the continent, much of it covered by the Sahara Desert.
Traditional music and dance are integral to the culture, often featuring vibrant costumes and rhythmic drumming.
