A major West African river flows through this nation, providing a vital source of water and supporting agriculture in its fertile regions, and Niamey is its largest city.
This country faces significant challenges related to desertification and food security, but its people maintain a rich cultural heritage and resilience.
This populous West African nation spans rainforests, savannas, and a great river delta opening onto the Gulf of Guinea.
The most populous country on the continent, it borders Benin, Niger, Chad, and Cameroon, with hundreds of distinct ethnic groups.
Its booming Afrobeats music and prolific Nollywood film industry export culture across the world from a vibrant creative scene.
The sprawling coastal megacity of Lagos drives its economy, while the planned city of Abuja serves as the inland capital.
Home to the ancient Nok terracotta culture and a major oil-producing delta, it gained independence from Britain in 1960.
This East Asian nation occupies the upper half of a mountainous peninsula and is among the most isolated and secretive states on the planet.
Ruled by a single dynastic family across three generations, it follows a state ideology of self-reliance and maintains a vast standing military.
Its heavily fortified southern frontier, a buffer strip dividing two rival states, is among the most tense borders anywhere on Earth.
The capital, Pyongyang, features the towering Juche Tower and mass gymnastic spectacles, while the city of Kaesong preserves ancient royal heritage.
Its leaders have built a nuclear arsenal, run on a calendar starting from a founder's birth, and enforce a rigid social ranking called songbun.
This Middle Eastern nation sits on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, fronting both the Arabian Sea and a strategic gulf.
Long ruled by a sultanate, it built a maritime empire that once stretched to the East African coast and the island of Zanzibar.
Famed for trade in aromatic frankincense, it preserves mud-brick forts, terraced mountain villages, and dramatic flooded canyons called wadis.
Its capital, Muscat, hugs rugged coastal mountains, while the Jebel Akhdar range and the vast Empty Quarter dominate the interior.
It guards the Strait of Hormuz, follows the distinctive Ibadi branch of Islam, and is the only Arab state never colonized by a European power.
This South Asian nation stretches from the Arabian Sea coastline up to some of the highest mountains found anywhere on the continent.
Carved out as a Muslim homeland during a 1947 partition, it borders India to the east and Afghanistan and Iran to the west.
Its territory cradles the ancient Indus Valley civilization, vibrant truck art, Mughal-era gardens, and the soaring peaks of the Karakoram range.
Major hubs include the coastal megacity of Karachi and historic Lahore, while a famed highway threads through the mountains toward China.
It is home to K2, the second-highest peak on Earth, the Faisal Mosque, and was the birthplace of activist Malala Yousafzai.
This narrow Central American country forms the slender land bridge connecting two continents while separating two great oceans.
Once part of Colombia, it gained independence in 1903 with backing tied to a massive engineering project on its isthmus.
Lush rainforests, the roadless Darien Gap, and a famed waterway define a land blending Indigenous, African, and Spanish heritage.
Its skyline-filled capital shares a name with the country, and a celebrated canal lets ships cross from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The only nation bordering both Colombia and Costa Rica, it uses the U.S. dollar locally and lent its name to a famous brimmed hat.
This Oceanian nation occupies the eastern half of the world's second-largest island, deep in the southwestern Pacific.
It shares its main island with Indonesia and lies just north of Australia, from which it gained independence in 1975.
Boasting extraordinary biodiversity and over 800 languages, its highland tribes wear elaborate feathered headdresses at colorful sing-sing gatherings.
The capital, Port Moresby, sits on the southern coast, while rugged interior ranges and volcanic outer islands fill the rest of the territory.
Home to dazzling birds-of-paradise and the wartime Kokoda Track, it is one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth.
This landlocked South American nation sits at the continent's heart, split by a major river into wetlands and the dry Chaco plains.
Wedged between Argentina, Brazil, and Bolivia, it endured a devastating 19th-century war that wiped out much of its male population.
Indigenous Guarani is widely spoken alongside Spanish, and locals constantly sip a bitter herbal tea called yerba mate from gourds.
Its capital, Asuncion, sits on a riverbank, while the eastern city of Ciudad del Este borders a massive shared hydroelectric dam.
The only doubly landlocked country in the Americas, it co-owns the Itaipu Dam, once the world's largest power station by output.
This western South American nation stretches from a Pacific desert coast over towering Andean peaks into dense Amazon jungle.
Heart of a vast pre-Columbian empire conquered by Spain in the 1530s, it later became a key colonial viceroyalty.
Ancient stone citadels, the mysterious desert geoglyphs near Nazca, and floating reed islands on Lake Titicaca dot its landscapes.
Its coastal capital, Lima, is a culinary capital, while the highland city of Cusco served as the old imperial heart.
Home to the cloud-wrapped citadel of Machu Picchu and the lost city of the Incas, it remains famed for ceviche and llamas.
This Southeast Asian nation is a sprawling archipelago of over 7,000 islands scattered across the western Pacific Ocean.
Named after a Spanish king, it spent centuries under Madrid before passing to American rule, leaving it predominantly Catholic.
It sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire with active volcanoes, terraced rice fields, and famed diving sites among coral reefs.
Its dense capital, Manila, anchors the main island of Luzon, while Cebu and Boracay draw visitors with beaches and festivals.
Birthplace of the jeepney and lechon, it endures frequent typhoons and is the only Asian nation colonized by both Spain and America.
This small Western Asian nation juts northward as a thumb-shaped peninsula into the warm waters of the Persian Gulf.
Once reliant on pearl diving, this absolute monarchy grew immensely wealthy after discovering enormous offshore gas fields.
It funds a globally influential news network, owns prestigious foreign sports clubs, and has built futuristic museums in the desert.
Its glittering capital, Doha, bristles with skyscrapers along a crescent bay, while the town of Al Khor sits up the coast.
Holding the world's third-largest natural gas reserves, it hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the first ever held in the Arab world.
This nation is located in the central part of Africa, with most of its land lying within the dense rainforest belt near the equator.
It is a significant nation situated primarily within the equatorial rainforest region, with a narrow window opening onto the Atlantic Ocean.
Known for its vast rainforests, rich biodiversity, and significant oil reserves, this country has a complex history of colonial influence.
Brazzaville is its capital, sitting across a great river from a much larger neighbor of nearly identical name, and the nation borders Cameroon and Angola.
Often distinguished from its larger eastern neighbor by its capital city, this nation maintains a coastline on the Atlantic Ocean and a major equatorial river.
This Eastern European nation borders the Black Sea, with an arc of forested mountains curling through its interior.
Its Romance language descends from Latin amid Slavic neighbors, a legacy of ancient Roman conquest of old Dacia.
Painted monasteries, medieval Saxon towns, and hilltop fortresses in Transylvania reflect a turbulent history of empires and overthrown communism.
The capital, Bucharest, holds the colossal Palace of Parliament, while the Carpathian peaks shelter the famed Bran Castle.
Folklore tied to Vlad the Impaler inspired the Dracula legend, and the Danube spills into a vast biodiverse delta here.
This is the largest nation on Earth by land area, sprawling across eleven time zones from Europe deep into northern Asia.
Once an empire of tsars, it became the core of the Soviet Union before that union dissolved at the end of 1991.
Onion-domed cathedrals, ballet, and literary giants like Tolstoy mark a culture shaped by vast plains, taiga forests, and bitter winters.
Its capital centers on the Kremlin and Red Square, while a former imperial capital on the Neva holds the Hermitage museum.
Containing frozen Siberian tundra and deep Lake Baikal, it remains a nuclear superpower and one of the world's top energy exporters.
This small East African nation, nicknamed the land of a thousand hills, sits on rolling highlands near the Great Rift Valley.
Landlocked and densely populated, it borders Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the much larger Congo to its west.
It is remembered worldwide for a horrific 1994 genocide, after which it rebuilt into one of the continent's cleanest, fastest-growing states.
Its tidy capital, Kigali, sits on green hills, while volcanic peaks in the north shelter endangered mountain gorillas.
Famous for gorilla trekking and a monthly community cleanup called umuganda, it banned plastic bags and elected a majority-female parliament.
This tiny European microstate is completely surrounded by a single neighbor, perched in the hills near the Adriatic coast.
Entirely enclosed by Italy, it lies just inland from the resort city of Rimini in the Apennine foothills.
Claiming founding by a stonemason in 301 AD, it boasts of being one of the world's oldest surviving republics.
Its hilltop capital crowns the slopes of Monte Titano, guarded by three medieval towers visible for miles around.
Among the smallest sovereign states anywhere, it is led by two captains regent and issues prized collectible coins and stamps.
This Middle Eastern giant covers most of the Arabian Peninsula, dominated by scorching deserts including the vast Empty Quarter.
An absolute monarchy ruled by a single royal family, it holds some of the planet's largest proven petroleum reserves.
It contains Islam's two holiest cities, drawing millions of pilgrims yearly, and is launching a futuristic linear megacity called The Line.
Its capital, Riyadh, anchors the desert interior, while Jeddah on the Red Sea serves as the gateway toward Mecca and Medina.
Birthplace of Islam and home to the Kaaba, this oil kingdom drives the OPEC cartel and only let women drive starting in 2018.
This nation lies on the western edge of Africa, where dry savanna gives way to a long Atlantic coastline dotted with fishing communities.
It is a significant nation situated primarily within the semi-arid Sahel region, marking the westernmost point of the entire African mainland.
Known for its vibrant music, bustling markets, and stunning coastal dunes, this country boasts a rich history of trade and resistance.
The capital city of Dakar is a major port and cultural center, and the country is famous for its 'teranga' - a spirit of hospitality.
This westernmost mainland African nation almost completely surrounds the tiny country of Gambia, and its resilient people are known for strong democratic traditions.
This landlocked Southeastern European nation lies in the Balkans, where central plains rise toward rugged southern mountains.
Once the largest republic of the former Yugoslavia, this Orthodox, Slavic land uses the Cyrillic alphabet.
Brass-band festivals, plum brandy called rakija, and a turbulent 20th-century history mark a people fiercely proud of their roots.
Its capital, Belgrade, sits where the Sava meets the Danube beneath an ancient hilltop fortress, while Novi Sad hosts a famed music festival.
Birthplace of inventor Nikola Tesla's ancestry and tennis champion Novak Djokovic, it produces most of the world's raspberries by export.
This tiny island nation scatters across the western Indian Ocean, lying northeast of Madagascar and far off the East African coast.
A former British colony, this archipelago of 115 islands speaks a French-based Creole alongside English and French.
Its inner islands are unusual granite outcrops fringed by sculpted boulders, palm-shaded beaches, and rare giant tortoises.
Its capital, Victoria, is among the world's smallest, while Praslin and La Digue shelter the rare double coconut, the coco de mer.
Among the planet's least populous sovereign states, it protects nearly half its land as nature reserves and ranks high in African wealth per capita.
This West African nation fronts the Atlantic with tropical beaches and forested hills rising behind its coastline.
Its name, given by Portuguese sailors, means 'lion mountains,' and it later became a British colony for freed slaves.
It endured a brutal civil war fueled by so-called blood diamonds and a devastating Ebola outbreak in the 2010s.
Its capital, Freetown, sits on a hilly peninsula founded as a haven for liberated Africans returning across the ocean.
Home to one of the world's largest natural harbors and rich diamond fields, it speaks the Krio creole as a lingua franca.
This tiny Southeast Asian island state sits at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, just north of the equator.
Expelled from Malaysia in 1965, this multicultural city-state blends Chinese, Malay, Indian, and Tamil communities under four official languages.
Renowned for strict laws, spotless streets, and gleaming towers, it transformed from a colonial trading port into a global finance hub.
A waterfront crowned by a boat-topped resort and supertree gardens defines its skyline beside one of the world's busiest container ports.
Famous for its banned chewing gum, the Merlion statue, and Changi Airport, it commands the strait bearing its own name.
This landlocked Central European nation lies along the Carpathian arc, with the High Tatra peaks crowning its north.
It peacefully split from its western neighbor in 1993, parting ways with what is now the Czech Republic.
Hundreds of medieval castles, wooden churches, and folk traditions dot a country shaped by Hungarian and Austro-Hungarian rule.
Its riverside capital, Bratislava, sits at a meeting point of three countries, while Kosice anchors the east.
Home to the sprawling Spis Castle ruins and ice caves, it adopted the euro and borders Austria, Poland, Hungary, and Ukraine.
This small Central European nation nestles between the Alps and a short stretch of Adriatic coastline.
The first republic to break from the former Yugoslavia in 1991, it borders Italy, Austria, Hungary, and Croatia.
More than half-covered in forest, it boasts emerald rivers, vast limestone caves, and a green, postcard-perfect reputation.
Its compact capital, Ljubljana, is famed for dragon bridges, while an island church floats on a glacial lake near Bled.
Home to the spectacular Postojna Cave and the original Lipizzaner stud farm, it adopted the euro and joined the European Union in 2004.
This nation forms the tip of the Horn of Africa, boasting the continent's longest mainland coastline along the Indian Ocean.
Bordering Ethiopia, Kenya, and Djibouti, it descended into prolonged civil war and statelessness after its government collapsed in 1991.
A largely nomadic, camel-herding people share one language and faith, sustaining a rich tradition of oral poetry and storytelling.
Its seaside capital, Mogadishu, faces the ocean, while the northern city of Hargeisa anchors a breakaway region.
Notorious for offshore piracy off its waters, it includes the self-declared independent territory of Somaliland in its north.
This teardrop-shaped island nation lies in the Indian Ocean just off the southern tip of the Indian subcontinent.
Formerly called Ceylon, it endured Portuguese, Dutch, and British rule before independence and a long civil war.
Ancient Buddhist temples, hilltop fortresses, and misty highland estates produce some of the world's most prized tea.
Its commercial hub, Colombo, sits on the west coast, while the sacred city of Kandy holds a revered tooth relic of the Buddha.
Dubbed the Pearl of the Indian Ocean, it is famed for cinnamon, leopard safaris, and elephants bathing at Pinnawala.
This large Northeast African nation spans desert and savanna where two great branches of the Nile converge.
Once Africa's biggest country by area, it split in 2011 when its oil-rich southern region broke away to form a new state.
Ancient Nubian kingdoms left behind more steep-sided pyramids here than exist in all of Egypt to the north.
Its capital, Khartoum, sits where the Blue and White Niles meet, with Omdurman sprawling just across the water.
Home to the royal pyramids of Meroe and devastated by recent civil war, it borders the Red Sea and seven other African nations.
This compact nation sits on the northeastern shoulder of South America, its coastline facing the Atlantic and its interior swallowed by jungle.
It lies between Guyana and French Guiana, a tiny republic whose dense rainforest covers most of its land and shelters remarkable wildlife.
Uniquely for the continent, Dutch remains the official tongue here, a legacy of colonial rule that also shaped its riverside trading settlements.
Its capital, Paramaribo, sits on a major river and is famed for whitewashed wooden colonial buildings recognized as a World Heritage treasure.
Descendants of Javanese, Hindustani, Maroon, and Indigenous communities share this land, the smallest sovereign state on the South American mainland.
This western Asian nation occupies a crossroads of the ancient world, with a short Mediterranean coastline and a vast arid interior.
Bordering Lebanon, Turkey, Iraq, Jordan, and Israel, it sits at the heart of the Levant and the historic Fertile Crescent.
Crusader castles, Roman colonnades at Palmyra, and one of humanity's longest continuously inhabited regions mark its layered, war-scarred history.
Its capital claims to be among the world's oldest cities, home to the great Umayyad Mosque and a labyrinthine covered souk.
Devastated by years of civil war since 2011, this Arab republic flies a flag of red, white, and black bearing two green stars.
This East Asian island lies across a narrow strait from the Chinese mainland, with rugged mountains running down its eastern spine.
A self-governing democracy claimed by Beijing, it is famed for bustling night markets, hot springs, and elaborate temples.
Portuguese sailors once dubbed it Ilha Formosa, the 'beautiful island,' and its mountainous terrain rises sharply toward Yushan peak.
Its capital, Taipei, is crowned by a record-setting bamboo-shaped skyscraper that briefly reigned as the tallest building on Earth.
This high-tech powerhouse manufactures most of the world's advanced semiconductor chips through its globally dominant foundry industry.
This landlocked Central Asian republic is overwhelmingly mountainous, with glaciers and high valleys covering most of its rugged terrain.
A former Soviet state, it borders Afghanistan, China, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan, and speaks a Persian-related language.
Ancient Silk Road caravans crossed its valleys, leaving a heritage blending Persian poetry, Islamic art, and nomadic tradition.
The towering Pamir range, nicknamed the 'Roof of the World,' dominates its east, while Dushanbe serves as the capital city.
Famed for vivid suzani embroidery and the turquoise Iskanderkul lake, it holds Ismoil Somoni Peak, once the Soviet Union's highest summit.
This large East African nation stretches from the Indian Ocean inland to the great lakes, with savanna plains teeming with wildlife.
It borders Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, and several others, and includes the spice-scented archipelago of Zanzibar offshore.
Olduvai Gorge here yielded fossils that earned it the title of a cradle of humankind, and Swahili is widely spoken.
The continent's tallest mountain, snow-capped Kilimanjaro, rises within its borders near the vast Serengeti and Ngorongoro Crater.
Each year millions of wildebeest thunder across its plains in the Great Migration, drawing safari-goers chasing the Big Five.
This narrow West African nation is a slender strip running inland from a short Gulf of Guinea coastline.
Wedged between Ghana and Benin, it reaches north toward Burkina Faso, blending French colonial legacy with vibrant local cultures.
Rhythmic drumming, voodoo traditions, and brightly patterned textiles animate its markets and ceremonial dances.
Its seaside capital, Lome, is a major regional port hosting one of West Africa's largest open-air markets.
Cocoa, coffee, and cotton drive its economy, and this small republic was once a German colony before French rule.
This twin-island nation sits at the southern edge of the Caribbean, just off the coast of Venezuela.
Comprising one larger industrial island and a smaller tourist-favored one, it enjoys oil and natural gas wealth uncommon in the region.
Its exuberant pre-Lenten Carnival, with masquerade bands and soca music, ranks among the most famous festivals in the Americas.
The capital, Port of Spain, hosts a celebrated waterfront, while the Pitch Lake holds the world's largest natural asphalt deposit.
This dual-island republic invented the steelpan drum and is widely hailed as the birthplace of calypso music.
This North African nation faces the Mediterranean from the continent's northernmost tip, its south fading into Saharan dunes.
Bordered by Algeria and Libya, it blends Berber, Arab, and French influences in its language, cuisine, and architecture.
The ruins of ancient Carthage stand near its capital, recalling a powerful empire that once rivaled Rome.
Desert oasis towns near Tozeur served as filming sets for Tatooine in Star Wars, and Berber granaries dot the south.
Where the 2011 Arab Spring began, this olive-oil and date producer was the heart of Rome's province of Africa.
This transcontinental nation straddles Europe and Asia, with long coastlines on the Mediterranean, Aegean, and Black Seas.
Its vast Anatolian peninsula reaches from European shores to borders with Greece, Syria, Iraq, Iran, and the Caucasus.
Cradle of Hittite, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman civilizations, it is dotted with rock-cut churches and grand bazaars.
Its largest city straddles the Bosphorus strait, where hot-air balloons drift over the fairy-chimney rock formations of Cappadocia.
Once the seat of the Ottoman Empire, it is home to the soaring domed Hagia Sophia and Ankara as its capital.
This landlocked Central Asian republic is dominated by the vast Karakum Desert, with the Caspian Sea along its western edge.
A former Soviet state bordering Iran, Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan, it sits atop enormous natural gas reserves.
Its prized hand-knotted carpets, with deep red geometric guls, reflect a proud nomadic heritage celebrated nationally.
Its capital, Ashgabat, is renowned for gleaming white-marble buildings and gold-domed monuments, holding a record for marble-clad structures.
A flaming gas crater nicknamed the 'Door to Hell' has burned for decades in its desert, a relic of a Soviet drilling mishap.
This landlocked East African nation straddles the equator and borders Africa's largest lake, Lake Victoria.
Sharing frontiers with Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, the Congo, and South Sudan, it brims with lakes, forests, and highlands.
A young British explorer once called it the 'Pearl of Africa,' praising its lush greenery and abundant wildlife.
Markets bustle in its capital, Kampala, while the snow-fed Rwenzori range, the 'Mountains of the Moon,' rises in the west.
Its misty Bwindi forest shelters nearly half the world's surviving mountain gorillas, a magnet for conservation tourism.
This large Eastern European nation spreads across fertile plains, with a long southern shoreline on the Black Sea.
Bordering Russia, Belarus, Poland, and Romania, its dark, fertile soil long made it a vital grain exporter.
Famed for golden-domed Orthodox churches, intricate embroidery, and Cossack folk traditions, it has a fiercely independent spirit.
Its capital, Kyiv, sits on the Dnieper River, and the abandoned Chernobyl reactor zone lies within its northern territory.
The sunflower is its emblem, and since 2022 it has resisted a full-scale Russian invasion that captured global attention.
This Gulf nation occupies the southeastern Arabian Peninsula, where desert dunes meet warm coastal waters.
Bordering Saudi Arabia and Oman, it is a federation of seven sheikhdoms transformed by oil into a global trade hub.
Beneath its glittering modernity lies a Bedouin heritage of falconry, camel racing, and pearl diving along the coast.
Its glamorous city of Dubai boasts the world's tallest skyscraper, the Burj Khalifa, while Abu Dhabi serves as capital.
Its dirham currency, indoor ski slopes, and palm-shaped artificial islands symbolize breakneck petro-fueled development.
This vast country is located in the central and northern part of its continent, spanning an entire landmass between two great oceans.
It is a vast federal nation known for its enormous size and diverse landscapes, stretching from one ocean coast to the other.
This country boasts a rich history of innovation and a culture deeply influenced by immigration, with iconic music and a love for baseball.
You can find bustling cities like New York and Los Angeles within its borders, alongside national parks like Yellowstone and the Grand Canyon.
Home to the Statue of Liberty and a symbol of freedom worldwide, this nation's flag features stars and stripes.
This small South American nation sits on the continent's southeastern Atlantic coast, a land of gently rolling grasslands.
Tucked between Argentina and Brazil, it borders the wide Rio de la Plata estuary and ranches stretch across its plains.
Cattle-herding gaucho culture, mate tea, and a strong European immigrant influence define its easygoing identity.
Its capital, Montevideo, is a lively port, while beach resorts like Punta del Este draw summer crowds.
Often called Latin America's most progressive country, it legalized recreational cannabis and same-sex marriage early on.
This doubly-landlocked Central Asian nation spreads across deserts and oasis valleys between two great rivers.
Bordering Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, and others, it lay at the heart of the historic Silk Road.
Dazzling turquoise tilework crowns its madrasas and mosques, and the two-stringed dutar accompanies traditional song.
Ancient Samarkand and Bukhara dazzle with Islamic monuments, while Tashkent serves as the bustling modern capital.
The once-mighty Aral Sea has shriveled to a fraction of its size here, ravaged by Soviet-era cotton irrigation.
This northern South American nation faces the Caribbean, with Andean peaks in the west and vast plains in the interior.
Bordering Colombia, Brazil, and Guyana, it possesses some of the planet's largest proven oil reserves.
Flat-topped tepui mountains rise from its jungles, including the cliff that feeds the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall, Angel Falls.
Its capital, Caracas, nestles in a coastal mountain valley, while economic collapse has driven mass emigration in recent years.
Explorers named it for stilt houses resembling Venice; today it is famed for beauty queens and a long Caribbean coastline.
This Southeast Asian nation forms a long, narrow S-curve along the coast, with deltas at each end fed by major rivers.
Bordering China, Laos, and Cambodia, it is famed for terraced rice paddies and farmers wearing conical straw hats.
Its history bears the marks of French colonialism and a brutal war against American forces in the twentieth century.
Its capital, Hanoi, lies in the north, while emerald Ha Long Bay bristles with thousands of limestone karst islands.
A leading exporter of coffee and rice, it is celebrated worldwide for the fragrant noodle soup known as pho.
This nation occupies the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, facing the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea.
Bordering Saudi Arabia and Oman, it guards the strategic Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the gateway to the Suez shipping route.
Its ancient skyscraper cities of mud-brick towers and terraced mountain farms reflect a heritage stretching back to the Queen of Sheba.
Its capital, Sana'a, holds a World Heritage old city of gingerbread tower-houses, and Socotra island hosts otherworldly dragon's-blood trees.
Gripped by years of devastating civil war and famine, this land gave its name to the coffee port of Mocha.
This landlocked southern African nation is a high plateau crossed by mighty rivers and dotted with wildlife-rich parks.
It borders eight countries, including Zimbabwe, the Congo, and Tanzania, and its economy leans heavily on copper mining.
The mighty Zambezi River carves through it, plunging over a thunderous mile-wide curtain of water along its southern frontier.
Its capital, Lusaka, anchors the nation, while the Copperbelt to the north feeds one of Africa's great mineral industries.
It shares Victoria Falls, locally called 'the smoke that thunders,' with its southern neighbor across the great river.
This landlocked southern African nation rests on a high plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers.
Bordering South Africa, Botswana, Mozambique, and Zambia, it boasts abundant wildlife and significant tobacco and lithium output.
Massive medieval drystone ruins built by ancestral kingdoms gave the modern nation its very name and identity.
Its capital, Harare, governs the country, while the spectacular Victoria Falls thunders along its northwestern border.
Once known as Southern Rhodesia, it endured hyperinflation so severe that trillion-dollar banknotes were printed.
This twin-island nation lies in the eastern Caribbean among the Leeward Islands, ringed by coral reefs and white beaches.
Comprising one larger populated island and a smaller, flatter sister isle, it gained independence from Britain in 1981.
Locals boast a beach for every day of the year, and the Georgian dockyard once anchored Britain's Caribbean naval fleet.
Its capital, St. John's, welcomes cruise ships, while Nelson's restored harbor recalls the famed admiral's stationing here.
A cricket-mad nation that produced legends like Viv Richards, it remains a Commonwealth realm under the British crown.
This island nation scatters across the western Atlantic just southeast of Florida, famed for shallow turquoise shallows.
Made up of around seven hundred islands and countless cays, it blends African and British colonial heritage.
Christopher Columbus made his first New World landfall on one of its islands in 1492, near coral reefs and blue holes.
Its capital, Nassau, charms visitors with pastel colonial buildings, a busy cruise harbor, and the giant Atlantis resort.
A top cruise destination, this archipelago is famous for the wild swimming pigs paddling in its clear Exuma waters.
This single coral island sits in the eastern Caribbean, the easternmost outpost facing the open Atlantic Ocean.
A former British colony, it built its early wealth on sugarcane plantations and the rum distilled from them.
Its deep colonial ties and cricket obsession earned it the affectionate nickname 'Little England' among the islands.
Its capital, Bridgetown, holds a historic garrison recognized by UNESCO, and rum here claims to be the world's oldest.
Birthplace of the global pop superstar Rihanna, it became a parliamentary republic, dropping the British monarch in 2021.
This tiny, oil-rich nation clings to the northern coast of Borneo, surrounded on land by Malaysian territory.
Split into two enclaves by a slice of Malaysia, it is cloaked in pristine rainforest and devout Islamic tradition.
Vast petroleum and gas reserves fund a wealthy welfare state with no income tax and free healthcare for citizens.
Its capital, Bandar Seri Begawan, gleams with gold-domed mosques and a sprawling water village built on stilts over the river.
Ruled by one of the world's longest-reigning monarchs, an immensely wealthy sultan, its name means 'Abode of Peace.'
Tucked into the eastern Caribbean, this mountainous tropical island sits between Guadeloupe and Martinique amid the volcanic Lesser Antilles arc.
A small, English-speaking republic, it remains far less developed for tourism than its neighbors, prizing rainforest hiking over crowded resort beaches.
Its rugged interior holds a boiling lake, sulphur hot springs, and hundreds of rivers, plus Morne Trois Pitons National Park, a protected wilderness.
The capital, Roseau, sits beneath steep green ridges, and the island is the last refuge of the rare Sisserou parrot pictured on its flag.
Marketed as the 'Nature Island' of the Caribbean, it was reputedly the only place Columbus would still recognize today, ringed by World Heritage rainforest.
In Southeast Asia, this half-island state lies northwest of Australia at the eastern tip of the long Lesser Sunda chain of islands.
Sharing its single island with Indonesia, it blends Catholic Portuguese heritage with indigenous Austronesian custom across rugged coffee-growing highlands.
After centuries of Lisbon's colonial rule and a brutal occupation, it endured a long independence struggle before a UN-supervised restoration of sovereignty.
Its seaside capital, Dili, faces a coral-rich coast, and Tetum and Portuguese serve as official languages of this young democracy.
Among the world's newest nations, it formally restored independence in 2002 and counts an exclave, Oecusse, surrounded by Indonesian territory.
In southern Africa, this tiny landlocked country occupies hilly terrain almost entirely encircled by one giant neighbor, with a sliver touching another.
Bordered by South Africa and Mozambique, it ranges from cool highveld to hot lowveld and remains one of the world's last absolute monarchies.
Vibrant beadwork, traditional dance, and reed-gathering ceremonies define its culture, while game reserves shelter rhinos, elephants, and antelope.
Its royal and administrative capitals, Mbabane and Lobamba, host the king who renamed the nation in 2018 to shed its colonial-era title.
Famous for the colorful Umhlanga reed dance and the kingship rite of Incwala, it was long known to the world as Swaziland.
Near the southern end of the Caribbean's island arc, this small tropical nation lies just north of Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela's coast.
A Commonwealth island state with lush rainforest interior, it became briefly notorious for a 1983 coup that prompted a United States invasion.
Once fought over by France and Britain, its volcanic soils made it a leading grower of nutmeg, mace, cloves, and other fragrant spices.
Boats crowd the harbor of its capital, St. George's, ringed by red-roofed colonial houses overlooking the Carenage waterfront.
Dubbed the 'Spice Isle,' its flag uniquely features a nutmeg pod, reflecting an export that once supplied much of the world's supply.
Straddling the equator in the central Pacific, this dispersed island republic spreads across an ocean area larger than India yet holds little land.
Made up of 33 atolls and reef islands in three groups, its low-lying coral terrain makes it acutely threatened by rising seas.
Seafaring culture runs deep here, with traditional voyaging, stick-fighting dances, and a maritime way of life shaped by surrounding lagoons.
Its capital, Tarawa, saw fierce Pacific fighting in 1943, and the nation later absorbed Christmas Island and other former British line islands.
Uniquely, it is the only country sitting in all four hemispheres, and it shifted the date line so its eastern islands greet each new day first.
In southeastern Europe's Balkan Peninsula, this small landlocked territory sits ringed by Serbia, Montenegro, Albania, and North Macedonia.
Its disputed sovereignty is recognized by many Western states but not by Serbia, Russia, or several others, leaving its status partly contested.
Layered with Ottoman mosques and medieval Serbian Orthodox monasteries, its rugged mountains and fertile basins shaped centuries of competing rule.
Pristina serves as its capital, and a 1999 NATO bombing campaign preceded years of UN administration before a unilateral declaration in 2008.
Europe's youngest country, predominantly ethnic Albanian, it uses the euro despite not belonging to the eurozone and honors a 1389 battlefield in its name.
Scattered across the central Pacific north of the equator, this remote republic comprises chains of low coral atolls and tiny reef islets.
In free association with the United States, which uses its dollar, the nation hosts an American missile-testing range on Kwajalein Atoll.
Navigators here once read swells using woven stick charts, a unique wayfinding tradition passed down across generations of canoe sailors.
Bikini and Enewetak atolls became Cold War nuclear test sites, including the Castle Bravo blast, displacing islanders for decades.
Its capital, Majuro, hugs a narrow lagoon ring, and the country's name commemorates an 18th-century British sea captain who charted these waters.
In the western Pacific north of the equator, this dispersed federation stretches across hundreds of islands spanning thousands of ocean kilometers.
Bound to the United States in free association, it unites four states, each with a distinct language, from Yap to Pohnpei and Kosrae.
Star-path navigation and outrigger canoes shaped its seafaring culture, while Yap is famed for enormous stone discs once used as money.
The ruined basalt city of Nan Madol, a UNESCO site built on coral reefs, hints at a powerful chiefdom that once ruled these islands.
Its capital, Palikir, ranks among the world's smallest by area, and the federation flag bears four white stars on an ocean-blue field.
At the western edge of the Pacific's Micronesia region, this small archipelago lies east of the Philippines and north of Indonesia's seas.
In free association with the United States and using its dollar, the nation is celebrated as one of the planet's premier scuba-diving destinations.
Its mushroom-shaped Rock Islands, a UNESCO World Heritage site, rise from turquoise lagoons studded with sunken World War II wrecks.
Its capital, Ngerulmud, ranks among the world's least populous, while the former hub Koror remains the main commercial center.
A marine sanctuary nation, it is famed for a saltwater lake where millions of harmless golden jellyfish pulse daily toward the sun.
In the northern Leeward Islands of the Caribbean, this two-island federation lies near Antigua, with green volcanic peaks rising above the sea.
The smallest sovereign state in the Americas by both area and population, this Commonwealth nation built its wealth on centuries of sugar plantations.
A massive 17th-century hilltop citadel, Brimstone Hill Fortress, now a UNESCO site, guards the larger island once dubbed the 'Gibraltar of the West Indies.'
Its capital, Basseterre, sits on the bigger island, while a narrow channel separates it from a smaller round island crowned by a cloud-wreathed peak.
A pioneer of selling citizenship, this dual-island state takes its names from a Christian saint and a Spanish word for snow-capped heights.
An island nation in the eastern Caribbean's Windward chain, it sits between Martinique and the islands of Saint Vincent to the south.
Lush volcanic rainforest covers its interior, and its creole-speaking culture fuses African, French, and British colonial influences.
A drive-in volcano with bubbling sulphur springs lies near the southwest coast, and the island changed hands between rival powers fourteen times.
Its capital, Castries, overlooks a harbor, while two dramatic forested cones, the Pitons, soar from the sea near the town of Soufrière.
Tiny yet remarkable, it has produced two Nobel laureates, including poet Derek Walcott, and its flag depicts those twin volcanic spires.
In the eastern Caribbean's Windward Islands, this multi-island country lies south of Saint Lucia and north of Grenada near the chain's end.
A single larger volcanic island anchors a string of smaller cays and islets prized by yachters for sailing and secluded anchorages.
Its active volcano, La Soufrière, erupted explosively in 2021, and its lush valleys served as a filming backdrop for a famous pirate movie series.
Its capital, Kingstown, sits beneath green ridges, while exclusive Mustique and the Tobago Cays draw celebrities and divers offshore.
Its flag bears three green diamonds nicknamed the 'gems of the Antilles,' and it was the last territory in its chain to gain independence in 1979.
In the South Pacific's Polynesian heart, this island nation lies near Fiji and Tonga, west of an American-administered territory of the same culture.
Two main volcanic islands, Savai'i and Upolu, dominate it, where village life follows a customary chiefly order known as fa'a.
Intricate hand-tapped tattooing, the tatau, is a revered rite of passage, and author Robert Louis Stevenson spent his final years here.
Its capital, Apia, lines a curved harbor, and in 2009 the country switched to driving on the left, aligning with Australia and New Zealand.
In 2011 it jumped the date line eastward to skip a day, ensuring this Pacific kingdom-turned-republic shares business days with its trading partners.
In the southwestern Pacific's Melanesia, this rugged archipelago lies east of Papua New Guinea and northeast of Australia's Coral Sea.
Hundreds of volcanic and coral islands make it up, where dozens of languages are spoken and shell money still circulates in some markets.
Wood carvings inlaid with shell depict ancestral spirits, and its dense jungles harbor rare birds, megapodes, and giant coconut-eating crabs.
Its capital, Honiara, sits on Guadalcanal, scene of a pivotal World War II campaign that left sunken warships in 'Iron Bottom Sound.'
Named centuries ago by a Spanish explorer who imagined a biblical king's gold here, it remains a Commonwealth realm under the British crown.
Deep in East-Central Africa, this landlocked nation of vast grassy plains lies south of its larger northern parent and borders Ethiopia and Uganda.
Pastoralist and farming peoples live across its flat lowlands, where the White Nile feeds the immense Sudd, one of the world's biggest wetlands.
Oil-rich but conflict-scarred, it broke away after decades of civil war between the largely Christian south and the Arab Muslim north.
Its capital, Juba, rose on the riverbank as the seat of the planet's most recently founded internationally recognized country.
Born by referendum in 2011, it is the youngest UN member state, its flag bearing a golden star symbolizing unity of its long-divided peoples.
In the South Pacific's Polynesia, this island kingdom lies south of Samoa and east of Fiji, scattered along the edge of a deep ocean trench.
Spread over many coral and volcanic islands, it is the region's last remaining Polynesian monarchy, ruled by a long-standing royal dynasty.
Custom prizes woven pandanus mats and respect for elders, and its waters host migrating humpback whales that gather to calve each winter.
Its capital, Nuku'alofa, sits on the main island, and a nearby undersea volcano erupted spectacularly in 2022, triggering a Pacific tsunami.
Never formally colonized, this 'Friendly Islands' kingdom keeps close ties to Britain and once sat just west of the international date line.
In the central Pacific between Australia and Hawaii, this scattered nation comprises just nine tiny atolls and reef islands of barely coral land.
Among the smallest and lowest-lying countries on Earth, its highest point rises only a few meters, making it acutely menaced by rising seas.
Ocean-centered culture, seafaring tradition, and dance define life here, with subsistence fishing on lagoons sustaining a few thousand residents.
Its capital, Funafuti, spreads thinly along a reef rim, and the country famously earns income leasing its '.tv' internet domain suffix.
Facing possible submersion, this Commonwealth realm has begun building a 'digital nation' to preserve sovereignty even if its land disappears.
In the southwestern Pacific's Melanesia, this volcanic archipelago lies east of Australia, northeast of New Caledonia, and west of Fiji.
Dozens of rugged islands make it up, where over a hundred indigenous languages plus the creole Bislama coexist with deep custom traditions.
Once jointly ruled by Britain and France as the New Hebrides, it became a republic in 1980 and ranks among the world's most disaster-prone states.
Its capital, Port Vila, sits on Efate, while Tanna island's accessible Mount Yasur volcano glows nightly above ash plains and cargo-cult villages.
On Pentecost island, men leap from tall wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, the ritual 'land diving' that inspired modern bungee jumping.
In southern Europe, this minuscule sovereign enclave lies entirely surrounded by a single major city on the banks of the Tiber.
The smallest independent state on the planet by area and population, it serves as the spiritual and governing center of the Roman Catholic Church.
Behind its medieval walls lie priceless Renaissance treasures, including Michelangelo's frescoed Sistine Chapel ceiling and Raphael's painted rooms.
Pilgrims fill its great colonnaded square before St. Peter's Basilica, while Swiss Guards in striped uniforms protect the surrounding museums.
Ruled by the Pope and created by the 1929 Lateran Treaty, this walled microstate elects its leader by cardinals' secret conclave behind locked doors.
In the Middle East along the eastern Mediterranean, this contested entity occupies two separated territories bordered largely by Israel.
Recognized by most UN members but not all, it comprises the West Bank inland and the coastal Gaza Strip, divided by Israeli-held land.
Ancient olive terraces, Bethlehem's Church of the Nativity, and Hebron's old city anchor a deeply layered religious and agricultural heritage.
Its administrative seat lies in Ramallah, while it claims contested East Jerusalem, a city holy to Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike, as its capital.
Born of a decades-long conflict with Israel, it holds permanent observer status at the UN and is governed by a divided national authority.
Sitting just south of the equator in the central Pacific, this isolated speck of raised coral is among the most remote inhabited places on Earth.
A single oval island with no official capital, it ranks as the smallest republic in the world and one of the least visited nations anywhere.
Decades of strip-mining phosphate left its interior a moonscape of jagged limestone pinnacles after the rich guano deposits were exhausted.
Its government district clusters around Yaren, and once-immense mining royalties briefly made its tiny population among the world's wealthiest.
Now reliant on Australian aid and an offshore asylum-processing center, this ring-road island circles a stranded plateau in barely twenty minutes by car.
In the South Pacific's Polynesia, this lone raised coral island lies east of Tonga and west of the Cook Islands, far from any neighbor.
One of the world's largest uplifted coral atolls, it has no central lagoon but instead steep limestone cliffs riddled with caves and chasms.
Its small population shares deep Polynesian roots, and the nation governs itself in free association with New Zealand, whose citizenship its people hold.
Its village capital, Alofi, perches on the western coast, and the island became one of the first nations to offer free nationwide Wi-Fi.
Nicknamed 'the Rock of Polynesia,' its name means 'behold the coconut,' and clear surrounding waters make it a haven for swimming with whales and snakes.
In the South Pacific's Polynesia, this scattered island group lies northeast of New Zealand and west of French Polynesia's Tahiti.
Fifteen islands, some volcanic and some low atolls, make it up, self-governing in free association with New Zealand and using its dollar.
Energetic drum dances, woven crafts, and black-pearl farming reflect a thriving culture named long ago for a famous British navigator.
Its main hub, Rarotonga, rises in jagged green peaks ringed by reef, while Aitutaki's vast turquoise lagoon draws honeymooners and divers.
Its people are New Zealand citizens, yet it issues its own coins and stamps, including a triangular coin and a famed pineapple-shaped dollar.
In the South Pacific north of Samoa, this dependent territory of just three coral atolls is among the tiniest and most isolated inhabited places.
A territory of New Zealand whose people hold its citizenship, it has no airport, reachable only by a long boat voyage across open ocean.
Its few hundred residents live by fishing and copra, governing themselves through village councils of elders on each separate ringed atoll.
Each of its atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu, and Fakaofo, runs its own affairs, and it remarkably draws nearly all its electricity from solar power.
With one of the smallest populations of any polity on Earth, its citizens vote in New Zealand elections and twice declined full self-rule by referendum.
Far out in the North Atlantic east of the Carolinas, this isolated subtropical island group lies hundreds of kilometers from the nearest mainland.
A self-governing British Overseas Territory, it is famed for pink-sand beaches, pastel cottages, and a thriving offshore insurance and finance industry.
Settled after a 1609 shipwreck that inspired Shakespeare's storm-tossed play, it became Britain's oldest continuously inhabited colony in the New World.
Its capital, Hamilton, lines a colorful harbor, while the old town of St. George's preserves a World Heritage colonial streetscape and stone fort.
Lending its name to a mythic ocean 'triangle' of vanished ships and planes, it is the place where businessmen still wear knee-length tailored shorts.
In northern Britain, a colossal red steel structure spans a saltwater estuary, an enduring icon of Victorian engineering ambition.
Found in Scotland, it carries railway traffic across a wide firth just west of the nation's capital city, Edinburgh.
Opened in 1890, its cantilever design uses three giant diamond-shaped towers and was once Britain's longest such span.
Crossing the estuary near Queensferry, it stands alongside two newer road crossings, dominating the skyline with rusty oxide-red girders.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, its endless repainting inspired a famous idiom about tasks that never truly reach completion.
In the western United States, a vast volcanic wilderness sits atop a supervolcano, famed for steaming geysers and bubbling hot springs.
Spanning mostly Wyoming with edges in Montana and Idaho, it became the world's first national park in 1872.
Known for grizzly bears, bison herds, and a rainbow-colored prismatic spring, it boasts half the planet's geothermal features.
Its most famous geyser erupts on a reliable schedule, drawing crowds who gather to watch the predictable plume shoot skyward.
The supervolcano caldera and that punctual geyser, nicknamed Old Faithful, make this America's iconic geothermal playground.
In southern Europe, a historic northern city sits on a winding river, beloved for romance and remarkably preserved Roman ruins.
Located in Italy's Veneto region, west of Venice, this UNESCO city draws opera lovers and literary pilgrims alike.
Its ancient pink-stoned Roman amphitheater still hosts grand summer opera festivals, rivaling the famous Colosseum in preservation.
Straddling the Adige river, it's forever linked to a Shakespearean tragedy about two feuding families and star-crossed teenage lovers.
Tourists flock to a balcony said to belong to Juliet, the heroine of the world's most famous doomed love story set here.
In South America, a planned capital rose from empty highland savanna in the late 1950s, a showcase of modernist design.
This Brazilian seat of government replaced Rio de Janeiro as capital in 1960, built from scratch in the country's interior.
Designed on a layout resembling an airplane or bird, its sweeping concrete government buildings define mid-century modernist architecture.
Architect Oscar Niemeyer shaped its cathedral, congress, and palaces, earning the young city UNESCO World Heritage status.
Lúcio Costa's Pilot Plan and Niemeyer's curves made this purpose-built federal district Brazil's audacious 20th-century capital.
In western Europe, an enormous gilded royal residence with sprawling formal gardens symbolizes absolute monarchy at its most extravagant.
Just southwest of Paris, this French chateau became the seat of royal power under a famously powerful 17th-century king.
Louis XIV transformed a hunting lodge into a dazzling court, complete with fountains, geometric gardens, and a mirrored gallery.
Its Hall of Mirrors hosted the 1919 treaty ending the First World War, beneath chandeliers reflecting endless windows.
Home to the Sun King and later Marie Antoinette, this opulent estate's name became shorthand for royal excess before the Revolution.
This North African city sits along the Atlantic coast, blending old medieval quarters with the administrative offices of a modern kingdom.
It serves as the seat of government for Morocco, a quieter alternative to the larger commercial hub of Casablanca to its southwest.
Founded as a fortified Almohad settlement, its kasbah and ramparts overlook the mouth of the Bou Regreg River.
Across the river lies the commuter town of Sale, while a tall unfinished 12th-century minaret and a royal mausoleum dominate the heart of the city.
Home to the Hassan Tower and the tomb of Mohammed V, this UNESCO-listed capital balances Andalusian gardens with the residence of Morocco's monarch.
This location is situated in a country renowned for its ancient dynasties and bustling modern cities.
You'll find this protected park within a mountainous region of China, offering breathtaking views and diverse geological formations.
This park preserves dramatic landscapes shaped by past ice ages, displaying distinctive U-shaped valleys and ancient glacial deposits scattered across the slopes.
Near the city of Jiujiang, this park focuses on the geological impact of ancient ice-age activity, specifically showcasing moraines and sculpted valleys within Jiangxi Province.
Sitting in Jiangxi Province, this reserve offers a unique glimpse into China’s glacial past, featuring prominent moraine ridges and evidence of ancient ice sheet retreat across its terrain.
This East Asian natural wonder lies high in a rugged mountain range famous for rare wildlife and turquoise waters.
Set in northern Sichuan Province, China, it occupies an alpine valley fed by mineral-rich hot springs.
Calcium-laden water cascades down thousands of terraced travertine pools, creating golden and blue basins along the slope.
Near Songpan and the Min Mountains, its tiered pools snake downhill in a shape locals liken to a scaly golden dragon.
A UNESCO World Heritage site famed for its Five-Flower Pond, this gilded limestone staircase glows beneath snow-capped peaks of western China.
This East Asian valley is renowned for dramatic alpine scenery and vivid blue-green waters.
Tucked into northern Sichuan Province, China, it lies amid forested peaks long inhabited by Tibetan herding communities.
Its terraced lakes glow in turquoise and emerald hues, fed by countless cascading waterfalls and ancient old-growth forest.
Named for the nine traditional Tibetan settlements scattered through it, the reserve sits near the Min Mountains and the town of Songpan.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site boasting over a hundred multi-coloured lakes and dozens of waterfalls, this fairy-tale gorge draws millions each year.
This East Asian landmark is a sprawling imperial garden retreat tied to the rulers of a former dynasty.
Located on the northwestern edge of China's capital, it served emperors and empresses escaping the heat of the inner city.
Its grounds combine an artificial lake, a man-made hill, ornate pavilions, and one of the world's longest covered painted corridors.
Within Beijing, it surrounds Kunming Lake and Longevity Hill, and is famously linked to the powerful Empress Dowager Cixi.
Known in Chinese as Yihe Yuan, this UNESCO-listed Qing-era garden features a marble boat and classical landscaping unrivalled in the empire.
This Western European landmark is a colossal Gothic church towering over a major Rhine-side city.
It rises in Germany, serving as the seat of a Catholic archbishopric beside one of the country's busiest railway stations.
Construction began in the 13th century but stalled for centuries, finally finished only in 1880 to twin soaring openwork spires.
Overlooking the Rhine in the city it shares its name with, it survived heavy World War II bombing and shelters a famed golden shrine.
Called the Kolner Dom, this UNESCO World Heritage church holds the reputed relics of the Three Kings and remains Germany's most visited landmark.
This Asian scenic area is celebrated for thousands of towering quartz-sandstone pillars rising from misty forest.
Set in Hunan Province, China, it spreads across a subtropical landscape riddled with caves and deep ravines.
Its eroded stone columns soar hundreds of metres, while limestone caverns below hold vast calcite formations and a record-setting natural arch.
Near Zhangjiajie, the dramatic spires here reportedly inspired the floating mountains of a famous science-fiction film.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, this pillar forest features one of the world's highest natural bridges and glass walkways drawing crowds of hikers.

medium.name: Sheikh Safi al-Din Khānegāh and Shrine Ensemble

clues.description: This site is found in a country known for its ancient history and vibrant culture.
You'll discover a significant religious and architectural complex within a major urban center of that nation.
This is a stunning mausoleum complex featuring intricate tilework, a mosque, and a caravanserai, located in the historic city of Ardabil, Iran.
This UNESCO World Heritage site houses the tomb of a 14th-century Sufi mystic and order founder, and sits within the walled city of Ardabil in northern Iran.
A beautifully preserved Sufi spiritual retreat, it stands prominently in Ardabil, Iran, showcasing exquisite turquoise and ceramic tile designs around the revered scholar's resting place.
This location resides within the Middle East, in an ancient city that has long served as a crossroads for caravans and overland traders.
It is a significant historical marketplace, functioning for centuries as a central hub for commerce, craftsmanship, and everyday social life.
This is a vast, covered market renowned for its intricate architecture, diverse stalls selling everything from carpets to spices, and bustling atmosphere.
Located in the northwest of Iran, this covered market is a designated UNESCO World Heritage Site, celebrated for its traditional layout and vibrant commercial activity.
Also historically called Qeysarieh, this sprawling roofed marketplace in northwestern Iran is famous for hand-knotted carpets and its role as a vital trading center for centuries.
This South Asian shrine is among the holiest pilgrimage sites for a major world religion born in the region.
It rises in the state of Bihar, India, drawing devotees to a small town famous for spiritual awakening.
A tall pyramidal brick spire marks the spot, beside a sacred fig tree said to descend from one rooted there millennia ago.
In the town of Bodh Gaya, tradition holds that a prince named Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment beneath this very tree.
A UNESCO World Heritage complex over two thousand years old, it preserves the Vajrasana stone seat marking the Buddha's moment of awakening.
This Middle Eastern monument is one of the largest historic public plazas in a country famed for Persian heritage.
It lies at the centre of a celebrated city in Iran, once the dazzling capital of a 17th-century empire.
Enclosed by tiled mosques, a royal palace, and a grand bazaar gate, it was designed as a stage for polo, parades, and trade.
Set in Isfahan, it is framed by the Imam Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, and the balconied Ali Qapu Palace.
A UNESCO World Heritage plaza built under Shah Abbas the Great, this Safavid-era square glitters with blue mosaics and is nicknamed the 'Image of the World'.
This enormous reserve lies on a rugged tropical island shared between Asia and the Pacific world.
It occupies the highlands of Indonesia's Papua Province, the biggest protected area in all of Southeast Asia.
Its terrain rises from steamy lowland rainforest to glacier-clad summits, harbouring countless endemic plants and animals.
Indigenous Dani communities and ancient rock art lie within its bounds, beneath some of the only permanent ice in the tropics.
Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999, this Papuan wilderness safeguards an unbroken ecological transect from snowfield to coast.
This Middle Eastern ruin is an ancient open-air performance venue set amid a stark desert oasis.
It stands within a famed caravan city in Syria, once a wealthy trading hub linking Rome with the East.
Built in the second century CE during the Severan period, its semicircular stone tiers face a richly columned stage backdrop.
Surrounded by the colonnaded avenues of an oasis once ruled by Queen Zenobia, it lies near the modern town of Tadmur.
Tragically seized and partly demolished by militants in 2015, this desert theatre witnessed staged executions before later being recaptured and assessed for restoration.
This location lies within Italy, hidden among the dense streets of a historic port city on a large Mediterranean island.
You will find this ancient historical site in a Mediterranean city known for its vibrant culture, dark volcanic stone, and lively street markets.
This ancient venue features a grand, open-air theatre alongside a smaller, semicircular Odeon, showcasing impressive classical architectural design.
Located within the Parco Archeologico Greco-Romano, this theatre offers a glimpse into the city's rich ancient past and boasts a stage once capable of seating thousands.
Dating back to the 2nd century BC, this venue retains original seating tiers and a restored facade, standing as a prominent landmark in a historic city beneath Mount Etna.
This Southern European ruin is an ancient curved performance venue surviving in the heart of a famous capital.
It stands in central Rome, Italy, a short walk from the Tiber River and the island in its waters.
Begun under one ruler and completed by Augustus, its arched travertine facade later inspired the design of a much larger arena nearby.
Sitting in the Sant'Angelo district near the old Jewish quarter, its upper levels were converted into a Renaissance noble palace.
Dedicated to a nephew and heir of Augustus who died young, this two-story arcade once seated thousands and now hosts apartments above ancient stone.
This Southern European ruin is an ancient performance venue in a coastal city long fought over by rival empires.
It lies in northeastern Italy, in a port on the Adriatic Sea near the modern border with Slovenia.
Built into a gentle hillside in the first century AD, its curved seating once faced the sea before later buildings rose around it.
Set within a historic city overlooking the Gulf that shares its name, it sat hidden for centuries until excavated in the 1930s.
Commissioned in the age of Augustus and framed by a bustling Habsburg-era harbour city, this restored theatre again stages summer performances.
This Southern European ruin marks the first permanent stone performance venue of an ancient republic's capital.
Its remains lie in central Rome, Italy, buried beneath a busy square ringed by Republican-era temple foundations.
Completed in 55 BC by a celebrated general, it included a vast portico and a curia chamber attached to its grounds.
On the Largo di Torre Argentina, its curia was the spot where Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March.
Now overlapping a famous cat sanctuary among four ruined temples, this complex was the grandest entertainment venue of the late Republic.
This location lies within a country known for its rich European history, particularly its many remarkably preserved ancient monuments.
You will find this site in a southern region with a significant legacy of ancient imperial influence and remarkably preserved antiquities.
This is a remarkably preserved theatre constructed during the early years of an ancient empire, showcasing impressive classical architectural design.
Located in southern France, this theatre is a municipal landmark and hosts the internationally renowned Choregies summer opera festival each year.
Identifiable by its towering stage wall and seating tiers, this venue stands as a testament to ancient engineering and remains a celebrated stage for classical performances.
This Western European ruin is an ancient performance venue in a sun-baked town beloved by painters.
It lies in the Provence region of southern France, near the marshy delta where the Rhone meets the sea.
Two lone marble columns nicknamed the 'two widows' still mark its stage, the survivors of a once-grand colonnade.
In the same town a celebrated Dutch painter created masterpieces, and a nearby amphitheatre hosts Provencal bullfights.
A UNESCO World Heritage venue from the first century BC, this excavated theatre yielded the famed Venus statue now displayed in the Louvre.
This Balkan ruin is a strikingly preserved ancient performance venue carved into a hillside.
It crowns one of the seven hills of an old city in Bulgaria, often called one of Europe's oldest continuously inhabited places.
Built in the early second century AD under Emperor Trajan, its marble tiers once seated thousands of spectators.
Rediscovered after a landslide in the 1970s, it overlooks the cobbled Old Town with its colourful National Revival mansions.
Restored and still hosting concerts and opera today, this hillside theatre in Bulgaria's second-largest city seats around six thousand beneath the open sky.
This Southern European ruin is an ancient hillside performance venue in a romantic northern Italian city.
It sits in the Veneto region of Italy, climbing a slope on the far bank of the Adige River.
Built in the late first century BC, its tiered seats rise above the water and look across to the historic centre opposite.
The city around it is famed for a star-crossed Shakespearean love story and a vast, separate ancient amphitheatre arena.
Distinct from that more famous arena, this riverside theatre hosts a summer festival of classical drama in the city of Romeo and Juliet.
Tucked into southwestern Europe, this ancient stone performance venue sits in a sun-soaked country with a deep Iberian and classical past.
It rests within an old Andalusian port founded by Phoenicians, one of the most enduring continuously inhabited settlements in all of Spain.
Carved into a hillside two thousand years ago, its tiered seating and broad stage were rediscovered only in the twentieth century beneath later buildings.
A medieval fortress raised by King Alfonso X of Castile was built atop part of this venue, layering a thirteenth-century stronghold over classical foundations.
Dating to the first century BC and once among the empire's largest such venues, it lies in the Barrio del Pópulo of this Atlantic-facing Andalusian port.
Found in a small northwestern European nation famous for waffles, chocolate, and lace, these tranquil walled enclaves dot its northern half.
They cluster in the Dutch-speaking northern region of Belgium, near canal cities celebrated for medieval brickwork and quiet inner courtyards.
Established in the Middle Ages as gated communities for devout but unmarried laywomen, they feature whitewashed cottages around enclosed gardens and chapels.
Surviving examples grace Bruges, Kortrijk, Ghent, and Leuven, each a peaceful retreat of small homes ringing a central green and church.
A collection of these unique semi-religious women's settlements across the Flemish lands was inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1998.
Deep in South America, this protected wilderness shelters dramatic rock formations alongside some of the continent's oldest evidence of human presence.
It lies in the dry interior of northeastern Brazil, within the semi-arid caatinga scrubland of the state of Piauí.
Towering sandstone cliffs and canyons here are painted and engraved with thousands of ancient images of animals, hunters, and dancing figures.
Researchers led by archaeologist Niède Guidon argued its pigments and artifacts may push human arrival in the Americas back tens of thousands of years.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this reserve guards over a thousand decorated rock shelters, the densest concentration of prehistoric art in the Americas.
Set in the largest country on Earth, this walled religious compound rises beside a riverbend in its sprawling capital city.
It stands in southwestern Moscow, a fortified nunnery long tied to the political fortunes of Russia's ruling dynasties.
Grand Duke Vasily III founded it in 1524 to mark the reconquest of Smolensk, and royal women were later confined within its walls.
Its red-and-white belltower and ornate Moscow Baroque churches survive remarkably intact, ringed by an adjoining cemetery holding many famous Russians.
Peter the Great imprisoned his half-sister Sofia here, and this UNESCO-listed cloister now anchors a famed burial ground for Soviet-era luminaries.
On a tropical island in South Asia, an immense isolated rock erupts from the surrounding jungle plain, crowned by ancient ruins.
It sits in the dry-zone heartland of Sri Lanka, near the historic cities of Dambulla and Anuradhapura.
A fifth-century king built a palace and pleasure gardens atop this two-hundred-meter monolith, fleeing his half-brother after seizing the throne.
Visitors climb past colorful cliff-face frescoes of celestial maidens and enter through giant carved paws that once formed a colossal lion gateway.
Often dubbed the eighth wonder of the ancient world and tied to King Kassapa, this UNESCO rock citadel features mirror walls and symmetrical water gardens.
In the Middle East, this ancient ruined town carries layers of Nabataean, Roman, Byzantine, and early Islamic history in its black volcanic stone.
It lies in the Hauran plain of southern Syria, north of the Jordanian border and once a caravan crossroads toward the desert.
Its centerpiece is a superbly preserved Roman theater built of dark basalt, later wrapped inside a citadel that shielded it for centuries.
Once a Nabataean stronghold and later capital of the Roman province of Arabia, it sat on routes linking Damascus to the Red Sea.
A UNESCO World Heritage site dating to the second century AD, its basalt arena seats thousands and stands among the world's best-kept Roman theaters.
Hidden beneath North American rainforest, this overgrown ancient metropolis lies in a southern country celebrated for its Mesoamerican civilizations.
It sits deep in the jungles of Campeche state in southern Mexico, only about twenty miles from the Guatemalan frontier.
Towering limestone pyramids, plazas, and thousands of structures here mark the heart of one of the mightiest Maya city-states, rich in carved stelae.
Known anciently as the Kingdom of the Snake, it waged a long rivalry against Tikal for dominance across the Maya lowlands.
A UNESCO mixed cultural and natural site within a vast biosphere reserve, its tallest pyramid rises above the unbroken Yucatán forest canopy.
Far out in the Indian Ocean off Africa, this remote ring of raised coral encircles a vast tidal lagoon rather than holding any town.
It belongs to an outlying island group of the Seychelles, lying roughly seven hundred miles southwest of that nation's capital, Victoria.
Largely untouched by humans, the atoll hosts the planet's greatest population of giant tortoises plus endemic birds found nowhere else on Earth.
Once eyed for a military airbase before conservationists intervened, it is now a strict nature reserve and UNESCO World Heritage site.
Home to over one hundred thousand giant tortoises and the western Indian Ocean's last flightless bird, this coral atoll is a living natural laboratory.
In a southern European nation that shaped Western civilization, this sprawling imperial retreat spreads its ruins across a green countryside estate.
It lies in the Lazio region of Italy, just outside the hillside town of Tivoli east of the capital.
A second-century emperor built this enormous complex of baths, pavilions, theaters, and libraries as a luxurious escape from the imperial court.
Its famous Canopus, a long reflecting pool lined with statues, recreated an Egyptian sanctuary the ruler had visited along the Nile.
Commissioned by the emperor who built Britain's great northern wall, this UNESCO-listed retreat near Tivoli is among antiquity's grandest residential estates.
On Europe's Atlantic edge, this vast monastic complex stands in a seafaring country that once pioneered ocean exploration.
It rises in the Belém district of Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, near the mouth of the Tagus River.
Built in the elaborate Manueline style with intricately carved stone, it served as a royal church and burial place for the nation's monarchs.
Its tomb holds the navigator Vasco da Gama, while nearby a riverside fortress and discoveries monument honor the Age of Exploration.
Completed in the sixteenth century and funded by spice-trade riches, this UNESCO World Heritage cloister entombs King Manuel I and the poet Camões.
In a large country famed for deserts and mountains, this protected area hides an astonishing world of caves beneath an arid surface.
It lies in the southwestern United States, within the Guadalupe Mountains of southeastern New Mexico near the Texas border.
Below the desert floor stretches a labyrinth of limestone chambers dripping with stalactites, stalagmites, and delicate mineral decorations.
Its enormous main chamber, the Big Room, ranks among the largest underground rooms in North America and dwarfs visitors who descend into it.
Each summer evening, hundreds of thousands of Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral out of this UNESCO-listed cave's natural entrance to feed.
Rising in the highlands of East Africa, this winding watercourse cuts through rugged, undeveloped terrain on its long southward course.
It runs wholly inside Ethiopia, descending from the central plateau near the upper reaches above the Gibe gorges.
Its banks support diverse tribal communities and archaeological sites, and a controversial dam now regulates much of its seasonal flow.
The flow ultimately empties into Lake Turkana, forming a vital part of the closed Turkana drainage basin shared with Kenya.
Its floodplain sustains the Karo and Nyangatom peoples, whose body-painting traditions have made this remote valley world-famous among photographers.
In East Asia's most populous nation, tens of thousands of religious figures were chiseled into riverside cliffs over many centuries.
These carvings line a river gorge in Henan province, near the ancient capital of Luoyang in central China.
Buddhist images fill more than two thousand niches cut into limestone, from tiny figures to colossal seated Buddhas dozens of meters tall.
Sculpting spanned the Northern Wei through Tang dynasties, and the grandest Vairocana statue is said to bear an empress's serene features.
A UNESCO World Heritage site facing the Yi River, this cliffside gallery preserves over one hundred thousand carved Buddhist statues and inscriptions.
In the southeastern United States, this enormous protected wetland spreads as a watery plain of sawgrass teeming with wildlife.
It occupies the southern tip of Florida, a subtropical mosaic of marsh, mangrove, and slow-moving water below Miami.
Often called a river of grass, it is a shallow sheet of freshwater creeping seaward, sheltering alligators, manatees, and wading birds.
It is the only place on Earth where American alligators and crocodiles coexist, with restoration efforts battling decades of drainage.
Spanning roughly 1.5 million acres, this UNESCO World Heritage site and International Biosphere Reserve protects North America's largest subtropical wilderness.
On the Balkan Peninsula, this small medieval place of worship hides extraordinary painted treasures at the foot of a forested mountain.
It sits on the outskirts of Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria, near the slopes of Vitosha mountain.
Built in stages from the eleventh century, its modest stone walls conceal remarkably lifelike frescoes added by an anonymous master in 1259.
Those paintings, depicting saints and donors with startling realism, are often hailed as forerunners of the European Renaissance in art.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this tiny Orthodox sanctuary is prized above all for its vivid thirteenth-century murals of biblical and courtly scenes.
In East Asia, a scattering of ancient earthen burial mounds preserves the legacy of a vanished warrior kingdom on a divided peninsula.
They lie in the secretive northern state of the Korean peninsula, several clustered near its capital, Pyongyang.
These were the graves of the rulers and nobles of an ancient kingdom that once stretched across northern Korea and into Manchuria.
Inside the mounds, vivid wall paintings dating from the fourth to seventh centuries show hunting scenes, dancers, and mythical guardian animals.
Inscribed by UNESCO in 2004, this group of decorated royal mounds offers rare surviving murals from one of Korea's three legendary early kingdoms.
On the Pacific coast of the Americas, the eroded mud walls of a once-mighty desert metropolis stretch across an arid plain.
It lies near the city of Trujillo in northern Peru, just inland from the ocean shore.
This was the royal capital of the Chimú people, a sophisticated pre-Inca culture whose craftsmen excelled in gold and textiles.
Its compounds enclose palaces, plazas, and reservoirs decorated with friezes of fish, seabirds, and waves molded into the adobe.
The largest earthen city of pre-Columbian South America and a UNESCO World Heritage site, it was eventually absorbed by the conquering Inca empire.
Within the world's largest country, a remote flat-topped highland of basalt rises in near-total isolation across the far north.
It sits in Arctic Siberia, east of the Yenisei River and the mining city of Norilsk in northern Russia.
Layered volcanic rock here is sliced by deep canyons holding countless cold lakes and some of the highest waterfalls in the country.
Reachable only by helicopter or boat, it hosts vast reindeer migrations and lies among the planet's least-visited wilderness regions.
A UNESCO World Heritage site straddling the Arctic Circle, this trap-basalt tableland preserves a complete subarctic ecosystem largely untouched by humans.
In a country renowned for its immense Siberian wilderness, a wall of soaring rock spires lines a great northern river.
This protected nature park lies in the Sakha Republic of eastern Russia, also known as Yakutia, one of Earth's coldest inhabited regions.
Towering limestone columns up to three hundred meters tall rise sheer from the riverbank, sculpted over ages by frost and erosion.
The rock here formed in ancient Cambrian seas and preserves early fossils, while extreme freeze-thaw cycles continue carving the cliffs today.
A UNESCO World Heritage site along one of Russia's mightiest rivers, this stone palisade glows pillar-red above the water at sunrise.
Across the heart of South America stretches a vast tropical grassland dotted with twisted trees and teeming with unusual wildlife.
This immense savanna covers much of central Brazil, sitting between the Amazon rainforest and the country's drier eastern lands.
Its gnarled, fire-adapted vegetation and deep-rooted plants make it one of the world's most biodiverse savanna ecosystems, rich in endemic species.
