Home to giant anteaters, maned wolves, and the headwaters of major rivers, much of it has been converted into soy and cattle farms.
Often called the cradle of the waters and an inverted forest, this threatened biome ranks among the planet's most endangered tropical ecoregions.
In a southern European country famed for classical art and cuisine, the buried remains of an imperial palace lie beneath a modern capital.
The ruins sit in the historic center of Rome, hidden on a hill not far from the great ancient arena of the Flavian amphitheater.
This lavish first-century residence pioneered bold concrete vaults and once shimmered with frescoes, gilding, and a revolving dining room.
Built by the tyrant Nero after the great fire, its octagonal hall and painted grottoes later inspired Renaissance grotesque ornament.
After Nero's fall it was stripped and buried beneath later building works, this UNESCO-area palace lying hidden until rediscovered in the fifteenth century.
Set on the African continent, this walled royal compound sits in the highlands of a landlocked empire famed for ancient Christian traditions.
Found in northern Ethiopia, it is a fortified enclosure of stone palaces, churches and banqueting halls built for emperors.
Raised in the 17th century by Emperor Fasilides, it became the center of imperial power and shows surprising Indian and Portuguese influences.
Crowning the old capital of Gondar, the castle-like complex houses imperial tombs and was sometimes called the Camelot of Africa.
A UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979, this remarkably preserved 17th-century palace city was the seat of Emperor Fasilides and his successors.
In East Asia lies this archaeological zone preserving the remains of a Bronze Age capital from over three thousand years ago.
Located near Anyang in China's Henan province, it marks the last great royal seat of the Shang Dynasty.
Excavations revealed palace foundations, vast royal burials, bronze ritual vessels and the tomb of a famous warrior queen.
Rediscovered around 1899, the site yielded inscribed turtle shells and ox bones used by kings for divination near the Huan River.
This UNESCO World Heritage site holds the earliest known Chinese characters carved on oracle bones, a crucial window into early Chinese civilization.
On a volcanic island in the Atlantic, this old port town lies in an archipelago off the West African coast.
Founded in 1462 within Cape Verde, it became the first European-built settlement in the tropics and a hub of the slave trade.
Ruined colonial buildings survive here, including a roofless cathedral and a hilltop bastion guarding the harbor below.
Near the modern capital Praia on the island of Santiago, it preserves a pillory column where enslaved people were once punished.
Now a UNESCO World Heritage site, this former Portuguese capital blended European, African and Atlantic cultures and was originally known as Ribeira Grande.
In western Europe, this serene monastic complex represents the austere ideals of a famous medieval reforming order.
Tucked into a wooded Burgundy valley in France, it is one of the oldest surviving Cistercian houses.
Founded in 1118 under the influence of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, its Romanesque church, cloister, dormitory and forge survive nearly intact.
Lying near Montbard in the Côte-d'Or, the self-sufficient monastery even ran an early metalworking forge powered by a stream.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this 12th-century abbey is the most complete Cistercian monastery in France, lacking only its refectory.
This location is situated in a country celebrated for its rolling hills and ancient traditions.
You'll find this historical site within a region known for its dramatic coastal scenery and Neolithic monuments.
A large, flat stone slab rests atop a series of smaller upright stones, forming a distinctive tomb structure amidst a rugged, limestone landscape.
Located in the Burren, a unique karst region of Ireland, this portal tomb sits on a windswept hillside overlooking the surrounding valley.
A remarkably preserved Neolithic portal tomb, it stands prominently in the Burren, offering panoramic views and providing a tangible connection to Ireland’s early inhabitants.

medium.name: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites

clues.description: Scattered across a peninsula in East Asia, these clusters of prehistoric stone tombs lie near coasts and low hills.
Spread over three counties in South Korea, they hold one of the world's densest concentrations of megalithic graves.
Hundreds of capstones rest on supporting boulders, marking burials from a bronze-using culture more than two thousand years old.
Found in the southwestern provinces and on a strategic island in the Han River estuary, the tombs come in table and go-board styles.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this trio of locations preserves over a thousand of the country's iconic prehistoric capstone tombs.
On the Balkan Peninsula, this layered ruin overlooks a tranquil lagoon near the Ionian Sea.
Lying in southern Albania across the strait from the Greek island of Corfu, it is a fortified ancient city.
Its stones reveal Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Venetian phases, including a theater, baths and an early Christian baptistery.
Set within a national park near Saranda, the site is guarded by a Venetian castle and walls dating to the 4th century BC.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this once-thriving city linked to the legend of Aeneas preserves a baptistery with stunning mosaic floors.
In East Asia stands this dazzling hilltop fortress, the finest surviving example of its country's feudal castle design.
Located in Japan's Hyogo Prefecture, it is a sprawling complex of more than eighty timber and plaster buildings.
Built atop earlier works and completed in the early 1600s, its mazelike passages and gates were designed to confuse attackers.
Its brilliant white plaster walls earned it the nickname White Heron Castle, soaring over the city that shares its name west of Kobe.
A UNESCO World Heritage site and national treasure, this is the largest and most-visited original castle in the country, never destroyed in war.
On a subtropical Atlantic archipelago belonging to Spain, this reserve protects a misty ancient woodland.
Covering the interior heights of the small island of La Gomera, it preserves a rare type of evergreen cloud forest.
Trade winds bathe its peaks in fog, sustaining a relict laurel forest that once blanketed Mediterranean lands millions of years ago.
Its highest summit, ringed by legend of two doomed lovers, rises above ravines feeding six surrounding municipalities.
Established in 1981 and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986, it shelters Europe's best-preserved laurisilva forest.
In the Middle East lie the ruins of a fortified desert city that twice repelled Roman legions.
Located in northern Iraq, southwest of Mosul, it was a caravan capital flourishing under the Parthian Empire.
Its great circular walls enclosed temples blending Hellenistic and Mesopotamian forms, dedicated to a sun god and other deities.
Roughly 290 kilometers northwest of Baghdad, the columned sanctuaries appeared in the opening scene of the film The Exorcist.
A UNESCO World Heritage site damaged by militants in 2015, it is the richest surviving Parthian-era city, long capital of an Arab kingdom.
In central Europe sits this modest city whose cultural weight far outstrips its size.
Located in the German state of Thuringia, it became a golden-age hub of literature and the arts around 1800.
Home to Goethe and Schiller, its palaces, parks and libraries embody a flowering of German classicism.
It gave its name to the fragile German republic founded here in 1919 and later hosted the first Bauhaus art school.
A UNESCO World Heritage ensemble, this city pairs poets' houses with the nearby Buchenwald memorial, a stark twist of history.
On the grasslands of East Asia lie the earthwork ruins of a once-glorious imperial capital.
Located in Inner Mongolia, China, it was the summer seat of a Mongol dynasty that ruled the largest land empire in history.
Built around 1256 for Kublai Khan, its palaces, walls and canals fused Mongol nomadic life with Chinese court tradition.
Visited by Marco Polo, its fabled pleasure-dome inspired a famous opium-fueled poem by Coleridge centuries later.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this grassy ruin north of Beijing was the first capital of Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty.
In a major East Asian capital lies this royal palace prized for blending architecture with its natural setting.
Found in Seoul, South Korea, it is one of the Five Grand Palaces of the Joseon Dynasty.
Built in 1405 as a detached residence, it became the kings' favorite seat after the main palace burned during war.
Its famed rear garden, the Huwon, hides pavilions and a lotus pond, and it was long paired as the East Palace beside Changgyeonggung.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this is the best-preserved royal palace of its dynasty, celebrated for harmony with the surrounding hills.
In the far north of Europe's largest country stands an all-timber complex on a remote island.
Set on an isle in Lake Onega within the Republic of Karelia, Russia, it gathers historic wooden religious buildings.
Two churches and a bell tower rise here, the larger crowned with twenty-two silvery aspen-shingled cupolas.
Legend says a carpenter built the soaring Transfiguration church using a single axe and not one nail, then threw the tool away.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this open-air collection is the masterpiece of Russian wooden architecture, fenced by a log palisade.

medium.name: Incense Route – Desert Cities in the Negev

clues.description: This location lies within the eastern Mediterranean region, in an arid land at the meeting point of three continents and ancient trade worlds.
You'll find significant geological formations and remnants of ancient settlements scattered within a dry, sun-baked southern landscape of crater valleys here.

An arid country hosts settlements that flourished along a historic spice-trading corridor, featuring fortified towns, trading posts, and elaborate caravanserais built to support the lucrative commerce passing through.
Exploring this dry region reveals sites like Tel Beersheba and ancient settlements near Makhtesh Ramon, showcasing the impact of long-distance trade routes on the landscape and architecture.
Set in a southern desert, this area preserves ruins of fortified caravan towns like Tel Beersheba, positioned along an ancient aromatic-resin trading corridor amid dramatic eroded crater canyons.
In a low-lying European nation famed for water management, this ring of waterways defines a great trading city.
Encircling the old heart of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, it is a planned belt of concentric urban waterways.
Dug during a 17th-century golden age, the semicircular waterways guided expansion and lined the banks with gabled merchant houses.
Spanned by countless bridges and dotted with houseboats, the principal channels bear names like Herengracht and Keizersgracht.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this Canal Belt is the iconic emblem of the Dutch capital, drawing boats past narrow tilting facades.
In East Asia stands a great walled stronghold built to honor a tragically slain royal father.
Encircling the city of Suwon in South Korea, it dates from the late Joseon Dynasty.
Constructed in the 1790s, its nearly six-kilometer wall combined Korean tradition with Eastern and Western military engineering.
Lying about thirty kilometers south of Seoul, it shelters the Haenggung palace built by King Jeongjo for his exiled court.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this fortress is tied to King Jeongjo and his father Prince Sado, who died sealed inside a rice chest.
In central Europe sits this riverside town, a quiet cradle of 20th-century modern design.
Located in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, it lies where the Mulde River joins the Elbe.
When a famous avant-garde art and design school was forced from Weimar, it relocated here in 1925.
Walter Gropius designed its landmark glass-walled school building, and nearby stand the cubic Masters' Houses for its teachers.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this town hosts the most famous surviving Bauhaus building, an icon of functionalist architecture.
In a major East Asian capital stands a solemn shrine devoted to dead kings and queens.
Located in Seoul, South Korea, it is the royal ancestral temple of the Joseon Dynasty.
Its long, austere wooden halls hold spirit tablets of monarchs and consorts, set apart from the city's busier palaces nearby.
Ritual music and dance once performed for departed rulers survive here as a living ceremony recognized worldwide.
A UNESCO World Heritage site, this is the oldest preserved royal Confucian shrine in the country, home to centuries-old memorial rites.

medium.name: Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon, the Depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana Woodblocks

clues.description: This location resides in East Asia, on a peninsula reaching south toward Japan between the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan.
You'll find this remarkable place high within a forested national park, set among mountain slopes as a long-revered religious site.
This mountain temple houses a vast collection of ancient wooden printing blocks containing Buddhist scriptures, a testament to many centuries of careful preservation.

Located in the southern part of a peninsular nation, this temple complex is renowned for its meticulously maintained repository safeguarding the carved scripture blocks, a celebrated national treasure.

A UNESCO World Heritage site, this temple repository protects 81,350 carved printing blocks holding the Buddhist canon, completed in the 14th century and preserved within climate-controlled wooden chambers.
In a southeastern corner of the Korean Peninsula lies a sprawling open-air museum of ancient royal heritage and ruins.
This South Korean district preserves palaces, temples, pagodas, and grass-covered burial mounds from a kingdom that ruled for nearly a thousand years.
It served as the capital of the Silla realm, and its tombs, statues, and stone monuments mark one of Asia's longest-lived dynasties.
Highlights include the Daereungwon mound cluster and Cheomseongdae, often called one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia.
Nicknamed the 'museum without walls,' this UNESCO World Heritage zone was the political and cultural heart of the Silla capital for centuries.

medium.name: Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty

clues.description: This location resides in East Asia, on a mountainous peninsula whose long history was shaped by powerful royal dynasties and Confucian tradition.
It is a significant historical site featuring elaborate burial complexes set within carefully chosen landscapes of hills, forest and flowing water.
This network of regal burial complexes encompasses earthen mounds, stone guardians and ceremonial pavilions spread across numerous sites throughout the peninsula's countryside.
These tombs represent the final resting places of a long-ruling royal house and their families, showcasing intricate stonework and traditional funerary practices rooted in geomancy.
Documented in the early 20th century, these regal burial grounds hold resting places of kings and queens, revealing opulent funerary rituals of the peninsula's last ruling house.
This bustling South Asian metropolis anchors a desert state famous for its maharajas, fortresses, and dazzling palaces.
Capital of India's Rajasthan, it forms one point of the country's celebrated tourist 'Golden Triangle' alongside Delhi and Agra.
Its walled old quarter, washed in a uniform rosy hue since a royal welcome in 1876, earned it a colorful and enduring nickname.
Lying about 270 kilometers southwest of the national capital, it is crowned by the hilltop Amber Fort and the rooftop Jantar Mantar observatory.
Its honeycombed 'Palace of Winds,' the Hawa Mahal, and thriving gemstone and textile bazaars make this 'Pink City' instantly recognizable.
In the reclaimed lowlands of northwestern Europe sits a curious relic of humanity's long struggle against the sea.
Set in the Netherlands' Noordoostpolder, this former island now rises slightly above drained farmland that was once open water.
For centuries its inhabitants clung to a narrow peat ridge, repeatedly battered by floods until the government evacuated them in the 19th century.
Today a museum and preserved church mark its village core, and the old shoreline is still visible where dry polder meets the elevated mound.
When the surrounding sea was pumped dry in the 1940s, this UNESCO World Heritage site became the first symbol of Dutch land reclamation triumph.
Beside a river in northern Central Europe stands one of the mightiest fortified complexes ever raised in red brick.
Set in Poland's Pomerania near the Nogat River, it was begun by a crusading military monastic order in the 13th century.
Expanded dramatically over the 1300s, it grew into three connected castles with vast halls, defensive walls, and a grand church.
Long the seat of the Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, it ranks as the largest castle on earth measured by land area.
This UNESCO-listed Gothic brick stronghold, painstakingly rebuilt after wartime destruction, remains an icon of medieval crusader power and engineering.

medium.name: Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks World Heritage Site

clues.description: This location resides within a country renowned for its expansive wilderness and diverse landscapes.
You'll find this landmark nestled within a mountainous region, characterized by dramatic elevation changes and abundant natural resources.
The area is defined by towering, snow-capped peaks, vibrant turquoise lakes fed by glaciers, and expansive coniferous forests, offering unparalleled outdoor recreation opportunities.

Specifically, this protected area encompasses glacial valleys sculpted by ancient ice, supports a thriving population of wildlife like grizzly bears and elk, and is closely associated with the towns of Banff and Lake Louise.

Set in the highlands of western Canada, this protected reserve showcases the iconic views of Mount Rundle and the Bow River, representing a globally significant example of alpine and subalpine mountain ecosystems.

medium.name: Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region

clues.description: Along a remote coastline of East Asia, scattered islands and villages conceal traces of a faith once banned on pain of death.
Found in a southwestern Japanese prefecture facing the East China Sea, these places mark communities who worshipped in secret for generations.
Stone chapels, concealed shrines, and isolated settlements preserved a banned religion through more than two centuries of brutal national prohibition.
Centered on the Goto islands and villages near a famous port city, the sites include Oura, the church where these believers revealed themselves in 1865.
This UNESCO World Heritage grouping commemorates the underground Christians of southwest Japan, whose covert devotion endured until religious freedom finally returned.

medium.name: lifts on the old Canal du Centre

clues.description: This location resides within the borders of a small, densely populated nation in northwestern Europe known for its waterways and industry.
You'll find this site within a region known for its industrial past and dense networks of busy inland waterways crisscrossing the landscape.
These structures are historic boat elevators, originally part of a vital waterway in the country's former industrial heartland, built to raise loaded vessels between differing water levels.

Located near La Louvière, these four hydraulic boat elevators are remnants of a 19th-century waterway's engineering infrastructure, allowing barges to overcome substantial changes in elevation along the route.
The four historic boat elevators are iconic features of this region's industrial heritage, offering a glimpse into Victorian-era engineering while still raising vessels between the waterway's levels.
On the banks of a great river in northeastern Africa lie the remains of one of antiquity's most powerful capitals.
Set in southern Egypt around the modern town now called Luxor, this ancient metropolis was a center of religion and royal power.
Its sprawling temple precincts honored the sun god, while across the water lay valleys filled with the rock-cut tombs of pharaohs.
Mortuary temples here commemorate rulers like Hatshepsut and Amenhotep III, the latter once fronted by the colossal seated 'Memnon' statues.
The towering columned halls of Karnak and the nearby royal burial valleys make this UNESCO World Heritage site Egypt's greatest open-air monument.
This location resides in a nation renowned for its dramatic coastlines, green hills and ancient history along the windswept edge of the Atlantic.
You'll find this landmark within a region of Northern Ireland characterized by rugged sea cliffs, crashing waves and stunning panoramic ocean views.
This dramatic coastal feature is a unique geological formation consisting of interlocking basalt columns, created by ancient volcanic activity and the slow subsequent cooling of molten rock.
Located in County Antrim, just northeast of the village of Bushmills, this natural wonder presents a remarkable hexagonal stepped rock structure descending into the sea.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, this coastal wonder showcases columnar basalt formed by a 60,000-year-old lava flow, situated near a famous cliffside rope footbridge.
In a semi-arid stretch of Western Asia stands the legacy of an ancient Silk Road oasis ringed by desert.
Located in Iran's southeastern Kerman Province, this fortified settlement once thrived on caravan trade and silk weaving.
Its enormous citadel, the largest adobe structure ever built, was shattered by a devastating earthquake in 2003 and has since been carefully restored.
Built entirely of sun-dried mud brick, the Arg-e citadel rose with watchtowers, a bazaar, and a governor's quarter atop a fortified mound.
This UNESCO World Heritage oasis city showcases over two millennia of mud-brick engineering and ingenious underground qanat irrigation across the desert.
Rising above a city in northern Europe, this soaring Gothic church is among the tallest medieval cathedrals ever completed.
It dominates a French city in the historic Picardy region, perched on a ridge above the Somme River roughly 120 kilometers north of Paris.
Begun in the 13th century, it boasts the largest interior volume of any cathedral in France and an immense vaulted nave.
Its west front bristles with hundreds of carved figures, and a famous weeping-angel sculpture inside draws visitors to its choir.
A UNESCO World Heritage masterpiece of High Gothic art, this seat of a bishop is illuminated at night with reconstructed medieval color projections.
In a far-northern island nation of glaciers and volcanoes lies a rift valley where the earth itself is splitting apart.
This protected reserve sits on a continental boundary, its lava plains and clear lake fed by glacial meltwater filtering through porous rock.
Here visitors walk between the slowly separating North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, peering into deep water-filled fissures.
The dramatic Almannagja gorge cleaves the landscape, and divers explore the crystalline Silfra fissure within this geological frontier.
Located a short drive from Reykjavik, this UNESCO World Heritage park hosted the world's oldest surviving parliament, founded here in the year 930.
High in the mountains of Western Asia lie sacred ruins arranged around a mysterious volcanic spring-fed lake.
Set in northwestern Iran's West Azerbaijan Province near the town of Takab, this remote complex sits among rugged highlands.
It was a principal fire temple and royal sanctuary of the Sasanian empire, later partly rebuilt under Mongol rulers.
Lying roughly midway between Urmia and Hamadan, its remains ring a deep artesian lake once tied to Zoroastrian coronation rites.
Nicknamed the 'Throne of Solomon,' this UNESCO World Heritage site fused Zoroastrian, Sasanian, and later traditions in a singular mountain shrine.
On the southern edge of the Arabian Peninsula stretches a fragrant region that once supplied the ancient world's most coveted aromatic resin.
Found in Oman's southern Dhofar governorate, this area linked desert caravans and Indian Ocean ships in a lucrative incense trade.
Gnarled trees here ooze a prized white resin burned in temples across Rome, Egypt, and beyond for thousands of years.
Its sites include the oasis of Wadi Dawkah, the desert caravan post of Shisr, and the coastal ruins of Al-Baleed near Salalah.
This UNESCO World Heritage grouping preserves the harvesting groves, caravan routes, and ports that powered the legendary incense road of antiquity.
On an island in a large alpine-foothill lake in Central Europe stands an opulent palace that was never quite finished.
Set in Germany's Bavaria within the Chiemsee lake, it lies roughly 60 kilometers southeast of Munich amid forested grounds.
Its eccentric royal patron built it as a deliberate homage to a famous French Sun King's residence, sparing no expense on gilded halls.
A reflecting hall of mirrors and lavish state rooms mimic the grand palace near Paris, though many wings were left incomplete at his death.
Commissioned by the 'fairy-tale king' Ludwig II, this island chateau is a near-replica of Versailles, abandoned when the bankrupt monarch died in 1886.
In a mountainous province of East Asia rises a sacred summit revered for centuries by pilgrims of one major religion.
Located in northern China's Shanxi Province near the city of Taiyuan, it is the foremost of the country's four holy Buddhist mountains.
Its terrain forms five distinct flat-topped summits, ringing a high basin crowded with monasteries built across many dynasties.
More than fifty temples survive here, including some of China's oldest surviving timber halls dating to the Tang dynasty.
Nicknamed the 'Five Terrace Mountain' and a UNESCO World Heritage site, it is venerated as the earthly home of the bodhisattva of wisdom, Manjusri.
In an East Asian nation, this storied region brims with temples, raked gardens, and a deep link to a former imperial capital.
Set in Japan's Kansai area, it served as the country's imperial seat for over a thousand years before the capital moved east.
Vivid vermilion shrine gates, contemplative Zen gardens, and dense bamboo groves define its instantly recognizable cultural landscape.
Its Zen temple Ryoan-ji is famed for a minimalist garden of fifteen rocks set in raked white gravel, framed by autumn maples.
Home to seventeen UNESCO-listed monuments, this old capital region preserves geisha districts, golden pavilions, and centuries of refined court tradition.
In the northern uplands of the British Isles lies an excavated frontier garrison from the days of an ancient Mediterranean empire.
Set in northern England's Northumberland, it guarded the wild frontier just south of the famous wall built by Emperor Hadrian.
Generations of soldiers and civilians lived here, and ongoing digs have revealed barracks, workshops, bathhouses, and a bustling settlement.
Its waterlogged soil preserved hundreds of thin wooden writing tablets, including a soldier's birthday party invitation prized as Britain's oldest handwriting.
These Roman frontier ruins, yielding shoes, letters, and everyday objects across four centuries of occupation, sit among the most revealing archaeological digs in Britain.
Deep in the red heart of an island continent, this colossal stone rises abruptly from flat desert plains.
Located in the Northern Territory's arid center, it is one of the largest single rock formations on Earth.
Sacred to the Anangu Aboriginal people, its sandstone surface glows fiery orange and crimson at sunrise and sunset.
Near the resort town of Yulara and the domes of Kata Tjuta, climbing it was banned out of respect in 2019.
Once called Ayers Rock by colonists, this monolith is the spiritual and visual icon of the country's Red Centre.
Off the warm tropical northeast coast of an island continent stretches the world's largest living structure.
Running along Queensland's shoreline, it spans more than two thousand kilometres of coral and turquoise lagoons.
Built by billions of tiny coral polyps, it shelters turtles, clownfish and is visible even from outer space.
Accessed from Cairns and the Whitsunday Islands, it suffers bleaching events driven by warming seas.
A UNESCO World Heritage marvel, this vast coral system is the planet's most famous underwater wonder.
On a harbour in the southern hemisphere stands a performing arts venue whose roof mimics billowing white sails.
Sitting on Bennelong Point in Australia's largest city, it juts dramatically into a famous blue harbour.
Designed by Danish architect Jorn Utzon, its interlocking concrete shells took fourteen years to complete.
Beside the great steel arch bridge nicknamed the Coathanger, fireworks burst over it every New Year's Eve.
A UNESCO-listed icon completed in 1973, its gleaming tiled vaults host ballet, theatre and symphony performances.
Along a wild southern coastline of an island continent, towering limestone stacks rise from pounding ocean swells.
Found in Victoria within Port Campbell National Park, they line a famous scenic drive built by returned soldiers.
Carved by relentless erosion from soft cliffs, fewer than the namesake number actually remain standing today.
Reached via the Great Ocean Road near Loch Ard Gorge, the formations glow golden at dawn and dusk.
Despite a biblical name suggesting a dozen, only eight of these wave-battered pillars survive after recent collapses.
On the eastern seaboard of an island continent lies a crescent of golden sand synonymous with surf culture.
In a suburb of Australia's largest harbour city, it draws crowds of swimmers, surfers and sunbathers year-round.
Home to one of the world's oldest surf lifesaving clubs, its red-and-yellow flags guard against fierce rips.
A coastal walk leads south to Coogee, while a reality TV show about its lifeguards made it globally famous.
Just east of Sydney's center, this kilometre of sand is the continent's most celebrated urban surf beach.
In the tropical far north of an island continent sprawls a vast wetland teeming with crocodiles and birdlife.
Located in the Northern Territory east of Darwin, it is the country's largest terrestrial national park.
Rock shelters here preserve Aboriginal paintings tens of thousands of years old, among the oldest art on Earth.
Featuring waterfalls like Jim Jim and floodplains that inspired the film Crocodile Dundee, it floods each wet season.
A dual World Heritage site for nature and culture, this monsoonal reserve borders Arnhem Land's sandstone escarpment.
On the humid tropical northeast coast of an island continent lies one of the planet's oldest surviving jungles.
In far north Queensland, this ancient jungle meets the coral sea where two World Heritage areas adjoin.
Estimated at over 180 million years old, it shelters cassowaries, tree kangaroos and rare primitive flowering plants.
North of Cape Tribulation and Mossman Gorge, a river of the same name winds through its dense green canopy.
The continent's largest tropical jungle, it is the only place where such forest meets coral reef along the shore.
Off the eastern coast of an island continent lies the largest sand island in the world, draped in green forest.
Stretching along Queensland's southern coast, it astonishes visitors with rainforest somehow growing on pure sand dunes.
Crystal-clear freshwater lakes perch atop its dunes, and dingoes roam its long beach used as a highway.
Now officially renamed K'gari in honour of the Butchulla people, it is reached by ferry from Hervey Bay.
A World Heritage site since 1992, this 120-kilometre sand mass features the wreck of the SS Maheno on its shore.
On the temperate southern coast of an island continent sits a city famous for its laneways, coffee and trams.
The capital of Victoria, it sprawls around a bay and is often ranked among the world's most liveable cities.
It briefly served as the nation's federal capital and hosts a Grand Slam tennis tournament each January.
Home to the giant cricket ground that bears its name and a famous spring horse race that stops the nation.
Known for changeable weather and a graffiti-filled arts scene, this rival to the harbour metropolis crowns the country's south.
On the sunny west coast of an island continent lies one of the most isolated major cities on Earth.
The capital of Western Australia, it straddles a wide river before reaching long Indian Ocean beaches.
Founded as the Swan River Colony, its wealth has long flowed from the mining boom in the vast interior.
Sprawling Kings Park overlooks its skyline, and the port suburb of Fremantle guards the river's mouth nearby.
Closer to Southeast Asia than to Sydney, this sun-drenched metropolis is the largest city of the continent's western third.
In the dry interior of an island continent stands a granite cliff sculpted into the shape of a breaking surf swell.
Located in the wheatbelt of Western Australia near the small town of Hyden, it curves like a frozen ocean roller.
Around 15 metres high and 110 metres long, vertical streaks of mineral run down its smooth concave face.
Shaped over millions of years by water erosion and weathering, it lies hours inland from the state capital.
A natural granite formation resembling a giant cresting tide, it is the outback's most photographed surf-like cliff.
On a rugged island state south of an island continent rises a jagged alpine peak ringed by glacial lakes.
In Tasmania's cool highlands, it anchors a national park famed for its multi-day wilderness trek, the Overland Track.
Its serrated dolerite summit reflects in mirror-still Dove Lake, often dusted with snow even in summer.
Part of the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area, it shelters wombats, echidnas and the rare Tasmanian devil.
Named for its resemblance to a baby's rocking bed, this craggy peak is the island's most iconic mountain.
On the tropical northeast coast of an island continent lies a beach renowned for its blindingly white silica sand.
Set within Queensland's Whitsunday Islands, it fringes turquoise waters swirling against the Great Barrier Reef.
Its sand is so pure it squeaks underfoot and stays cool, often called the cleanest in the country.
At nearby Hill Inlet, tides swirl sand and sea into shifting marbled patterns photographed by helicopter tours.
A seven-kilometre crescent on Whitsunday Island, this dazzling strand regularly tops lists of the world's best beaches.
In the southeastern highlands of an island continent rises the highest point on the entire landmass.
Rising in the Snowy region of New South Wales, it tops the alpine ranges near the Victorian border.
At 2,228 metres, its rounded summit is reachable by a gentle walk, and snow blankets it each winter.
Named by a Polish explorer after a national hero, it sits within a national park sharing the Snowy River's source.
One of the famed Seven Summits, this modest rounded peak is the loftiest summit on the whole continent.
In the arid red center of an island continent, sheer sandstone walls plunge into a deep desert gorge.
Within the Northern Territory's Watarrka National Park, its 100-metre cliffs glow ochre under the outback sun.
A rim walk circles weathered beehive domes nicknamed the Lost City before descending to a lush palm-filled Garden of Eden.
Lying between Alice Springs and the great red monolith of Uluru, it ranks among the Red Centre's great chasms.
Carved into the George Gill Range, this dramatic ravine is one of the outback's most spectacular sandstone chasms.
On the steamy tropical top edge of an island continent sits its only major city in true monsoon climate.
The capital of the Northern Territory, it serves as the gateway to wetland parks and the Tip End wilderness.
Heavily bombed by Japanese aircraft in 1942 and flattened by Cyclone Tracy in 1974, it has been rebuilt twice.
Famed for vibrant night markets at Mindil Beach, it lies closer to Indonesia than to most of its own nation.
Named after the famous naturalist, this northernmost capital is the country's gateway to Asia and Kakadu.
On the tropical northeast coast of an island continent lies a city that thrives on reef and rainforest tourism.
In far north Queensland, it is the launching point for boats heading out to the Great Barrier Reef.
A scenic railway and cableway climb to the rainforest village of Kuranda above its cane-fields and mangroves.
Its waterfront esplanade lagoon substitutes for swimming beaches plagued by stingers and saltwater crocodiles.
Gateway to both the World Heritage reef and the Daintree, this humid hub is the tourism capital of the tropical north.
On the dry west coast of an island continent, thousands of eerie limestone spires jut from yellow sand.
Within Western Australia's Nambung National Park, this strange field lies a few hours north of the state capital, Perth.
Formed from ancient seashells and weathered over millennia, some columns stand several metres tall like petrified figures.
A loop drive winds among them, and they appear almost lunar under moonlight near the coastal town of Cervantes.
A surreal forest of stone needles in the sand, this desert is the western coast's most otherworldly landscape.
Off the southern coast of an island continent lies a small lake famous for its astonishing bubblegum-pink water.
On Middle Island in Western Australia's Recherche Archipelago, it sits near the port town of Esperance.
Its vivid rose colour, likely caused by salt-loving algae and bacteria, stays pink even when bottled in a glass.
A thin strip of eucalyptus separates its candy-coloured surface from the deep blue Southern Ocean alongside.
Best seen from the air, this permanently pink saltwater lake is one of the world's most surreal coloured lakes.
In the remote northwest of an island continent rise hundreds of striped beehive-shaped sandstone domes.
Hidden in Western Australia's Kimberley region, this maze of towers was largely unknown to outsiders until the 1980s.
Alternating orange and grey-black bands of silica and cyanobacteria give the rounded hills their tiger-stripe pattern.
Within Purnululu National Park, gorges like Cathedral and Echidna cut deep into the banded rock formations.
A World Heritage labyrinth of striped domes, this range is the Kimberley's most spectacular geological wonder.
On the easternmost edge of an island continent sits a laid-back coastal town beloved by surfers and backpackers.
In northern New South Wales, it marks the most easterly point of the whole Australian mainland at Cape headland.
A white lighthouse crowns its cliff, where whales pass offshore and the day's first sunrise touches the country.
Famed for its alternative bohemian vibe, yoga retreats and music festivals, it draws celebrities to its hinterland.
Named after a poet's grandfather by Captain Cook, this bohemian beach town is the continent's most easterly settlement.
In the scorching desert interior of an island continent lies a mining town where most residents live underground.
In the South Australian outback along the highway to the Red Centre, it endures blistering summer heat.
It supplies a large share of the world's opals, and dugout homes, churches and hotels burrow into the earth to stay cool.
Its lunar landscape of mullock heaps has stood in for alien worlds in films like Mad Max and Pitch Black.
Nicknamed the opal capital of the world, this subterranean settlement is the outback's most unusual underground town.
On the westernmost coast of an island continent lies a vast bay of seagrass meadows and turquoise inlets.
In Western Australia, it shelters the world's largest seagrass beds and a famous population of friendly dolphins.
At Hamelin Pool sit ancient living stromatolites, among Earth's oldest life forms still building rocky mounds today.
At Monkey Mia, wild dolphins swim ashore to be fed, while dugongs graze the shallows by the dazzling Shell Beach.
A World Heritage site at the continent's most westerly point, this bay is renowned for dolphins and primordial microbes.
Hugging the remote northwest coast of an island continent lies a fringing coral reef accessible straight from the beach.
In Western Australia near the Cape Range, it is far less crowded than the great reef on the opposite eastern coast.
Each autumn the world's largest fish, the gentle whale shark, gathers here to feed on coral spawn.
Snorkellers wade from the shore at Coral Bay and Exmouth to swim among manta rays and turtles.
A World Heritage fringing reef famous for whale shark encounters, it is the western coast's premier underwater playground.
At the geographic heart of an island continent sits a remote desert town surrounded by ancient red ranges.
In the Northern Territory's Red Centre, it is the main hub for the surrounding outback and Aboriginal communities.
Born as a telegraph repeater station, it gave rise to the Royal Flying Doctor Service and the School of the Air.
Nestled in a gap of the MacDonnell Ranges, it lies hundreds of kilometres from the nearest large city in any direction.
The unofficial capital of the outback, this isolated town is the gateway to Uluru and the continent's red interior.
Perched high in the Andes of western South America, this storied highland metropolis sits well above three thousand metres in elevation.
Once the dazzling capital of the Inca Empire, it lies in the southern highlands of Peru, in a valley ringed by terraced peaks.
Spanish colonial churches rise atop precise Inca stonework, and its name in Quechua is said to mean the navel of the world.
Travelers use it as the gateway to the Sacred Valley and the famous lost citadel reached by rail and the Inca Trail.
Its Plaza de Armas, Qorikancha sun temple foundations, and Sacsayhuamán fortress make it the historic heart of the former empire.
Sitting almost exactly on the equator in the northern Andes, this capital is one of the highest seats of government on Earth.
It serves as the capital of Ecuador, cradled in a long Andean valley beneath an active volcano named Pichincha.
Its sprawling colonial old town, one of the first World Heritage Sites ever listed, brims with gilded baroque churches.
A nearby monument marks the line of zero latitude, while a teleférico climbs the slopes overlooking the city center.
Locals call its historic core the Relicario de América, and La Compañía glitters with tons of gold leaf inside.
Spilling down a dramatic canyon in the high Andes, this South American seat of government is often called the world's highest.
Though not the constitutional capital, it is Bolivia's administrative heart, sprawling beneath the towering peak of Illimani.
Brick houses climb steep slopes up to the sister city of El Alto, set on the cold Altiplano plateau.
A vast network of cable cars known as Mi Teleférico glides above its bowl-shaped basin as urban public transit.
The eerie Valle de la Luna and a bustling Witches' Market selling llama foetuses sit within this dizzying metropolis.
On the warm Caribbean coast of northern South America, this walled port has long guarded ships against pirates and rivals.
A jewel of Colombia's coastline, its colonial quarter is enclosed by massive stone ramparts beside a tropical sea.
Spanish galleons once loaded silver here, defended by the imposing San Felipe de Barajas fortress on a hill.
Its candy-colored balconies, the Clock Tower gate, and the bohemian Getsemaní district draw visitors year round.
The novelist Gabriel García Márquez immortalized this Heroic City, famed for love in the time of cholera.
In a sunny valley of the southern Andes, this South American city is built largely from pale volcanic stone.
Peru's second-largest urban center, it lies beneath the snow-capped cone of the volcano El Misti.
Its luminous architecture of white sillar rock earns it a nickname referencing that bright building material.
The vast, candy-toned Santa Catalina Monastery forms a walled city within the city near its grand cathedral.
Known as the White City, it is the gateway to the deep Colca Canyon where Andean condors soar.
Overlooking a famous Andean city in South America, this ancient citadel features colossal stones fitted without mortar.
Built by the Inca above their capital in southern Peru, its zigzag walls crown a hill at high altitude.
Some of its limestone blocks weigh over a hundred tonnes yet join so tightly a blade cannot slip between them.
Each June the Inti Raymi sun festival reenacts imperial ceremonies on the great esplanade below the ramparts.
Its zigzag terraces are thought to form the head of a puma whose body is the city of Cusco itself.
On the green eastern slopes of the Andes in South America, this small resort town clings to a steep river gorge.
Set in central Ecuador where the highlands tumble toward the Amazon, it sits below the active Tungurahua volcano.
Famed for its thermal hot springs, it has become a magnet for waterfall hikes and adventure sports.
A giant garden swing called the Swing at the End of the World launches over a misty canyon on a cliffside.
Its full name honors the holy waters of the Virgin, drawing pilgrims and rafters along the Pastaza River.
On a windswept peninsula of the high Andean plateau in South America, ancient cylindrical towers rise beside still water.
This burial ground in southern Peru overlooks the reedy Lake Umayo, near the larger shores of Lake Titicaca.
The pre-Inca Colla people built tall stone funerary towers here to entomb nobles and their families.
These tapering tombs, called chullpas, often widen toward the top and face the rising sun across the altiplano.
Reached from the city of Puno, its lakeside necropolis of stone cylinders is among the finest of its kind.
On the cold, treeless plateau of the central Andes in South America, monumental ruins predate the Inca by centuries.
Lying in western Bolivia near the southern end of Lake Titicaca, it was once a vast ceremonial capital.
Its Akapana pyramid and sunken temple reflect a powerful pre-Columbian state that flourished around a thousand years ago.
A carved monolithic doorway known as the Gate of the Sun stands among andesite blocks fitted with metal clamps.
Stone faces stud the walls of its Kalasasaya platform, marking one of the highest urban centers of the ancient Americas.
Cutting through the southern Andes of South America, this gorge ranks among the deepest on the planet.
Located in the Arequipa region of Peru, it plunges far deeper than the better-known Colca to its southeast.
Its floor lies more than three thousand metres below the surrounding peaks, carved by a river of the same name.
Terraced villages, hot springs, and the Sipia waterfall dot its near-vertical walls in a remote highland reserve.
Often cited as roughly twice the depth of Arizona's Grand Canyon, this abyss is a favorite of extreme kayakers.
Rising as a glacier-clad giant in the equatorial Andes of South America, this dormant volcano dominates its skyline.
The highest summit in Ecuador, it towers over the central highlands within its own national wildlife reserve.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, its peak is the point on the surface farthest from the planet's center.
Herds of vicuña graze its lower slopes, and the city of Riobamba sits in its broad volcanic shadow.
Often called the closest point to the sun, its summit beats Everest in distance from the centre of the globe.
In the green highlands of northwestern South America, this lakeside town is famed for vividly painted houses.
A short drive east of Medellín in Colombia's Antioquia department, it sits beside a sprawling reservoir.
Every building wears colorful relief panels called zócalos depicting daily life, animals, and crafts along its streets.
A giant granite monolith nearby is climbed by more than seven hundred zigzagging steps for sweeping water views.
That towering rock, El Peñón, looms over its candy-colored lanes, making it one of the country's most photographed towns.
In the northern Andes of South America, this highland town is renowned for one of the continent's great markets.
Sitting in the Imbabura province of Ecuador, it lies among volcanoes north of the capital, Quito.
Its indigenous people are famed weavers and traders, selling textiles and crafts known across the Americas.
The bustling Plaza de los Ponchos fills each Saturday with woven blankets, alpaca goods, and Andean instruments.
Nearby Cuicocha crater lake and the Peguche waterfall frame this textile hub of the Otavaleño people.
High on a forested Andean ridge in South America, a massive stone fortress predates and rivals more famous ruins.
Hidden in the cloud forests of northern Peru's Amazonas region, it was raised by the Chachapoya people.
Its towering perimeter walls, up to twenty metres tall, enclose hundreds of round stone dwellings.
Built by the so-called Warriors of the Clouds, it long resisted Inca expansion from its mountaintop perch.
Reached by a cable car above the Utcubamba valley, it is dubbed the Machu Picchu of the north.
On the shore of a vast high-altitude lake in the central Andes, this pilgrimage town draws devout visitors.
Set in western Bolivia on the great inland sea shared with Peru, it sits at over three thousand metres.
Its whitewashed Moorish-style basilica houses a revered dark statue of the Virgin, patroness of the nation.
Boats leave its harbor for the sacred Isla del Sol, the mythic birthplace of the Inca dynasty.
Drivers bring cars to be blessed and adorned with flowers here, sharing its name with a famed Rio beach.
On a hillside in the Andes of South America, thousands of shallow terraced ponds shimmer white against red earth.
Set in the Sacred Valley of southern Peru near Cusco, these pools have been worked since pre-Inca times.
A briny spring feeds a maze of small evaporation pans that local families have harvested for many centuries.
As water evaporates in the mountain sun, crystallizing pink and white deposits are scraped by hand from each pan.
Cascading down the slope above the Urubamba River, these famous mineral pans near a small Andean town make a dazzling sight.
In the Andean highlands of northern South America, this colonial town centers on one of the continent's largest plazas.
Located in Colombia's Boyacá department, it preserves whitewashed houses and cobbled streets from the Spanish era.
Its enormous stone-paved main square, unusually empty of a central fountain, is among the biggest in the Americas.
Surrounding desert hills hold marine fossils and a full kronosaurus skeleton from when the area lay underwater.
Declared a national monument, its perfectly preserved sixteenth-century streetscape often stands in for period films.
A scenic neighborhood viewpoint in a southern Andean city of South America frames a snowy volcano through stone arches.
Found in Arequipa, Peru, this traditional district is built from the same pale volcanic rock as the wider White City.
Its famous mirador consists of carved sillar archways inscribed with verses praising the region's beauty.
Through the arches visitors photograph the perfect cone of El Misti rising beyond the rooftops.
