Salt flats, sand dunes, and eroded badlands bake here; Badwater Basin sinks 282 feet below sea level.
The planet's highest reliably recorded air temperature, 134 degrees Fahrenheit, was measured at its Furnace Creek in 1913.
Its ominous name, given by lost gold-rush pioneers, marks the largest protected reserve in the contiguous states, a furnace of extremes.
In Southeast Asia, this celebrated coastal wonder draws cruise boats threading among thousands of forested islets rising from emerald water.
Located in the Gulf of Tonkin in northeastern Vietnam, it is a UNESCO World Heritage seascape of dramatic karst pillars.
Limestone towers, hidden grottoes, floating fishing villages, and arching sea caves define this drowned landscape carved over millions of years.
Reached easily from Hanoi, its name in Vietnamese means roughly 'descending dragon', tied to a legend of beasts spitting jewels into the sea.
Junk boats with crimson sails glide past Ti Top Island here, the most photographed marine seascape in all of Vietnam.
On a Southeast Asian coast, this small riverside town is famous for lantern-lit evenings and superb tailors who stitch suits overnight.
Set in central Vietnam near Da Nang, it was a thriving trading port linking Chinese, Japanese, and European merchants for centuries.
Its preserved old quarter holds a Japanese covered bridge, ochre merchant houses, and Chinese assembly halls along narrow lanes.
Each full moon the town extinguishes electric light, releasing glowing paper lanterns onto the Thu Bon River.
A UNESCO-listed yellow-walled town, it sits just south of the ruins of My Son and is renowned across the country for silk lanterns.
This historic Southeast Asian city served as an imperial capital, leaving behind moated palaces and royal mausoleums.
Sitting on the Perfume River in central Vietnam, it was the seat of the Nguyen dynasty until the mid-twentieth century.
A vast walled citadel, the Forbidden Purple City, and elaborate emperors' tombs scattered in the hills define its grandeur.
Heavily fought over during the 1968 Tet Offensive, it lies between Da Nang and the former demilitarized zone.
Famed for its refined royal cuisine and the Thien Mu Pagoda, this is the old dragon-throne capital of the unified nation.
In maritime Southeast Asia stands the world's largest Buddhist temple, a colossal stepped pyramid of dark volcanic stone.
Built in the ninth century on the island of Java in Indonesia, it sits amid rice fields ringed by volcanoes.
Pilgrims climb nine stacked platforms past hundreds of relief panels and bell-shaped stupas containing seated Buddha figures.
Near Yogyakarta and overlooked by Mount Merapi, it was rediscovered under jungle and ash before colonial-era restoration.
Its summit holds dozens of latticed stone bells around a central dome, the most visited monument in the whole archipelago.
In Southeast Asia, this active volcano is famous for sunrise crowds peering across a smoking crater amid a fog-filled sea of sand.
Located in East Java, Indonesia, it sits within a vast caldera near the taller peak of Semeru.
Visitors cross a grey volcanic plain on horseback, then climb steps to a constantly steaming summit rim.
Home to the Tengger people, who hold the Yadnya Kasada festival tossing offerings into its crater.
Photographed at dawn from Penanjakan viewpoint, this perpetually fuming cone is the most iconic volcano on the island.
This Southeast Asian hill town is renowned as an arts and yoga retreat surrounded by emerald terraced paddies.
In the uplands of Bali, Indonesia, it became famous as a centre of painting, dance, and woodcarving.
A cheeky troop of long-tailed macaques inhabits its forested sacred sanctuary among mossy temples and banyan trees.
Featured in the memoir and film 'Eat Pray Love', it lies inland from Denpasar amid the Tegallalang rice terraces.
Known for the Monkey Forest and nightly Legong dance performances, it is the cultural heart of the Island of the Gods.
This Southeast Asian island is famous worldwide as the wild home of the planet's largest living lizard.
Part of an Indonesian national park in the Lesser Sunda chain, it features savannah hills and pink-tinged beaches.
Rangers escort visitors across dry scrubland to observe venomous reptiles that can grow three metres long.
Reached by boat from Labuan Bajo on Flores, its surrounding reefs draw divers to vivid coral gardens.
The fearsome 'dragon' that bears this island's name patrols here, found nowhere else on Earth but this small group of islands.
In a Southeast Asian capital, this dazzling royal complex glitters with gilded spires and mirror-mosaic walls.
Built in the eighteenth century beside the Chao Phraya River, it was the official residence of Thailand's kings.
Within its walls stands a revered chapel housing a small jade Buddha dressed in seasonal golden robes.
Mythical guardian statues and a model of Angkor Wat fill its courtyards in the heart of Bangkok.
Home to the Emerald Buddha temple, it is the most visited monument in the entire kingdom and demands modest dress.
This Southeast Asian ruined city was once a glittering royal capital that European traders compared to the great cities of the world.
Sitting on an island between rivers in central Thailand, it flourished for four centuries before being sacked in 1767.
Crumbling brick prangs, headless Buddhas, and a famous stone face entwined in tree roots fill its temple park.
A short trip north of Bangkok, it gave its name to the kingdom that preceded the modern Thai state.
A UNESCO World Heritage former capital, its most photographed image is a serene sandstone Buddha head cradled by banyan roots.
This Southeast Asian city is a beloved mountain hub known for temples, night bazaars, and elephant sanctuaries.
Capital of an old northern kingdom in Thailand, it sits in a valley ringed by forested hills.
A square moat and crumbling walls enclose its old town, packed with golden-spired Lanna temples.
A gilded hilltop temple, Doi Suthep, watches over it, and crowds release floating lanterns here during Yi Peng.
The 'Rose of the North' and former Lanna capital, it draws backpackers and digital nomads to the country's northern highlands.
This Southeast Asian island group is famed for turquoise lagoons enclosed by towering limestone cliffs and white sand.
Lying in the Andaman Sea off southern Thailand, they are reached by ferry from Phuket and Krabi.
Long-tail boats ferry snorkelers into a cliff-ringed bay made world-famous by a Leonardo DiCaprio film.
The smaller uninhabited isle hosts Maya Bay, while the larger has a bustling village rebuilt after the 2004 tsunami.
Setting for 'The Beach', these dramatic karst islands are among the most photographed tropical escapes in the entire kingdom.
This Southeast Asian highland lake is famous for fishermen who balance on one leg and row with the other.
Sitting in the Shan hills of Myanmar, it is dotted with stilted villages and floating tomato gardens.
The Intha people propel flat boats with a unique leg-rowing technique while casting cone-shaped nets.
Markets rotate among lakeside towns, and a temple here holds five gilded Buddha images blurred by gold leaf.
Renowned for its leg-rowing fishermen and floating gardens, it is the most celebrated freshwater lake in the country.
This Southeast Asian walled royal city is famed for stone towers carved with enormous serene smiling faces.
Built in the late twelfth century in northern Cambodia, it was the last great capital of the Khmer Empire.
Its central temple, the Bayon, bristles with over two hundred giant faces gazing in every direction.
Entered through gates topped with four-faced towers, it lies just north of the more famous moated temple of the same region.
Near Siem Reap and a celebrated nearby temple complex, this 'great city' of smiling stone faces was once among the largest cities on Earth.
This Southeast Asian lake is remarkable for a river that reverses direction with the seasons, swelling it enormously.
The largest freshwater body in Cambodia, it forms the beating heart of the lower Mekong basin.
Floating villages, stilted houses, and fish farms cluster on its surface, supporting millions who depend on its catch.
When monsoon rains push the Mekong backward, the lake can quintuple in size, flooding surrounding forests.
Reached from Siem Reap, this great pulsing lake is Southeast Asia's largest, feeding the nation with its astonishing fish harvest.
This Southeast Asian riverside town is famed for saffron-robed monks collecting alms along its streets at dawn.
A former royal capital of Laos, it sits where the Nam Khan meets the Mekong amid forested mountains.
Gilded temples, French colonial shophouses, and a hilltop shrine reached by hundreds of steps fill its peninsula.
Nearby cascade the turquoise Kuang Si waterfalls, and monks descend daily for the silent morning offering of sticky rice.
A UNESCO World Heritage town blending Buddhist and colonial architecture, it is the most beloved heritage gem of the landlocked nation.
This Southeast Asian region is a vast watery maze of channels, paddies, and orchards nicknamed the 'rice bowl' of its nation.
Where a mighty river splinters into the sea in southern Vietnam, fertile silt feeds endless green fields.
Vendors paddle laden sampans through bustling floating markets like Cai Rang near the hub city of Can Tho.
Coconut groves, fruit orchards, and fish farms line the labyrinth of waterways south of Ho Chi Minh City.
Fed by a river that crosses six countries, this fertile southern lowland is the most productive farming region in the land.
On the southern edge of the Sahara in West Africa, this fabled city became a byword for the remotest, most far-flung place imaginable.
Set in northern Mali near the great bend of a famous river, it once thrived as a hub of trans-Saharan caravan trade in gold and salt.
Its medieval scholars filled libraries with manuscripts, and its mud-brick mosques made it a renowned center of Islamic learning.
The Djinguereber and Sankore mosques rise here, sculpted from earth and timber on the desert's frontier near the Niger River.
English speakers invoke its name as shorthand for the end of the earth, a place so distant it seems almost mythical.
In the inland delta of West Africa stands a town celebrated for the world's largest building made entirely of sun-dried earth.
Located in central Mali on a flood-prone island, it has been a market and Islamic study center for over a thousand years.
Each spring the community gathers to replaster its towering mosque by hand, repairing damage from the rains.
Its Great Mosque, bristling with palm-wood beams and conical towers, anchors a lively Monday market in this Niger delta settlement.
The adobe sanctuary here is often called the finest example of Sudano-Sahelian architecture on the entire continent.
This rapidly growing West African capital straddles a great river and is one of the fastest-expanding cities on the continent.
It serves as the political and cultural heart of Mali, sprawling along both banks of the Niger River.
Famous for vibrant music, its clubs and griots helped launch internationally acclaimed desert-blues and kora performers.
The Hippodrome district, the National Museum, and bridges over the river link the city's busy left and right banks.
Its name is said to mean 'crocodile river,' and three crocodiles feature on the emblem of this Malian metropolis.
Deep in the forest belt of West Africa lies a bustling inland city long regarded as a proud cultural capital.
It is the historic seat of the Ashanti kingdom in central Ghana, ruled from a palace by a revered traditional monarch.
The Golden Stool, symbol of the nation's soul, belongs to its royal court, surrounded by goldsmithing and kente weaving.
Nicknamed the 'Garden City,' it hosts the vast Kejetia market, one of the largest open-air bazaars in West Africa.
As the Asantehene's capital, it is the spiritual heartland of Ashanti gold, drums, and elaborate adinkra symbolism.
Sprawling across a West African nation is an immense man-made reservoir, among the largest such surface areas on Earth.
Created in the 1960s by damming a major river in Ghana, it submerged vast lands and displaced tens of thousands.
The Akosombo Dam at its southern end generates much of the country's electricity and supplies neighboring states.
Long ferries and fishing canoes ply its waters, while drowned forests below the surface still snag nets near Yeji.
By surface area it ranks as the world's largest artificial lake, named for the river whose flow it tamed.
This sun-baked West African capital fronts the Gulf of Guinea and buzzes as a regional commercial and diplomatic hub.
It is the largest city and seat of government of Ghana, sprawling along the Atlantic coastline.
Independence Square and the Black Star Gate commemorate the nation's break from colonial rule in 1957.
The Kwame Nkrumah Mausoleum, Jamestown lighthouse, and bustling Makola Market define its energetic seafront districts.
It hosted the continent's first sub-Saharan independence celebration, with the iconic Black Star arch dominating its parade ground.
Built across islands and lagoons on a West African coast, this is among the most populous urban areas on Earth.
Once the capital of Nigeria, it remains the country's economic powerhouse and a magnet for migrants nationwide.
Its film and music scenes power Nollywood and Afrobeats, exporting culture far beyond the continent.
Victoria Island, the Third Mainland Bridge, and the affluent Ikoyi district crowd its sprawling, traffic-choked metropolis.
Often dubbed the megacity that never sleeps, it anchors a conurbation of tens of millions on the Bight of Benin.
On the dry savanna of West Africa lies one of the continent's oldest continuously inhabited commercial centers.
This northern Nigerian city was a key terminus of trans-Saharan caravans crossing toward the Mediterranean.
Ancient earthen walls once ringed it, and its indigo dye pits have colored cloth for over five centuries.
The Kurmi Market, the Emir's palace, and the Gidan Makama Museum recall its Hausa-Fulani heritage and emirate.
Famed as the leather and dye-pit city, its Hausa traders made it the great entrepôt of the region's groundnut trade.
Perched on the westernmost tip of mainland Africa, this Atlantic capital juts toward the Americas on a rocky peninsula.
It is the seat of government of Senegal and a major port at the crossroads of European, African, and American shipping.
A towering bronze monument of a family figure overlooks the city, among the tallest statues on the continent.
The famous off-road rally once finished here, on the Cap-Vert peninsula opposite the historic Gorée slave island.
Long the endpoint of a legendary motorsport raid from France, it sits at the African mainland's most westerly point.
On a West African coast lies a shallow body of water famous for an astonishing color that shifts with the light.
Found near Senegal's capital, it is separated from the Atlantic by only a narrow strip of dunes.
Salt-loving microorganisms tint its hypersaline waters a vivid strawberry hue, especially under the dry-season sun.
Workers wade in with canoes to harvest mounds of salt by hand near the village just northeast of Dakar.
Known in French as the 'Pink Lake,' its rosy waters and salt so dense bathers float effortlessly draw crowds of visitors.
Sitting where a great river meets the Atlantic in West Africa, this island city wears faded colonial elegance.
It was the first French settlement and former capital of both Senegal and a wider colonial federation.
Pastel two-story houses with wrought-iron balconies line its grid, linked to the mainland by the long Faidherbe Bridge.
An annual jazz festival fills its narrow streets, near the mouth of the Senegal River and the Langue de Barbarie.
Nicknamed the 'Venice of Africa,' its island core is a celebrated heritage town of crumbling French-colonial charm.
On the Atlantic coast of West Africa lies a holy town that swells to millions of pilgrims for one yearly gathering.
Located inland from Senegal's capital, it is the spiritual center of a major Sufi Muslim brotherhood.
Founded in the late 19th century by a revered religious leader, it functions almost as a city-state run by its caliph.
A vast green-and-white mosque dominates the town, drawing the enormous Grand Magal pilgrimage each year.
Home of the Mouride brotherhood and its founder's shrine, it hosts one of Africa's largest annual religious pilgrimages.
On a humid West African coast sits a small town steeped in spirituality and a tragic maritime past.
In southern Benin, it was a notorious departure port for enslaved Africans bound across the Atlantic.
A sandy avenue runs from the old slave-auction square to the shore, ending at a memorial arch on the beach.
Widely regarded as the cradle of Vodun, it hosts a major annual festival celebrating that traditional religion.
Its 'Route of Slaves' ends at the Door of No Return, and pythons are venerated in its famous temple downtown.
This humid West African port is the largest city and economic engine of a small coastal francophone nation.
Though not the official capital of Benin, it hosts most government offices, the main airport, and the country's chief seaport.
Motorbike taxis called zémidjans swarm its boulevards, weaving through markets between a lagoon and the Atlantic.
Its sprawling Dantokpa Market ranks among the biggest open-air markets in the region, near the Nokoué lagoon.
The de facto capital on the Bight of Benin, it lies just west of Nigeria and is famed for its swarming moped traffic.
Inland in a small West African country lie the earthen ruins of palaces built by a once-feared warrior kingdom.
This town in central Benin was the capital of the powerful Dahomey kingdom for over two centuries.
Twelve successive kings raised mud-walled compounds here, some decorated with bas-reliefs and, by legend, human blood.
Its royal palaces, now a museum and World Heritage Site, recall the famed all-female Dahomey Amazon regiments.
The seat of the Dahomey monarchs, its sprawling royal compounds are the chief surviving relic of that slave-trading empire.
A vast capital city sits on the southern South American coast, beside a famously wide muddy estuary opening to the Atlantic.
Argentina's largest metropolis blends European architecture with intensely local culture, its residents proudly called porteños of the port.
Birthplace of a passionate partnered dance, it cradles colorful immigrant neighborhoods, grand cafes, and an enormous central avenue claimed as the world's widest.
Visitors photograph the painted houses of La Boca, the pink presidential palace on Plaza de Mayo, and the elaborate Recoleta cemetery tombs.
Eva Perón addressed crowds from its government house balcony, and football devotion divides loyalties between River Plate and Boca Juniors here.
Deep in southern South American wilderness, jagged granite spires rise above turquoise glacial lakes and windswept golden grasslands.
This Chilean Patagonian reserve draws trekkers from across the globe seeking its dramatic mountain skyline and roaming guanaco herds.
Famous multi-day circuits like the W and O loops pass hanging glaciers, milky rivers, and steep granite walls sculpted by ice.
Three soaring rock towers give the park its name, while the horned Cuernos massif looms over glacier-fed Lake Pehoé.
Often crowned among the planet's most beautiful natural wonders, fierce Patagonian gales batter hikers chasing pink dawn light on the peaks.
On a subtropical South American border, a colossal curtain of waterfalls thunders through dense green rainforest teeming with toucans.
Straddling Argentina and Brazil, this system of hundreds of cascades dwarfs Niagara in width and sheer roaring spectacle.
Boardwalks carry visitors above and below the spray while coatis prowl the trails of the surrounding national parks.
Its most dramatic chasm, the Devil's Throat, swallows the river in a thundering misty horseshoe straddling the international frontier.
Eleanor Roosevelt reportedly gasped 'poor Niagara,' and the falls starred in the film The Mission as a Guaraní homeland.
In far southern South America, a vast wall of blue ice advances slowly toward a lake, occasionally cracking with cannon-like roars.
This Argentine Patagonian ice tongue flows from a huge continental ice field within Los Glaciares National Park.
Unusually, it remains stable rather than retreating, periodically damming an arm of Lake Argentino before the ice bridge spectacularly collapses.
Tourists walk steel boardwalks facing its towering front near El Calafate, watching house-sized chunks calve into the milky water.
Guides strap crampons on visitors for 'ice trekking' across crevasses, sometimes ending with whisky chilled by ancient glacial fragments.
At the very bottom of South America, a small port city huddles between snowy peaks and a frigid channel.
This Argentine town on the Tierra del Fuego archipelago markets itself as a gateway to the frozen continent south.
Cruise ships bound for Antarctica depart its harbor, and a scenic railway recalls the prison whose convicts once built the line.
Sitting on the Beagle Channel, it neighbors a national park and bills itself the southernmost city in the world.
Signs proclaim it the 'End of the World,' and a famous postcard lighthouse marks waters Darwin once charted nearby.
Along South America's Pacific edge, an immense rust-colored wasteland stretches between the Andes and the ocean under blistering sun.
This northern Chilean expanse ranks among the driest places on Earth, where some weather stations have never recorded rainfall.
Salt flats, steaming geysers, and Mars-like valleys make it a film stand-in for other planets and a copper-mining heartland.
Near the oasis town of San Pedro, observatories exploit the crystalline skies, including the giant ALMA radio telescope array.
Its Valley of the Moon and rare flowering 'desierto florido' blooms draw stargazers to perhaps the planet's clearest night skies.
On the Pacific coast of South America, a colorful port tumbles down steep hillsides above a busy working harbor.
This bohemian Chilean city, near the capital Santiago, is famed for street art splashed across its labyrinth of hills.
Once a vital stop for ships rounding Cape Horn, its fortunes faded after the Panama Canal opened, leaving faded grandeur.
Antique funicular elevators climb between alleys, and the poet Pablo Neruda kept a beloved quirky house called La Sebastiana here.
Nicknamed the 'Jewel of the Pacific,' its UNESCO-listed historic quarter overflows with murals, cafes, and tangled hilltop staircases.
In the South American lake country, an alpine-styled resort town nestles beside deep blue water ringed by forested mountains.
This Argentine Patagonian destination sits within Nahuel Huapi National Park, a magnet for skiers and summer hikers alike.
Swiss and German settlers gave it chalets and a famous chocolate industry, lending the streets a distinctly Alpine flavor.
Boats cross Nahuel Huapi Lake to the Llao Llao hotel and the Andean crossing toward Chile through Puerto Blest.
Argentines flock to its 'Cerro Catedral' slopes, and graduating students traditionally celebrate trips devouring its renowned artisanal chocolate.
On a South American river-mouth shore, a tiny old town of cobbled lanes faces a distant capital across the water.
This Uruguayan settlement on the Río de la Plata sits directly opposite Buenos Aires, a short ferry ride away.
Founded by Portugal in 1680, it changed hands repeatedly between Iberian crowns, leaving a rare blend of colonial street plans.
Its UNESCO-listed Barrio Histórico boasts a stout lighthouse, the Portón de Campo gate, and the lantern-lit Calle de los Suspiros.
Vintage cars sit parked among bougainvillea, while day-trippers from Argentina wander what is Uruguay's oldest European-founded town.
Where a South American coastline meets the Atlantic, a glittering peninsula of high-rise towers and beaches lures summer crowds.
This Uruguayan resort is the playground of wealthy Argentines and Brazilians escaping the southern winter for January sun.
A peninsula separates calm bay waters from rougher ocean surf, and a sculptural bridge undulates over a nearby lagoon.
Its most photographed sight is 'La Mano,' giant concrete fingers emerging from the sand on Playa Brava.
Often dubbed the 'Monaco of the South,' its casinos, yacht harbor, and Casapueblo villa define glamorous regional beach holidays.
On a South American estuary shore, a relaxed capital spreads along a long seaside promenade lined with beaches.
This Uruguayan capital, the country's largest city, holds nearly half the small nation's entire population.
Strollers walk its rambla beside the Río de la Plata, sipping mate, while a hilltop fortress overlooks the port.
Its old town centers on Plaza Independencia, where a mausoleum honors national hero Artigas beneath the Palacio Salvo tower.
Carnival here is among the world's longest, and candombe drumming with African roots echoes through the Barrio Sur streets.
In western South America, a sunny city sits in a high desert plain at the foot of towering snow-capped peaks.
This Argentine provincial capital is the country's wine capital, surrounded by vineyards irrigated by Andean snowmelt channels.
Rebuilt with wide tree-lined avenues after an earthquake, its plazas and acequias keep the dry climate green and shaded.
It serves as the launch point for climbers tackling Aconcagua, the Americas' highest summit looming to the west.
Famous for full-bodied Malbec, its bodegas host an annual grape-harvest festival, the Fiesta de la Vendimia, each autumn.
In the heart of South America, a landlocked nation's capital sits on a broad river bend amid humid subtropical heat.
This Paraguayan capital, one of the continent's oldest cities, perches on the eastern bank of a major navigable river.
Spanish colonizers made it a launching base, earning it the nickname 'Mother of Cities' for the settlements it later seeded.
Its riverfront skyline features the pink Government Palace and the Panteón Nacional honoring the country's heroes.
Both Spanish and Guaraní are spoken in its streets, and it overlooks the river forming the border with Argentina.
Off the misty Pacific coast of South America, a large green island of rolling pastures and dense forest endures frequent rain.
This Chilean archipelago lies south of Puerto Montt, separated from the mainland by a narrow channel of cold water.
Renowned for its folklore of ghost ships and forest sprites, it preserves distinctive stilt houses called palafitos over the tide.
Sixteen wooden churches built by Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries earned the island UNESCO World Heritage recognition.
Locals cook curanto in earth pits, and the colorful palafitos of Castro line the waterfront of its main town.
Near a great South American capital, a maze of leafy river channels and islands spreads where a major river fans into the sea.
This Argentine delta, just north of Buenos Aires, is a popular weekend escape reached by suburban train.
Wooden stilt cabins, rowing clubs, and provisioning boats serve island dwellers across the labyrinth of brown waterways.
Visitors ride wooden launches from its bustling waterfront, passing the riverside Puerto de Frutos craft market and amusement park.
Named for jaguars once hunted in its reeds, the delta forms where the Paraná empties into the Río de la Plata.
On a South American border river, a colossal concrete barrier harnesses immense flow to generate staggering amounts of electricity.
Shared between Paraguay and Brazil, this hydroelectric giant on the Paraná River supplies a vast share of both nations' power.
Completed in 1984, its spillways and turbines were once hailed among the seven wonders of the modern engineering world.
Lit-up nighttime tours run from nearby Ciudad del Este and Foz do Iguaçu, close to the famous triple-border waterfalls.
For years the planet's largest producer of hydroelectric energy, its reservoir flooded the once-mighty Guaíra Falls upstream.
In a remote corner of South American Patagonia, swirling stone formations glow turquoise where water laps eroded rock.
These Chilean rock chapels sit in a vast glacial lake straddling the border with Argentina along the Carretera Austral.
Thousands of years of wave action carved smooth caverns and pillars from solid calcium-rich stone reflecting the water's color.
Small boats ferry visitors from Puerto Río Tranquilo into the so-called 'Cathedral' and 'Chapel' along General Carrera Lake.
The blue-and-white veined walls shift hue with the seasons, making these glassy grottoes one of Patagonia's most photographed marvels.
In northern Europe sits a deep glacier-carved inlet of seawater, walled by towering cliffs and reachable mainly by boat or winding road.
This Scandinavian waterway lies in western Norway, a UNESCO-listed arm of the sea famous among cruise passengers exploring the country's coast.
Sheer rock faces plunge straight into the water, and thin cascades tumble hundreds of metres down the green walls all around vessels passing through.
Two waterfalls here are nicknamed the Seven Sisters and the Suitor, said to flirt across the channel near abandoned cliffside farms.
Often called the crown jewel of the country's fjords, this S-shaped passage near the village sharing its name draws sightseers each summer.
Somewhere in northern Europe a flat slab of rock juts horizontally from a mountainside, hanging high above a long lake far below.
This dramatic ledge sits in the Hardanger region of western Norway, reached only after a demanding multi-hour hike each way.
Formed by glacial frost shattering the cliff, the thin protruding shelf floats roughly 700 metres above the water of Ringedalsvatnet.
Hikers queue for hours to photograph themselves standing on the narrow tongue-shaped overhang near the village of Skjeggedal.
Its name literally means the troll's tongue, and the precarious viewpoint has become one of the country's most shared hiking photographs.
A compact island district of cobbled lanes and ochre buildings forms the medieval heart of a northern European capital.
This historic quarter occupies a small island in Sweden's capital, a city spread across many islands where a lake meets the Baltic.
Founded in the 1200s, its maze of alleys surrounds a royal palace, a cathedral, and Europe's narrowest street barely a metre wide.
Tourists crowd the colourful merchant houses of Stortorget square in Stockholm, site of a notorious medieval bloodbath.
Its name means simply the old town, and changing of the guard at the palace draws crowds to this islet daily.
A purpose-built hall in northern Europe shelters a single colossal exhibit: an almost fully intact wooden warship.
Found on the Djurgarden island in Sweden's capital, this museum preserves a 17th-century vessel raised from the harbour mud.
The top-heavy galleon capsized minutes into its 1628 maiden voyage and lay submerged for over three centuries before salvage.
Its ornate carved stern and original timbers tower inside a copper-clad building near the Nordic and amusement attractions of Stockholm.
It is the most visited single-object museum in Scandinavia, named after the doomed royal flagship it was built to display.
A twisting white skyscraper dominates a flat northern European skyline beside a strait crossed by a famous bridge-tunnel.
This residential tower rises in Malmo, a city in southern Sweden facing the Oresund strait toward Denmark.
Designed by Santiago Calatrava and based on a sculpture of a rotating human figure, it spirals ninety degrees from base to top.
Completed in 2005 at around 190 metres, it is the tallest building in Scandinavia and overlooks the bridge to Copenhagen.
Its nine stacked cubes spiraling skyward gave the structure its descriptive name evoking a body twisting in motion.
On a volcanic island in the far north Atlantic, milky turquoise water steams amid a black lava field.
This geothermal spa lies on the Reykjanes peninsula of Iceland, a short drive from the international airport at Keflavik.
The mineral-rich, silica-laden water is actually fed by runoff from a neighbouring geothermal power plant, warm year-round.
Bathers smear white silica mud on their faces while soaking in the pale, milky pools surrounded by jagged dark rock.
Its descriptive colour-based name marks the country's most famous spa, ranked among the world's great wonders by many travel lists.
In a treeless northern landscape, a glacial river plunges in two great steps into a deep rugged canyon.
This powerful waterfall sits in southwestern Iceland, a key stop along the popular sightseeing circuit near the capital.
Fed by the Hvita river from a glacier, its cascade drops at right angles, throwing spray and rainbows on sunny days.
It anchors the country's Golden Circle route alongside an erupting geyser and a famous rift valley national park.
Its name literally means the golden falls, named for the amber glow the mist takes in afternoon sunlight.
Along a southern coast in the far north, a slender ribbon of water drops from a tall green cliff onto the plain below.
This waterfall stands beside the ring road in southern Iceland, fed by meltwater from a glacier-capped volcano.
A walking path lets visitors pass completely behind the falling curtain of water, getting soaked by the spray.
It plunges roughly sixty metres near the hidden cascade of Gljufrabui, with the Eyjafjallajokull volcano looming inland.
Famed as one of the few cascades you can walk behind, it featured in a Justin Bieber music video shot on the island.
In a northern European capital sits an unusual place of worship carved directly down into solid bedrock.
This Lutheran sanctuary lies in central Helsinki, the capital of Finland, blasted out of a granite outcrop in a residential block.
Daylight floods in through a ring of skylights beneath a vast copper dome resting on the rough quarried rock walls.
Completed in 1969, its superb acoustics make the excavated space a favourite concert venue near the city centre.

Spongy paramo grassland and twisted quinoa-bark polylepis forests cling to its windswept rocky basins.
Its name evokes boxes or chests, referring to the steep glacial cirques cradling each tarn.
Over 270 lakes fill this UNESCO biosphere plateau, a key headwater feeding rivers toward both oceans.
A chain of glacier-capped peaks crowns the eastern range of South America's northern Andes.
It lies in Colombia's Boyacá department, holding the country's largest surviving tropical glaciers.
Jagged snowy summits rise above paramo where giant frailejon plants stand like sentinels.
Sacred to the U'wa indigenous people, the high ice fields here are retreating rapidly with warming.
Its serrated white range, sometimes dubbed a sierra nevada, towers above the village of Güicán.
A remote South American river bursts into vivid colours for only a few months each year.
It flows through Colombia's Meta department within the ancient Serrania de la Macarena rock formation.
An endemic aquatic plant turns the streambed brilliant red, joined by yellow, green and blue hues.
Locals call it the river of five colours or the liquid rainbow for its seasonal blaze.
Cascades and circular potholes scour quartzite bedrock dating back over a billion years here.
Buried in dense South American jungle, an ancient terraced settlement was rediscovered only in 1972.
It lies in Colombia's Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, near the Caribbean coast yet high in the mountains.
Built by the Tairona people centuries before a famous Andean citadel to the south, it predates the Inca empire.
Reaching it requires a multi-day jungle trek climbing roughly 1,200 mossy stone steps.
Indigenous Kogi descendants still guard the round stone terraces of this place known simply as the lost city.
On the northern edge of the African continent sits a fortified earthen village of reddish mudbrick rising above a seasonal riverbed.
It lies in southern Morocco along the old caravan route between Marrakesh and the Sahara, beyond the High Atlas passes.
Clustered houses and granaries crowned with corner towers form a classic ksar of rammed earth, repaired each year against the rains.
Near the town of Ouarzazate, it has doubled as ancient Jerusalem and Egypt for countless films and television epics.
Gladiator, Lawrence of Arabia and Game of Thrones all filmed here; UNESCO protects this most famous of Saharan-gateway clay citadels.
Tucked into a North African mountain range, this small town is famous for one overwhelming colour washing nearly every wall.
It sits in Morocco's Rif Mountains, founded in the late fifteenth century as a fortress against Portuguese incursions.
Andalusian refugees and Jewish settlers shaped its lanes, later painting the medina in countless shades of indigo and azure.
Travellers nickname it the Blue Pearl; goat-leather goods and woven wool fill its hillside market squares below twin peaks.
Its blue-rinsed alleys are among the most photographed streets on Earth, drawing visitors from nearby Tangier and Tetouan.
Among rolling grain fields in northwest Africa lie the most westerly ruins of a great Mediterranean empire.
This Moroccan archaeological site flourished as a provincial capital of Mauretania, exporting olive oil to imperial markets.
Triumphal arch, basilica, and dozens of mosaic floors survive, depicting Orpheus, Hercules, and the labours of mythic heroes.
It stands near the holy town of Moulay Idriss and the imperial city of Meknes, below Mount Zerhoun.
Excavated columns and the Arch of Caracalla mark this UNESCO-listed Roman city, the empire's farthest corner in the Maghreb.
On Africa's Atlantic coast, towering natural sandstone arches once spanned a windswept beach of red-tinged cliffs.
It lies in southern Morocco between the surf town of Mirleft and the port of Sidi Ifni.
Wave-cut openings in the rust-coloured rock framed the ocean until one celebrated arch collapsed in 2016.
At low tide visitors walked beneath the surviving span as the setting sun turned the cliffs deep crimson.
Famed for its dramatic ochre arches over the tide, this beach is among the Souss-Massa region's signature wonders.
In northern Africa a winding river has cut a deep canyon through layered red and ochre rock.
This Moroccan gorge slices the southern flank of the High Atlas, lined with palm groves and crumbling kasbahs.
Bizarre wind-eroded formations nearby, called monkey fingers, rise beside a road of famous hairpin switchbacks.
It forms part of the Route of a Thousand Kasbahs, threading between Boumalne and the Sahara's edge.
Photographers prize its serpentine highway twisting up the canyon wall along the river that shares this valley's name.
On the African continent a vast sea of wind-sculpted dunes rises abruptly from flat desert hammada.
This Moroccan sand sea reaches the Algerian frontier, its tallest crests towering some 150 metres high.
Camel caravans set out from a fringe village to watch dawn ignite the sand in glowing apricot and gold.
Travellers depart from the oasis town of Merzouga to camp among its rippling crests under brilliant Saharan stars.
These towering orange dunes are Morocco's most iconic Sahara landscape, a postcard image of the great desert itself.
In northwest Africa a river plunges over a tiered cliff in the largest waterfall of its country.
These Moroccan cascades drop roughly 110 metres through the Middle Atlas, often crowned by rainbows in the spray.
Old stone olive mills line the descent, and troops of Barbary macaques scamper among the surrounding groves.
Boat operators ferry visitors near the base; the name refers to the olive trees clinging beside the falling water.
Northeast of Marrakesh near Beni Mellal, these triple-tiered falls are the kingdom's most celebrated cascade.
In North Africa a great concrete arch holds back a turquoise reservoir cradled among arid mountains.
Built in the 1950s in Morocco's Atlas foothills, it was a pioneering hydroelectric project for the region.
Its emerald lake stretches between bare ridges, feeding irrigation canals across the plains toward Beni Mellal.
Anglers prize its pike and bass while paragliders launch from cliffs above the deep blue water near Azilal.
This double-curvature arch dam, one of Africa's earliest, takes its name from the gorge village it flooded.
On the North African highlands lie the grid-perfect ruins of a colony built for retired imperial soldiers.
Founded by Emperor Trajan in Algeria around AD 100, it shows textbook Roman town planning on a flat plateau.
A great triumphal arch, a library, theatre, and forum reveal streets laid out in immaculate squares.
Nicknamed the Pompeii of Africa, it sits near the Aurès Mountains and the modern town of Batna.
Sand preserved this perfectly orthogonal Roman city until rediscovery, making it a UNESCO showcase of colonial urban design.
High in North Africa's hills stand the ruins of a Roman town that bent its grid to fit steep terrain.
This Algerian site, once called Cuicul, sits about 900 metres up amid green mountains near Sétif.
Its forums, temples, and Christian basilicas survive beside one of the finest mosaic museums in the region.
The Arabic name means the beautiful, and its hillside setting distinguishes it from flatter imperial colonies nearby.
A UNESCO-listed mountain town of pagan and early Christian Rome, it overlooks deep ravines in Kabylie's highlands.
Deep in the African desert a sandstone plateau hides thousands of prehistoric paintings on its eroded rock walls.
This vast Algerian highland near the Libyan and Niger borders preserves art spanning herds, hunters, and giraffes.
Forests of weathered rock pillars and natural arches stand among canyons once green with savanna life.
Its name means plateau of rivers in Tuareg; cypress trees thousands of years old endure in its gorges.
Home to some of humanity's oldest cave art and bizarre stone forests, it is a UNESCO Saharan treasure.
In North Africa five fortified hilltop towns cluster in a desert valley, each crowned by a pyramidal minaret.
This Algerian oasis settlement anchors the M'zab Valley, built by a devout Ibadi Muslim community in the eleventh century.
Concentric streets spiral up toward the mosque, and palm gardens are fed by an ingenious traditional water-sharing system.
Le Corbusier admired its cubist white-and-ochre houses; its arcaded market square hums with Mozabite traders.
Capital of the M'zab pentapolis and a UNESCO site, this desert town's terraced architecture inspired modern designers.
In the heart of the Sahara a volcanic massif rises into jagged black peaks against the African sky.
This Algerian highland surrounds the oasis of Tamanrasset, homeland of the indigo-veiled Tuareg people.
Eroded volcanic plugs spear upward at Assekrem, where a French hermit-priest once built a remote mountain refuge.
Its highest summit, Mount Tahat, tops the country; sunrise from the plateau is a legendary desert spectacle.
Charles de Foucauld's hermitage and the spiky lava domes make this central Saharan range an icon of the deep desert.
On a North African mountain plain lie the ruins of a medieval Muslim capital abandoned after barely a century.
This Algerian site was founded around 1007 as the first seat of a Berber dynasty in the Maghreb.
A towering minaret over twenty metres tall survives beside palace foundations and a vast congregational mosque.
Set in the Hodna Mountains near M'Sila, it influenced later Norman and Andalusian architecture across the Mediterranean.
This UNESCO-listed fortified Hammadid royal city's striped minaret is among the finest survivals of eleventh-century Islamic Algeria.
On a North African hilltop overlooking olive-clad valleys spread the best-preserved Roman ruins of their country.
This Tunisian site began as a Numidian town before Rome enriched it with temples and a grand theatre.
A Punic-Libyan mausoleum and the towering Capitol temple to Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva dominate the ruins.
Set near Téboursouk in the country's interior, its streets still follow the old contours of the original hill town.
UNESCO calls it the finest example of a Romano-African town; its hilltop Capitol is a Tunisian emblem.
On a flat North African plain a colossal three-tiered Roman arena rises far from any sea.
This Tunisian monument once held around 35,000 spectators, rivalling the great amphitheatre of the imperial capital itself.
Built of golden limestone in the third century, its underground passages once caged beasts and gladiators.
Standing amid a small modern town south of Sousse, its sandy oval has hosted a renowned classical music festival.
One of the largest Roman amphitheatres ever built and a UNESCO site, its honey-coloured arches appear on Tunisian banknotes.
In a North African desert region, multi-storey vaulted granary chambers stack around courtyards like a honeycomb.
This Tunisian fortified storehouse belongs to the Berber south, where nomads once hoarded grain in cliffside cells.
Rows of cave-like ghorfas climb several levels, reached by external staircases of stone and mud.
Near the village of Tataouine, its courtyards were filmed as a slave quarter on Anakin Skywalker's desert homeworld.
A famous Star Wars filming location and the best-preserved fortified granary of its kind, its name honours a local tribe of sultans.
On the North African desert's edge a spring tumbles down a rocky cleft into a hidden palm grove.
This Tunisian mountain oasis nestles against the Atlas foothills near the Algerian frontier, beneath a ruined cliff village.
Locals once called it the castle of the sun; the old abandoned dwellings cling above the cool waterfall.
It featured in The English Patient and Star Wars, lying near sister oases Tamerza and Mides by the salt flats.
A mountain spring-fed palm refuge above the Chott el Gharsa, it is among the country's most cinematic desert oases.
In North Africa a shallow lake and surrounding wetland form a vital stopover on a great bird migration route.
This Tunisian reserve near Bizerte shelters hundreds of thousands of wintering ducks, geese, and flamingos each year.
A lone limestone hill rises beside the brackish lake, which swings between fresh and salt with the seasons.
Once a royal hunting ground, it is the last survivor of a chain of North African lakes drained over centuries.
A UNESCO site and Ramsar wetland, this lake-and-mountain refuge is among the Mediterranean's most important waterfowl havens.
In a North African desert, surreal chalk formations stand like giant white mushrooms across a pale plain.
This Egyptian protected area lies in the Western Desert, reached through the Bahariya and Farafra oases.
Wind and sand have carved the soft cretaceous rock into shapes resembling icebergs, chickens, and towering pillars.
At dusk the formations glow pink and gold, and at night they shine ghostly under the desert moon.
Egypt's Sahara el Beyda, this national park of wind-sculpted chalk monoliths is a famed overnight camping spectacle.
Far in a North African desert, a remote depression of salt lakes and palm groves preserves its own Berber tongue.
This Egyptian oasis near the Libyan border was home to a celebrated ancient oracle of a ram-headed god.
A young world conqueror trekked across the sands to consult its prophet and be hailed as divine.
The ruined mudbrick citadel of Shali crumbles above the town, and salt pools glitter across the basin floor.
Alexander the Great visited its Oracle of Amun; this isolated date-and-olive oasis lies hundreds of kilometres west of the Nile.
On a North African peninsula a narrow desert ravine reveals walls banded in red, purple, and gold.
This Egyptian canyon lies on the Sinai near the Gulf of Aqaba, between Nuweiba and the inland mountains.
Iron and manganese oxides streak the sandstone in swirling layers as hikers squeeze through its slot passages.
Bedouin guides lead trekkers down from the Red Sea coast into the cool shaded depths of the gorge.
Famed for its rainbow-streaked rock corridors, this Sinai slot canyon is a signature desert hike near the resort coast.
Against a sheer North African cliff a vast terraced shrine rises in colonnaded tiers from the desert floor.
This Egyptian mortuary monument honours a rare female pharaoh who ruled in the fifteenth century BC.
Long ramps connect three pillared terraces; reliefs record her divine birth and a famous trading voyage to Punt.
It nestles in a bay at Deir el-Bahari on the Nile's west bank, opposite the temples of Karnak and Luxor.
Designed by the architect Senenmut for Egypt's great queen-pharaoh, its colonnaded terraces face the Valley of the Kings.
In a corner of Central Europe stands a small grove of pines whose trunks defy every expectation of how a tree should grow.
Located in western Poland near the town of Gryfino, close to the German border and the Oder river valley.
Around four hundred trees each bend sharply northward at the base before curving back upright, a deformity probably caused by human intervention in the 1930s.
Planted shortly before the Second World War, the village that tended them was abandoned, leaving the mystery of the J-shaped trunks unsolved.
Photographers call it one of Europe's strangest woodlands, where every pine seems to take a deliberate bow before reaching for the sky.
Deep beneath a Central European town lies an underground world carved entirely from a mineral once worth its weight in coin.
Found in southern Poland just outside Kraków, this site was among the first ever inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
Labourers worked these tunnels for some seven centuries, sculpting chapels, statues and chandeliers from the rock they extracted.
Its grandest chamber, the Chapel of Saint Kinga, sits over a hundred metres down with floors, altars and reliefs all hewn from translucent crystal.
Visitors descend hundreds of wooden steps to find subterranean lakes and a cathedral lit by lamps glittering off walls of pure sodium chloride.
Snaking across the highest mountains of a Balkan nation, this serpentine ribbon of asphalt closes under snow for much of the year.
It crosses the Făgăraș range in central Romania, linking the historic provinces of Wallachia and Transylvania.
Built in the early 1970s on the orders of a communist dictator as a military route, it climbs above two thousand metres through tunnels and hairpins.
Near its summit lies glacial Lake Bâlea, and a famous British motoring show once crowned it the best driving road in the world.
Drivers tackle dozens of switchbacks past Vidraru dam, calling this dramatic alpine traverse one of the continent's ultimate road trips.
In a northern corner of a Balkan country, a graveyard celebrates death with colour and humour rather than solemn grief.
It lies in the village of Săpânța in Romania's Maramureș region, near the Ukrainian border.
Hundreds of carved oak crosses painted bright blue bear comic epitaphs and folk-art portraits depicting how each villager lived and died.
Begun in the 1930s by woodcarver Stan Ioan Pătraș, the tradition continues under his apprentice, drawing visitors to its cheerful rows.
The vivid azure pigment and witty rhyming verses make this the world's most light-hearted burial ground, a UNESCO-tentative folk treasure.
Hidden in the wooded hills of a Balkan land stands a small church famous for a single dazzling shade of pigment.
It rises in the Bukovina region of northern Romania, part of a celebrated cluster of UNESCO-listed painted churches.
Founded in 1488 by the warrior prince Stephen the Great, its exterior walls are covered with vivid frescoes still vivid after five centuries.
Its western façade depicts a sweeping Last Judgement against an intense blue so distinctive it earned the church the nickname 'the Sistine of the East'.
Scholars still debate the recipe behind its luminous cobalt background, a hue now named after this very monastery.
In the far west of a Balkan country, towers of red sandstone rise abruptly from forested hills like a petrified army.
These formations stand in northwestern Bulgaria near the Serbian border, sculpted over two hundred million years.
Folklore gives each weathered pillar a name and legend, from a schoolgirl to a horseman, shaped by wind and rain into uncanny figures.
A medieval fortress was built directly into the rocks, its defensive walls fused seamlessly with the natural cliffs above the town.
Rising up to two hundred metres, this crimson rock labyrinth was a finalist in a campaign to name new natural wonders of the world.
Atop a windswept peak in a Balkan country sits an abandoned saucer-shaped hall that looks beamed in from another planet.
It crowns a summit in central Bulgaria's Balkan range, a former rallying point for the country's communist party.
Completed in 1981, its vast circular interior once gleamed with mosaics of workers and leaders beneath a soaring concrete dome.
A slender tower beside the flying-saucer hall bears giant red stars, while the mosaics now crumble amid graffiti and broken glass.
Urban explorers flock to this decaying brutalist relic, often dubbed the eeriest socialist monument ever raised on a mountaintop.
Deep in a southern Balkan gorge, a stone arch spans a swift river beneath mist-shrouded mountain slopes.
It crosses the Arda river in Bulgaria's Rhodope Mountains, near the town of Ardino.
Ottoman builders raised it in the early sixteenth century along an old route linking the Aegean coast with the interior highlands.
Legend says the master mason walled in his wife's shadow during construction, and at certain hours the arch and its reflection form a perfect eye.
Locals tie its eerie name to nocturnal apparitions on the cobbles, making this humpbacked Rhodope crossing a magnet for folklore seekers.
In the rugged south of a Balkan nation, hundreds of slender earthen pillars crowned with stone caps cluster on an eroded hillside.
These formations stand on Radan mountain in southern Serbia, the product of volcanic soil and centuries of erosion.
Two acidic springs nearby bubble with mineral-rich water, and the towers grow or shrink as rain reshapes their soft conical bodies.
Local legend claims the spires are petrified wedding guests cursed by an evil spirit, giving the eerie site its sinister name.
Capped by flat boulders that shield them from the rain, these roughly two hundred 'earth pyramids' were a contender among new natural wonders.
In eastern reaches of a Balkan country lie the ruins of a fortified imperial palace from the late ancient world.
It sits near Zaječar in eastern Serbia, raised by a Roman emperor born in this very region.
Emperor Galerius built the complex around 300 AD and named it after his mother, surrounding it with massive towers and a triumphal mosaic floor.
Twin temples, imperial mausolea and a sacred hilltop where the ruler was deified lie within, all now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Its surviving floor mosaics of Dionysus and a labyrinth mark one of the best-preserved tetrarchic palaces of the dying Roman Empire.
On a peninsula jutting into the northern Adriatic, a hidden canyon bristles with towering limestone pillars beloved by rock climbers.
It cuts through the Učka massif on Croatia's Istrian peninsula, near the Gulf of Kvarner.
Sheer karst columns rise dozens of metres from the gorge floor, a protected geomorphological wonder within a nature park.
A viaduct of the old road soars above the chasm, while marked trails descend past free-standing stone towers shaped by erosion.
Climbers from across Europe come to scale its slender pinnacles, hailing this dramatic ravine as the region's finest vertical playground.
On a hilltop in a Mediterranean country sits a settlement so tiny it claims a record few places would dare contest.
It perches in the heart of Croatia's Istrian peninsula, surrounded by vineyards and oak forests.
Just two short streets and a few dozen residents fit inside its medieval walls, entered through a single fortified gate.
Stone inscriptions in the ancient Glagolitic script line the nearby lane, and the town is famed for a potent local mistletoe brandy.
Guinness recognises it as the smallest town on Earth, with a population barely scraping past twenty souls.
Scattered across an azure Mediterranean sea lies one of Europe's densest island archipelagos, mostly barren and uninhabited.
This cluster lies off the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, near the towns of Zadar and Šibenik.
Nearly ninety islands and reefs fill a compact national park, their seaward cliffs called 'crowns' plunging dramatically into the deep.
A playwright described them as a labyrinth of stone scattered by a god in a moment of inspiration, ringed by drystone walls and olive groves.
Sailors thread its maze of channels past karst islets, where sheep graze and tiny stone cottages dot a sun-bleached, treeless seascape.
In a corner of Eastern Europe, a disused railway threads through a leafy green archway formed entirely by overgrown trees.
It runs near the village of Klevan in the Rivne region of western Ukraine.
An industrial train serving a plywood factory still trundles along the track, its passing having sculpted the foliage into a perfect tunnel.
Couples walk the rails believing that a wish made here, hand in hand, will come true beneath the verdant canopy.
Photographers from around the world flock to this romantic three-kilometre corridor of intertwined branches, especially when summer turns it emerald.
On the bank of a great river in Eastern Europe stands a mighty stronghold whose towers have witnessed centuries of siege.
It rises above the Dniester river in western Ukraine, near the border with Moldova in the Bukovina region.
Its stone walls and round towers, raised across the medieval and early modern eras, guarded a crossroads fought over by Poles, Ottomans and Cossacks.
A famous 1621 battle here halted an Ottoman advance into Europe, and its dramatic silhouette has featured in many historical films.
Soaring directly from the riverbank, this Podolian citadel is celebrated as one of the seven wonders of its nation.
Beneath the gentle farmland of Eastern Europe winds the longest gypsum cave system anywhere on the planet.
It lies in the Ternopil region of western Ukraine, in the historic borderland of Podolia.
Discovered by speleologists in 1966, its mapped passages now exceed two hundred and sixty kilometres, all carved through soft sulphate rock.
Delicate crystal formations line a near-flat maze so vast that explorers can spend days underground without retracing their steps.
Its hopeful name reflects the cavers' optimism, and it ranks as the world's second-longest cave overall behind only Mammoth in Kentucky.
High on a windswept plateau in a Balkan country, a weathered crag bears an uncanny resemblance to a human face in profile.
It stands atop a high plateau in the southern Carpathians of central Romania, above the resort towns of Bușteni and Sinaia.
Frost and wind eroded the megalith over millennia until, viewed from the right angle, it mirrors the famous Egyptian monument it is named after.
Nearby rise the mushroom-shaped rock outcrops known as the Babele, fuelling local legends of ancient energy and lost civilisations.
Every year on a late-November dawn, mystics gather as the rising sun aligns with this stony Carpathian face at over two thousand metres.
In the arid American Southwest sits a slot carved through sandstone by flash floods over countless centuries of erosion.
Located on Navajo Nation land in northern Arizona, it is famous among photographers for its narrow, sculpted corridors.
Shafts of sunlight pierce the upper passages at midday, illuminating swirling orange and purple walls of Navajo Sandstone.
It lies near the town of Page and the vast reservoir of Lake Powell, split into upper and lower sections by guides.
Beams of light famously spotlight the dusty floor here, making it perhaps the most photographed slot of its tiny kind on Earth.
High on a forested plateau in North America, ancient peoples built elaborate stone homes tucked beneath sheltering cliffs.
In southwestern Colorado, this UNESCO site preserves dwellings of the Ancestral Puebloans abandoned around the late 13th century.
Its Cliff Palace, with over 150 rooms and ceremonial kivas, is the largest such alcove village in the United States.
The name describes the flat-topped 'green table' landform; nearby lie Durango and the Four Corners region.
Visitors climb ladders into sandstone alcoves to tour Balcony House and Spruce Tree House, masterpieces of Puebloan masonry.
Rising abruptly from the plains of the American interior, a flat-topped column of igneous rock dominates the surrounding grassland.
In northeastern Wyoming, this striking butte became the very first national monument designated in the United States in 1906.
Its sides are scored by enormous hexagonal columns of phonolite porphyry, sacred to many Plains tribes who call it Bear Lodge.
Near the Belle Fourche River and the Black Hills, it famously appeared as an alien landing site in a Spielberg film.
Climbers scale its vertical cracks while Indigenous peoples leave prayer bundles at the base of this 386-meter monolith.
In a high desert valley of North America stands a multi-storied adobe settlement continuously inhabited for roughly a thousand years.
Set in northern New Mexico, this living Native American community is a designated UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Its terraced earthen apartments, reached by wooden ladders, rise beside a mountain creek used for drinking water.
Nestled beneath the Sangre de Cristo Mountains near an artists' town, it features the San Geronimo mission church.
The reddish stacked dwellings of Hlauuma and Hlaukwima form the most famous Indigenous village of the Rio Grande region.
In the American South, naturally heated mineral waters bubble up from the earth, drawing bathers for over a century.
This unusually urban national park sits within a small Arkansas city, wrapped around a historic bathhouse district.
Forty-seven thermal sources emerge here at around 62 degrees Celsius, channeled into ornate early-20th-century spa houses.
Its Bathhouse Row along Central Avenue once earned it the nickname 'The American Spa' and hosted gangsters and ballplayers.
Once a federal reservation protected before national parks existed, this Ouachita Mountains resort town shares its name with its steamy waters.
In a remote desert canyon of North America lie the ruins of a vast, astronomically aligned ancient civilization's hub.
This UNESCO site in northwestern New Mexico was the ceremonial center of Ancestral Puebloan society around 850 to 1150 CE.
Its great houses, like Pueblo Bonito, contained hundreds of rooms and were linked by hundreds of miles of engineered roads.
Buildings here align with solstices and lunar cycles; the remote site near Farmington is treasured by dark-sky astronomers.
The sun dagger on Fajada Butte marked the seasons in this canyon, North America's grandest pre-Columbian masonry complex.
On a North American floodplain rose the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, built entirely of earth.
In southern Illinois near the Mississippi River, this UNESCO site preserves the heart of the Mississippian culture.
Its central earthen pyramid, Monks Mound, covers more ground at its base than the Great Pyramid of Giza.
A timber circle dubbed 'Woodhenge' tracked solstices here, just across the river from modern St. Louis.
Around 1100 CE this metropolis of perhaps 20,000 people thrived; its 80-plus surviving earthworks bear the name of a later tribe.
A vast, blackened lava landscape in North America looks so otherworldly that astronauts once trained here for space.
Spread across the Snake River Plain of southern Idaho, this national monument preserves a young volcanic wilderness.
Cinder cones, spatter cones, and lava tube caves formed from eruptions along the Great Rift over the past 15,000 years.
Apollo astronauts studied basalt here near Arco; the rolling fields of dark rock evoke a barren lunar surface.
Its very name compares the cratered, ashen terrain to humanity's nearest celestial neighbor, the gray cratered satellite above.
In the Pacific Northwest of North America, a powerful cataract plunges into a deep amphitheater gouged by ancient megafloods.
Located in southeastern Washington State, this waterfall is the official state waterfall, set amid rolling wheat country.
The river drops nearly 60 meters over a basalt rim into a churning plunge pool carved during the Missoula floods.
Surrounded by the hilly farmlands that share its name, it lies near the Snake River in arid Whitman County.
Kayaker Tyler Bradt set a world record by paddling over this single basalt drop, the region's most dramatic cataract.
In a remote desert wilderness of North America, undulating sandstone ridges resemble a frozen, multicolored ocean swell.
Straddling the Arizona-Utah border in the Paria Canyon area, access requires a hard-to-win permit lottery.
Thin layers of Jurassic Navajo Sandstone form swirling bands of red, orange, and yellow rippling across the slickrock.
Part of the Coyote Buttes within Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, only a few dozen hikers are admitted daily.
Photographers prize its trough of rippling rock; the formation's name evokes the surfing crest its curves so perfectly imitate.
Along a rugged North American coastline, the sea appears to vanish into a churning hole in the volcanic rock.
On the central Oregon coast, this saltwater feature draws photographers at high tide and storm swells.
A collapsed sea cave forms a bowl that fills and violently drains with each surging wave of the Pacific.
Found at Cape Perpetua near Yachats, it is nicknamed the 'drainpipe of the Pacific' for its gulping motion.
Said to be a bottomless sinkhole swallowing the ocean, it borrows the name of the Norse god of thunder.
Where a mighty North American river finally meets the ocean stands a beacon guarding one of the world's deadliest bars.
At the mouth of the Columbia River in Washington State, this rocky headland marks where Lewis and Clark reached the Pacific.
Its lighthouse, among the oldest on the West Coast, warns ships of the treacherous shoals called the 'Graveyard of the Pacific'.
Named by a frustrated British explorer who missed the river entrance, it sits near the town of Ilwaco and Fort Canby.
The Corps of Discovery carved their names here in 1805; this headland's gloomy title reflects a sea captain's failed, frustrated search.
In the southeastern United States, a river slices a dramatic chasm hundreds of meters deep through ancient hard quartzite.
Located in the Blue Ridge foothills of northeastern Georgia, this chasm is among the deepest east of the Mississippi.
A series of six waterfalls tumbles through the two-mile canyon, where a famous tightrope walker once crossed on a wire.
Karl Wallenda walked above the chasm in 1970; a swaying suspension bridge now lets hikers peer down at the cascades.
Its name comes from a Cherokee word; the rushing falls inspired one of the South's earliest river-tourism resorts.
In a remote desert of North America, balanced rock pillars capped with harder stone stand like petrified mushrooms.
Found in southern Utah within Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, they form along a short hiking trail off a highway.
Softer Entrada Sandstone erodes beneath protective caprocks, leaving slender stems topped by broad resistant boulders.
Located near the town of Kanab and the Paria badlands, the formations glow red and white against the desert sky.
These fragile capped spires are named for the fungi they resemble, a whimsical wonder of differential erosion.
In the northeastern United States, a stream tumbles through a narrow shale gorge past a stone walkway carved into cliffs.
At the southern tip of one of New York's Finger Lakes, this state park is famous for nineteen waterfalls in two miles.
A path winds behind cascades and beneath dripping overhangs, crossing stone bridges built by 1930s work crews.
The village sharing its name, near Seneca Lake, also hosts a legendary motor-racing circuit in the wine country.
Hikers pass through the famous Cavern Cascade and Rainbow Falls in a ravine whose name matches its lakeside town.
Scattered across a remote North American desert mesa stand the stone towers of a vanished ancient farming people.
Spanning the Utah-Colorado border, this national monument preserves Ancestral Puebloan villages around shallow canyon heads.
Square, round, and D-shaped masonry towers cluster at the rims of small canyons, some seemingly aligned to the sun.
Near the Four Corners and Cortez, its ruins like Square Tower and Hackberry date to around the 13th century.
Its name is a Ute word meaning 'deserted valley,' fitting these silent stone towers abandoned over 700 years ago.
In a remote North American desert, a surreal field of eroded clay forms a maze of fantastical, alien rock shapes.
Located in northwestern New Mexico south of Farmington, this wilderness has no marked trails across its eroding mudstone.
Hoodoos, petrified logs, and 'cracked egg' formations emerge from ancient Cretaceous seabed and coastal swamp deposits.
Managed by the Bureau of Land Management near the Navajo Nation, it pairs with the De-Na-Zin wilderness next door.
Its name comes from a Navajo word describing such eroded terrain; photographers prowl its otherworldly hoodoo gardens at sunrise.
Beneath the wooded hills of the American South lies a still-growing limestone cave glittering with mineral formations.
Located in the Ozark Mountains of north-central Arkansas, this cavern system is managed by the U.S. Forest Service.
An underground stream flows through the chambers past towering flowstone, soda straws, and a massive cathedral-like room.
Near the towns of Mountain View and Fifty-Six, a clear creek emerges from the bluff that lends this cave its name.
Among the most beautiful 'living' caves in the country, its Dripstone Trail showcases actively forming calcite wonders.
In the Pacific Northwest of North America, a soaring two-tiered waterfall drops down a mossy basalt cliff beside a busy highway.
Located in a forested river gorge in northern Oregon, it is the tallest such cascade in the state.
Spring-fed water plunges 189 meters in two steps, crossed midway by an arched stone footbridge built in 1914.
Set within the Columbia River Gorge near Portland, it is the region's most visited natural attraction.
Its name honors a local Indigenous people; the iconic Benson Bridge frames the upper drop in countless postcards.
In the western United States, dramatic fins of red sandstone jut vertically from the earth against a backdrop of high peaks.
At the foot of the Rocky Mountains in central Colorado, this free public park sits within a sprawling Front Range city.
Towering tilted slabs of crimson rock were thrust upward when the mountains rose, forming balanced and pierced formations.
Near Pikes Peak and the city of Colorado Springs, landmarks include Balanced Rock and the soaring Kissing Camels.
Two surveyors in 1859 joked it was fit for a beer hall, but a grander divine name stuck to these scarlet spires.
In western North America's prairie heartland, eroded badlands hide one of Earth's richest beds of prehistoric remains.
Carved by the Red Deer River in southern Alberta, its hoodoos and coulees break an otherwise flat grassland.
Late Cretaceous strata here have yielded fossils of more than fifty reptilian species from around 75 million years ago.
Northeast of Brooks and near Drumheller's museum country, the moon-like terrain is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Its very name advertises the extinct giants whose skeletons emerge from these crumbling, layered cliffs.
On the grassy plains of western North America, a sandstone cliff records thousands of years of Indigenous ingenuity.
In southern Alberta near Fort Macleod, Blackfoot peoples drove herds of bison off this escarpment for millennia.
Bone deposits beneath the precipice run metres deep, among the oldest and best-preserved hunting complexes anywhere.
An interpretive centre built into the cliffside lies along the Porcupine Hills, recognised by UNESCO in 1981.
Its grisly English name supposedly recalls a young hunter crushed beneath the falling animals he came to watch.
Along an Atlantic Canadian shoreline, eroding sea bluffs reveal a 'coal age' rainforest frozen in solid stone.
Beside the Bay of Fundy in Nova Scotia, the world's highest tides constantly expose fresh Carboniferous rock.
Upright petrified tree trunks and the earliest known reptiles inspired ideas that influenced Charles Darwin himself.
Near the Cumberland Basin and the village sharing its name, the layered seaside bluffs became a UNESCO site in 2008.
Spanning roughly 300 million years of the 'Coal Age,' it is hailed as the most complete record of terrestrial life from that era.
In an arid valley of western North America, a shallow lake transforms each summer into a polka-dotted mosaic.
Near Osoyoos in British Columbia's Okanagan, intense evaporation concentrates minerals into hundreds of separate pools.
Magnesium sulphate, calcium and sodium leave rimmed circles of yellow, green and blue as the water recedes.
Sacred to the Syilx Okanagan people as Kliluk, it sits just off the highway toward the United States border.
Its mineral-rich brine was once mined for munitions, and the colourful spots give the lake its plainly descriptive name.
In the far northern reaches of North America, a near-perfect circular lake marks a violent visitor from space.
On the tundra of Nunavik in northern Quebec, this meteorite scar holds some of the purest freshwater on the planet.
Formed by an impact about 1.4 million years ago, its rim rises starkly above the flat Ungava plateau.
Once dubbed the 'Crystal Eye of Nunavik,' it lies within a provincial park accessible only by chartered aircraft.
Its Inuktitut name meaning 'where the land rises' describes the raised rim of this 3.4-kilometre-wide cosmic bowl.
On a foggy Atlantic headland of North America, layered seaside rock preserves some of Earth's earliest complex life.
At the southeastern tip of Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, sloping cliffs guard thousands of ancient impressions.
Fossils here record the Ediacaran biota, soft-bodied organisms living over 560 million years ago on a deep sea floor.
Ships once steered onto these rocks thinking they had reached Cape Race, giving the treacherous promontory its rueful name.
Inscribed by UNESCO in 2016, its bedding planes show the oldest known large, architecturally complex multicellular fossils.
Visible from orbit, an enormous ring-shaped lake scars the boreal forest of northeastern North America.
On Quebec's Côte-Nord, this annular waterway encircles a central island left by an ancient cataclysm.
A meteorite roughly five kilometres wide struck here some 214 million years ago, near the Triassic mass extinction.
Astronauts call it the 'Eye of Quebec,' its central René-Levasseur Island larger than the surrounding water ring.
A hydroelectric dam on the local river flooded the impact moat, creating the distinctive doughnut shape seen from space.
Above the Arctic Circle on a vast North American island, granite spires and ice fields rise from polar tundra.
On Baffin Island in Canada's far north, sheer rock towers loom over a glacier-carved pass through the mountains.
The Akshayuk Pass corridor and the sheer face of Mount Thor offer the planet's greatest vertical cliff drop.
Reached from the Inuit hamlets of Pangnirtung and Qikiqtarjuaq, its summits include the pyramid-like Mount Asgard.
Its Inuktitut name, meaning 'the land that never melts,' refers to the enduring Penny Ice Cap at its frozen heart.
On a windswept northern tip of North America, turf mounds mark the earliest known European foothold on the continent.
At the northern point of Newfoundland, Norse seafarers built sod dwellings around the year 1000 AD.
Excavated iron nails, a bronze pin and a spindle whorl confirmed a Viking presence centuries before Columbus.
Reconstructed longhouses overlook the strait toward Labrador, possibly the 'Vinland' of the Icelandic sagas.
Made a UNESCO site in 1978, this French-named meadow is the only confirmed Norse settlement in the Americas.
In the high mountains of western North America, a long glacial lake mirrors snow-capped peaks in turquoise water.
Within Jasper National Park in the Canadian Rockies, it is the largest natural lake in the region.
Its waters glow blue-green from glacial rock flour, fed by ice and drained partly through underground channels.
Boat tours cross to tiny Spirit Island, perhaps the most photographed islet in the entire Rocky Mountains.
Its French name, meaning 'wicked' or 'malignant,' was given for the river that disappears into a karst sinkhole nearby.
On the northern Great Plains of North America, sandstone hoodoos shelter the continent's densest concentration of rock art.
In southern Alberta along the Milk River, weathered cliffs are carved and painted with thousands of Indigenous images.
Blackfoot peoples recorded battles, spirits and the arrival of horses and guns across these eroded canyon walls.
Known to the Niitsitapi as Áísínai'pi, the park lies near the Sweetgrass Hills and the United States border.
Granted UNESCO status in 2019, its very name announces the petroglyphs and pictographs etched into the soft rock.
Straddling a provincial-territorial line in northern North America, this is the continent's largest national park.
Spanning Alberta and the Northwest Territories, its boreal plains host one of the world's biggest inland river deltas.
Home to the largest free-roaming herd of its namesake beast and the last natural nesting ground of whooping cranes.
The Peace and Athabasca rivers form a vast delta here, recognised by UNESCO in 1983 for its wetlands and wildlife.
From orbit, the world's largest beaver dam, over 850 metres long, was discovered hidden within this remote reserve.
Far out in the North Atlantic off eastern North America, a thin crescent of sand drifts amid treacherous shoals.
Roughly 175 kilometres from Nova Scotia, this shifting sandbar lies alone in the open ocean with no trees.
Hundreds of feral horses roam its dunes, descendants of animals left here centuries ago to fend for themselves.
More than 350 shipwrecks earned it the chilling nickname 'Graveyard of the Atlantic' among mariners.
Now a protected national park reserve, this crescent-shaped 'sand' island also hosts the world's largest grey seal colony.
On an Atlantic coast of North America, a colourful colonial port preserves a meticulously planned British grid town.
Founded in 1753 on Nova Scotia's south shore, it was settled largely by German and Swiss Protestant colonists.
Brightly painted wooden houses, including the overhanging 'bump' dormers, rise above a still-active fishing harbour.
Its waterfront once built the famed racing schooner Bluenose, the vessel pictured on the Canadian dime.
Inscribed by UNESCO in 1995 as the best surviving planned British colonial settlement in North America.
In far northern Europe sits a sheer cliff plateau beloved by hikers, rising hundreds of metres above a deep glacial inlet.
Found in southwestern Norway, this flat-topped granite shelf overlooks the Lysefjord and draws crowds along a steep marked trail.
The square, almost perfectly level summit drops roughly 600 metres straight down to the water with no railing at the edge.
Reached from the town of Forsand near Stavanger, its name in Norwegian means a preacher's elevated platform of stone.
This iconic flat outcrop has featured in a Tom Cruise spy thriller and is one of the most photographed viewpoints in the fjordlands.
Along a northern European harbour stands a row of tall, narrow wooden buildings leaning together, painted in ochre, red and cream.
