In the Norwegian coastal city of Bergen, this old quayside district recalls a medieval German trading league's outpost.
Repeatedly burned and rebuilt on its original foundations, its crooked timber facades enclose narrow alleys and merchant houses.
Once a Hanseatic League stockfish trading hub, this UNESCO-listed wharf faces the Vagen bay below Mount Floyen.
Its leaning gabled warehouses are the city's postcard symbol, a survivor of fires that shaped the entire fjord-port skyline.
In northern Europe a small medieval timber sanctuary survives, its dark wooden walls carved with intertwining animal motifs.
Perched above a Norwegian fjord arm in Sognefjord country, it is the oldest surviving wooden mast-built house of worship.
Its north portal preserves elaborate Viking-age carvings of serpents and beasts that lend their name to a whole art style.
Standing on a hillside at the Ornes hamlet in Luster municipality, it dates partly from the twelfth century.
This UNESCO-listed mast-framed chapel gives its name to a distinctive Scandinavian style of looping zoomorphic ornament.
In northern Europe a dramatic mountain road climbs a steep wall in eleven tight hairpin bends past a thundering waterfall.
Set in western Norway's fjord country, this serpentine pass links valleys near the town of Andalsnes.
Its switchbacks ascend a near-vertical face beside the Stigfossen falls, with viewing platforms cantilevered over the drop.
Named in Norwegian for a mythical path of giants, it sits along the route toward the Geiranger region.
Closed by snow much of the year, this folkloric staircase of asphalt is one of the country's most famous scenic drives.
On a north Atlantic island a beach of jet-black sand stretches beneath cliffs of hexagonal stone columns.
On the southern coast of Iceland near the village of Vik, dangerous sneaker waves crash against this dark shore.
Offshore stand pointed basalt sea stacks, said in legend to be trolls frozen while dragging a ship to land.
A cave of stacked columnar basalt frames the beach, with the Dyrholaey promontory rising nearby.
This jet-black volcanic strand is repeatedly named among the world's most striking beaches despite its deadly surf.
On a far northern Atlantic island a massive waterfall thunders through a barren volcanic canyon, throwing up constant spray.
In northeastern Iceland it pours over a basalt lip within the Vatnajokull National Park along a glacier-fed river.
Reckoned among Europe's most powerful falls by sheer water volume, its grey glacial torrent drops about 45 metres.
Fed by the Jokulsa a Fjollum river, it lies near the Asbyrgi canyon north of Lake Myvatn.
Its raw cascade opens a Ridley Scott science-fiction film about humanity's origins, framed against black desert.
On a north Atlantic island a glacial lake glows with floating blue and white ice that drifts slowly toward the sea.
On Iceland's southeastern coast, calved ice from an outlet of the Vatnajokull ice cap fills this deepening lagoon.
Stranded ice chunks wash onto a nearby black beach so polished they make it look strewn with diamonds.
Crossed by the ring road bridge along Route 1, it has grown rapidly as the Breidamerkurjokull glacier retreats.
Its iceberg-dotted waters have doubled as a backdrop in James Bond and Batman films and Iceland's deepest lake.
In northern Europe a sprawling sea fortress spreads across a cluster of linked islands guarding a Baltic harbour.
Off the capital of Finland, its ramparts and bastions were begun under Swedish rule in the eighteenth century.
Once nicknamed the Gibraltar of the North, it later fell to Russia and served under three different flags.
A short ferry from Helsinki's market square reaches its grass-topped walls, dry dock, and a submarine on display.
This UNESCO-listed island stronghold remains an inhabited district, blending barracks, cannons, and homes among the skerries.
In northern Europe a tidy old town survives entirely in painted wooden houses lining narrow cobbled lanes.
On Finland's western coast by the Gulf of Bothnia, this is one of the largest preserved Nordic wooden townscapes.
Long famous for handmade bobbin lace, its pastel cottages cluster around a medieval Holy Cross stone church.
An old Hanseatic-era port, it holds an annual lace week and sits in the Satakunta region near Pori.
This UNESCO-listed grid of timber homes is celebrated as a rare intact example of old Scandinavian wooden urban building.
In northern Europe a log-built country chapel combines a sturdy timber cross plan with a separate freestanding bell tower.
In central Finland's lake district, it was raised by a self-taught peasant master builder in the 1760s.
Its interior fuses Renaissance vaulting ideals with rustic Gothic carpentry, all hewn from notched horizontal logs.
Standing near Jyvaskyla, the structure was preserved when a newer house of worship replaced it, saving it intact.
This UNESCO-listed Lutheran log sanctuary is hailed as a masterpiece of northern wooden ecclesiastical architecture.
On a Baltic island in northern Europe a complete medieval ring wall encircles a town of church ruins and rose-clad lanes.
The chief town of Sweden's largest island, Gotland, it flourished as a wealthy Hanseatic trading centre.
Its limestone curtain wall with dozens of towers is among the best-preserved fortified town walls in the north.
Each August it hosts a celebrated medieval week, while ruined Gothic churches stud the slope down to the harbour.
This UNESCO-listed walled town inspired the seaside setting of a famous Studio Ghibli witch-delivery film.
In northern Europe a vast treeless limestone plain stretches flat to the horizon, thin-soiled and dotted with rare orchids.
Covering much of a long narrow Baltic island off southeastern Sweden, this barren pavement supports unique steppe-like flora.
Grazed for thousands of years, its sparse turf over bare bedrock harbours plants found almost nowhere else in the region.
Spanning the southern half of the island of Oland near Kalmar, it forms part of a UNESCO agricultural landscape.
This great alvar barren is among Europe's largest such limestone heaths, prized by botanists and birdwatchers alike.
In northern Europe a rugged shoreline of steep forested hills and islands rises from a brackish northern sea.
On the eastern coast of Sweden along the Gulf of Bothnia, this land is still visibly lifting out of the water.
Freed from the weight of vanished ice sheets, the ground rebounds here faster than almost anywhere on Earth.
A long suspension bridge spans its inlet near Kramfors, while the highest ancient shoreline towers nearly 290 metres up.
This UNESCO-listed coast is the global type site for measuring post-glacial isostatic land rise.
In northern Europe a walled medieval core of spires, towers and cobbled lanes crowns a low hill above a Baltic port.
Forming the historic heart of Estonia's capital, it preserves merchant houses from its Hanseatic golden age.
An upper town of cathedrals and a lower town of guild halls are linked by gates beneath cylindrical defensive towers.
Landmarks include the onion-domed Alexander Nevsky cathedral on Toompea hill and the squat Fat Margaret tower.
This UNESCO-listed enclave is rated among the best-preserved medieval town centres in all of northern Europe.
In northern Europe a low coastal reserve mixes pine bogs, erratic boulders, and quiet bays along a chilly sea.
On the northern shore of Estonia east of the capital, it was the Soviet bloc's first designated national park.
Its name means land of bays, describing fingers of forested peninsula reaching into the Gulf of Finland.
Restored manor houses, fishing villages, and giant glacial boulders dot its raised-bog hiking trails.
This pioneering Baltic protected area shelters bears, elk, and one of the region's most extensive coastal wetlands.
In northern Europe a long thin sand peninsula separates a brackish lagoon from the open Baltic Sea.
Shared between Lithuania and Russia's Kaliningrad enclave, it is famed for towering migrating dunes.
Once threatened by sand drift, its forests were replanted to halt the moving dunes that buried whole villages.
Resort hamlets like Nida cluster beneath the great Parnidis dune near the city of Klaipeda.
This UNESCO-listed barrier of windblown sand stretches roughly 98 kilometres, a fragile human-shaped cultural landscape.
In northern Europe a small mound bristles with hundreds of thousands of crucifixes left by countless pilgrims.
In northern Lithuania near the city of Siauliai, this folk shrine became a symbol of national and religious defiance.
Soviet authorities bulldozed it several times, yet locals returned each night to replant the sacred timber emblems.
A visiting pope prayed here in 1993, cementing its fame as a place of Catholic pilgrimage and resistance.
Today its tangled forest of crucifixes, rosaries, and effigies grows endlessly as visitors keep adding their own.
In northern Europe a winding river has cut a broad wooded valley exposing tall reddish sandstone cliffs and caves.
In northern Latvia it is the country's largest and oldest national park, centred on a meandering namesake river.
Its sandstone outcrops include a vast cave whose walls bear inscriptions carved over many centuries.
The medieval castle town of Sigulda and the brick ruins of Turaida overlook this so-called Switzerland of the region.
Famous for autumn colour, its valley draws hikers, bobsledders, and cable-car riders above the forested gorge.
In West Africa, a long sandstone cliff rises abruptly from arid plains, sheltering villages clinging improbably to its towering vertical face.
Found in central Mali southeast of the Niger River, this dramatic ridge is home to the Dogon people and their ancestral terraced settlements.
Ancient mud granaries and abandoned cliff dwellings of the earlier Tellem people honeycomb the rock high above the modern villages below.
Famous for elaborate masked Dama funeral dances and toguna shelters, the area centers on the town that shares the cliff's name in the Mopti region.
This UNESCO-listed cultural landscape is renowned for cosmological astronomy tied to the Sirius star and intricate carved wooden door lintels.
On a West African floodplain stands the largest structure on Earth built entirely from sun-dried mud bricks and plaster.
Located in central Mali on an island in the inland delta of the Niger River, it dominates a historic market town.
Bristling wooden beams called toron project from its walls, serving as scaffolding for the annual communal replastering festival each spring.
Three towering minarets crowned with ostrich-egg finials overlook the weekly Monday market in the old caravan town sharing its name.
Rebuilt in 1907 in the Sudano-Sahelian style, this UNESCO icon is the most famous earthen place of worship in the world.
Beside a great West African river sits a stepped pyramidal monument of packed earth, bristling with protruding timbers like a spiny hill.
In eastern Mali's Gao region, this 17-metre earthen structure was raised by a powerful emperor of a vast medieval trading empire.
Built around 1495 by the ruler who expanded the Songhai Empire after returning from a famous pilgrimage to Mecca.
Flanked by two flat-roofed mosques and a cemetery, it stands in the city that once rivalled nearby Timbuktu as a Saharan trade hub.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, this conical mausoleum honors the emperor Mohammad, the dynasty's greatest sovereign and namesake of the dynasty itself.
In West Africa stands a tiny whitewashed earthen sanctuary, its pyramidal towers studded with horizontal timbers in a striking Sudanese style.
Set in northern Ghana's Savannah Region near the entrance to Mole National Park, it is among the oldest such buildings in the country.
Local legend says a 15th-century trader dreamed its foundations, and an ancient baobab beside it supposedly grew from his grave.
Nicknamed the Mecca of West Africa, the small village mosque guards a centuries-old handwritten Quran said to have arrived by divine gift.
Coated brilliant white with conical buttresses, this revered shrine shares its name with the surrounding settlement near the White Volta.
In a West African coastal wetland, an entire village floats on stilts above the water, reached only by dugout canoe.
Located in southwestern Ghana's Western Region on a freshwater lagoon, this settlement sits a long paddle from the nearest dry land.
Oral tradition holds that its founders were guided here from ancient Walata by a snail, settling them permanently over Lake Tadane.
Raised wooden walkways link homes, a school and a chapel, all perched above the water near the village of Beyin.
A UNESCO tentative-list community whose name means surface of water, it is West Africa's most celebrated stilt village.
In West Africa, water plunges in twin cascades down a forested escarpment, the highest such drop in the region.
Found in eastern Ghana's Volta Region near the border with Togo, it lies within the Agumatsa Wildlife Sanctuary.
Thousands of fruit bats roost on the cliffs surrounding the upper pool, swirling above the spray in dense clouds.
Reached by a forest trail near the town of Hohoe, the lower cataract feeds a swimming pool ringed by rainforest.
Straddling an international frontier, this is the tallest waterfall in the country, named for the village at its base.
On a West African shore stands a vast whitewashed fortress, its cannon facing an ocean that carried millions into bondage.
Located on the central coast of Ghana, it is one of dozens of European slave-trading forts dotting the Gulf of Guinea.
Built by Swedes in 1653 and later seized by the British, its dank dungeons held captives before the infamous Door of No Return.
A short drive from Elmina, the seaside town sharing its name became Britain's colonial capital of the Gold Coast.
A UNESCO World Heritage fort visited by President Obama in 2009, it is the most prominent memorial of the transatlantic slave trade.
In a West African rainforest, visitors sway hundreds of feet above the canopy on a swaying suspended rope-and-plank trail.
Located in Ghana's Central Region inland from the coastal slave forts, it protects a rare surviving tract of tropical jungle.
Forest elephants, bongo antelope and over 250 bird species inhabit its dense understory, best glimpsed at dawn from the treetops.
Its famous walkway, strung between giant emergent trees near the city of Cape Coast, is one of only a few canopy bridges in Africa.
Established in 1992 from a former logging reserve, this protected forest is celebrated for that vertiginous aerial walkway above the leaves.
In West Africa, a hilltop kingdom of terraced fields and stone-paved paths preserves a chiefdom largely unchanged for centuries.
Perched in the Mandara Mountains of northeastern Nigeria near the Cameroon border, it overlooks the plains of Adamawa State.
Ceremonial flagstone avenues, sacred trees and the imposing palace of its hereditary chief reflect an ancient iron-smelting society.
Dry-stone walls, ruined furnaces and granaries dot the slopes above the village from which this cultural landscape takes its name.
Inscribed in 1999, it was the first cultural landscape in sub-Saharan Africa added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
In West Africa, dense riverside forest shelters shrines and sculptures dedicated to a goddess of fertility and water.
Located in southwestern Nigeria's central Yorubaland, this woodland on the edge of a city is sacred to local devotees.
Fantastical clay and iron statues by artist Susanne Wenger guard winding paths along the river to the deity's principal shrine.
Each August an immense festival draws pilgrims who carry offerings to the riverbank in the city sharing the grove's name.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, it is among the last intact remnants of primary forest once typical of southern Yorubaland.
In West Africa, immense rounded granite domes rise sheer from the forest, their bald gray faces glinting in the sun.
Located in southwestern Nigeria's Ondo State, these inselbergs sheltered an entire community atop their summits for over eight centuries.
A flight of 660 steps climbs past an old palace, court and shrines to the abandoned hilltop town the people only left in the 1920s.
A mysterious unreadable inscription, Agboogun's footprint and a thunder god's shrine draw visitors near the town of the same name.
On Nigeria's UNESCO tentative list, this dramatic cluster of ancient settlement-topped boulders is among the country's most striking landscapes.
In West Africa, a colossal solitary monolith looms over the highway, dwarfing everything around it like a natural watchtower.
Located in central Nigeria just outside the planned capital, it rises some 300 metres straight from the surrounding plain.
Local lore reads a face into the weathered rock, and the Gwari people once used it as a defensive refuge against invaders.
Standing near Madalla on the road from Abuja to Kaduna, it appears on the back of the Nigerian 100-naira banknote.
Often nicknamed the Gateway to Abuja, this immense igneous outcrop is one of the largest monoliths on the continent.
In West Africa, a fortress of stacked granite boulders riddled with caves and tunnels shelters a city grown up around it.
Located in southwestern Nigeria's Ogun State, this outcrop gave refuge to a people fleeing 19th-century intertribal wars.
Egba settlers hid in its crevices, and the town that arose at its base takes its name from the rock that means God molded this.
Ancient shrines, a centuries-old cottage and aged priestesses still occupy the formation in the heart of the city of Abeokuta.
A staircase and elevator now carry visitors to its summit, the most famous landmark of the Yoruba town beneath it.
In West Africa, a vast prehistoric earthwork of ditches and ramparts encircles a territory larger than many modern cities.
Located in southwestern Nigeria's Ogun State, this rampart system winds for around 160 kilometres through the rainforest.
Reaching twenty metres in places, the moat is attributed to a wealthy noblewoman some link to the biblical Queen of Sheba.
Centered on the town of Ijebu-Ode, the immense rampart may be the largest single ancient monument in all of Africa.
Built around the 10th century and bearing the name of its legendary patron Bilikisu, it sits on Nigeria's UNESCO tentative list.
Off a West African coast lies a small island of pastel colonial houses, its cobbled lanes haunted by a brutal trade.
Located just offshore from Senegal's capital, this car-free isle was contested by Portuguese, Dutch, English and French powers.
Its salmon-pink slave house preserves cramped holding cells and a doorway opening straight onto the open Atlantic.
A short ferry ride from Dakar, the island's famous Maison des Esclaves draws pilgrims mourning the Middle Passage.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978, it is the most visited memorial to the slave trade in francophone Africa.
In West Africa, a shallow lagoon glows a startling strawberry pink, its waters saltier than almost any sea.
Located northeast of Senegal's capital near the Atlantic dunes, it is separated from the ocean by only a thin sandy ridge.
A salt-loving alga tints the brine, while laborers wade in to harvest mounds of salt heaped along the shore.
Once the finish line of the famous Paris-Dakar Rally, it sits a short drive from the city of Dakar.
Known locally as Retba, this hypersaline body is celebrated for a rosy hue that deepens under the midday sun.
In West Africa, a vast wetland of channels and lagoons teems with millions of migratory birds arriving from European winters.
Located in northern Senegal on the delta of a great river bordering Mauritania, it is one of the world's premier bird refuges.
Great white pelicans nest in immense colonies here, alongside flamingos, herons and waves of ducks that darken the sky.
Lying near the historic colonial town of Saint-Louis, the reserve forms a crucial stopover on the East Atlantic Flyway.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Senegal River delta, it ranks among the three most important ornithological sanctuaries on Earth.
In West Africa, terraced hills and laterite plateaus shelter peoples whose initiation rites and farming have endured for centuries.
Located in southeastern Senegal near the Guinea border in the Kédougou region, it spans rugged, isolated highlands.
Distinctive villages, sacred groves and elaborate masked coming-of-age ceremonies mark the Bedik and Fula communities living here.
Set amid the foothills of the Fouta Djallon near the town of Salémata, its inhabitants are renowned for vivid initiation festivals.
A UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape inscribed in 2012, it bears the name of one of the three peoples who shaped it.
In West Africa lie the earthen ruins of a powerful slave-trading kingdom's seat, a sprawl of mud-walled compounds and shrines.
Located in southern Benin, these dozen royal enclosures were raised by successive kings of a fearsome militarized realm.
Polychrome bas-reliefs depicting wars and the all-female warrior corps, the so-called Amazons, decorate the walls of the throne rooms.
Built between 1625 and 1900 in the town sharing their name, they housed monarchs like Ghezo and Behanzin of the Dahomey kingdom.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, this complex is the most important surviving monument of the pre-colonial Dahomey civilization.
In West Africa, a town of tens of thousands lives entirely on stilts above a lagoon, navigating its lanes by pirogue.
Located in southern Benin on Lake Nokoué near the economic capital, it is the largest lake settlement on the continent.
The Tofinu people built here to escape slave-raiders forbidden by religious taboo from entering the water, and never left.
Floating markets, a stilted mosque and church, and fish-farming pens fill the village a short boat ride from Cotonou.
Nicknamed the Venice of Africa, this aquatic town's name reportedly means we survived, recalling its origin as a refuge.
In West Africa, fortress-like mud dwellings shaped like little castles dot a remote range, livestock below and granaries above.
Located in northwestern Benin's Atacora hills near the Togo border, these towered homes belong to the Betammaribe ethnic group.
Each two-storey structure mixes living quarters, animal byres and turret-like silos, designed to repel raiders and the elements.
Concentrated in the Koutammakou landscape around Natitingou, the same architecture extends across the frontier into Togo.
Their Togolese counterparts are UNESCO-listed; the Beninese fortified mud houses are best known by a two-word local name meaning ethnic-group house.
In West Africa, a vast savanna reserve shelters one of the last viable populations of big game left in the region.
Located in northwestern Benin against the Atacora range and the Burkina Faso border, it forms part of a huge transboundary park complex.
Elephants, hippos, lions and the rare West African cheetah roam its grasslands, drawn to a meandering river and seasonal pools.
Named for the winding watercourse threading through it near the town of Tanguiéta, it is Benin's premier wildlife stronghold.
Part of a UNESCO-listed transboundary complex shared with Burkina Faso and Niger, it harbors the largest elephant herds remaining in West Africa.
On a beach in the southern Pacific lies a cluster of remarkable rounded stones, eroding slowly from the coastal cliffs behind them.
Found along the Otago coast of New Zealand's South Island, these spherical concretions formed over millions of years within ancient seabed mudstone.
Each grey sphere can reach two metres across, some cracked open to reveal honeycomb interiors of yellow calcite and dark veining.
Maori legend says they are gourds and food baskets washed ashore from a great wrecked canoe near a small fishing village.
Photographers flock at dawn to capture these famous 'dragon eggs' scattered along Koekohe Beach, between a small settlement and Hampden.
Set among rolling green farmland in the southwestern Pacific, a fantasy village of round doors and gardens was built into a hillside.
Located near Matamata on New Zealand's North Island, this permanent attraction recreates a fictional rural community of small folk.
Dozens of colourful burrow homes dot the slopes, complete with a mill, a stone bridge, and a tavern called the Green Dragon.
It served as the cinematic dwelling of Bilbo and Frodo in Peter Jackson's epic Middle-earth trilogies, set in the Shire.
Fans tour the famous Bag End and sip ale beside the pond in this carefully preserved set on the Alexander family sheep farm.
In a volcanically restless region of the southwestern Pacific, a steaming hot spring fizzes within a brilliantly coloured geothermal field.
This vivid hot spring lies near Rotorua on New Zealand's North Island, within the Wai-O-Tapu thermal wonderland.
Bubbling carbon dioxide rises through scalding water, while arsenic and antimony deposits paint its rim a striking orange ledge.
Formed some seven hundred years ago by a hydrothermal eruption, its effervescent surface inspired a fittingly bubbly beverage nickname.
Steam drifts across the emerald-and-orange basin beside the Artist's Palette and the famous Lady Knox Geyser of the Taupo Volcanic Zone.
In a geothermal corner of the southwestern Pacific, an abandoned settlement lies buried beneath ash and mud from a catastrophic eruption.
Near Rotorua on New Zealand's North Island, this excavated village once served tourists visiting the celebrated Pink and White Terraces.
A volcanic blast in 1886 from a nearby mountain entombed homes, a hotel, and a flour mill under metres of debris overnight.
Now an open-air heritage attraction, its unearthed whare and the tohunga's hut sit beside Lake Tarawera's shore.
Known as the 'Buried Village,' it preserves the lost gateway settlement destroyed when Mount Tarawera erupted, killing over a hundred people.
A vast field of steaming craters and rainbow-hued pools spreads across a volcanic plateau in the southwestern Pacific.
This thermal park sits south of Rotorua on New Zealand's North Island, fed by ancient hydrothermal activity beneath the surface.
Boardwalks wind past collapsed craters, sulphurous terraces, and a multicoloured mineral expanse known as the Artist's Palette.
Each morning at 10:15, a geyser is coaxed into eruption with soap, named after a colonial-era governor's wife, Lady Knox.
Its Maori name meaning 'sacred waters' marks this geothermal wonderland, home to the bubbling Champagne Pool and Devil's Bath.
A celebrated day-long trek crosses a volcanic plateau of steaming vents and vivid lakes in the southwestern Pacific.
This high mountain route traverses a dual World Heritage national park in the central North Island of New Zealand.
Hikers climb past the Red Crater and descend to the Emerald Lakes, their startling colours born of dissolved minerals.
The conical peak of Ngauruhoe alongside the trail doubled as the brooding Mount Doom in a famous film trilogy.
Often called the country's finest one-day walk, it skirts the active volcanoes of a vast massif near Mount Ruapehu.
Deep in the rainforest of the southern Pacific, a narrow rocky ravine cradles water of an almost unreal turquoise blue.
This gorge lies on the West Coast of New Zealand's South Island, fed by glacial meltwater from the Southern Alps.
The milky aquamarine colour comes from finely ground 'rock flour' suspended in water flowing from distant glaciers.
A swing bridge spans the chasm near a town once famed for gold rushes and now for carving local greenstone.
Reached from a coastal pounamu-trading town, its glowing blue waters wind between schist boulders and dense native bush.
At the windswept northern tip of a southwestern Pacific island nation, two great oceans collide in churning lines of foam.
This headland marks the far north of New Zealand, where the Tasman Sea meets the Pacific Ocean in visible turbulence.
A lone white lighthouse stands above the cape, and a solitary ancient pohutukawa clings to the cliff face below.
In Maori belief, spirits of the dead depart here, sliding down the tree's roots to begin their journey to the ancestral homeland.
Known to Maori as Te Rerenga Wairua, the 'leaping place of spirits,' it lies at the end of Ninety Mile Beach.
A symmetrical volcanic cone rises straight from the sea near a major harbour in the southwestern Pacific.
This island shield volcano sits in the Hauraki Gulf, a short ferry ride from New Zealand's largest city.
The youngest of its volcanic field, it erupted only about six hundred years ago, witnessed by early Maori settlers.
Its broad black basalt slopes host the world's largest pohutukawa forest, with lava caves threading beneath the scrub.
Visible on Auckland's eastern skyline, its near-perfect cone is reached by ferry from the downtown waterfront for summit hikes.
On a tropical Polynesian island, a deep circular swimming hole plunges through lava rock to brilliant turquoise water below.
This natural pool lies on the southeastern coast of Upolu in independent Samoa, ringed by lush gardens and palms.
A long wooden ladder descends sheer into the collapsed lava tube, where the sea connects through hidden underwater channels.
Its name in the local language means 'giant swimming hole,' a favourite of travel photographers across the region.
Near the village of Lotofaga, this famed sinkhole's deep emerald basin is reached by a steep ladder from the cliff top.
Hidden in jungle on a Polynesian island lies the largest ancient stone structure in the South Pacific, long overgrown.
This great earthen-and-stone pyramid stands on the island of Savai'i in independent Samoa, near former plantation land.
Built perhaps a thousand years ago, its flat-topped rectangular platform rises about twelve metres across a broad base.
Its purpose remains debated, possibly a chiefly residence, ceremonial site, or a platform for the traditional pigeon-snaring sport.
Locally nicknamed the 'Big Star,' this monumental Polynesian platform near Palauli is the region's largest pre-contact construction.
On a Melanesian island in the southwestern Pacific, an accessible active volcano hurls glowing lava into the night sky.
This stratovolcano rises on Tanna island in the archipelago nation of Vanuatu, drawing visitors to its crater rim.
Among the most continuously active volcanoes on Earth, its Strombolian explosions have erupted for centuries with reliable regularity.
Local cargo cults and the John Frum movement regard its fiery summit as a sacred and powerful spiritual place.
Often dubbed the 'world's most accessible volcano,' its booming crater can be approached on foot for nightly eruption displays.
In a Melanesian archipelago of the southwestern Pacific lies the first World Heritage site recognised for this island nation's heritage.
Spread across three sites in central Vanuatu, it preserves the residence, death place, and burial island of a legendary paramount leader.
Oral tradition recounts the powerful ruler who ended warfare among clans, his story confirmed by twentieth-century archaeological excavation.
His mass burial on the small island of Artok, with retainers laid alongside him, matches the legends passed down for generations.
Honouring a peacemaking ruler near Efate, this protected cultural landscape links Mangaas village, Lelepa island, and his sacred grave site.
In mainland Southeast Asia, this multi-tiered cascade tumbles through jungle into a series of turquoise mineral pools beloved by swimmers.
It lies in northern Laos, a short drive from the old royal capital famed for its riverside temples and saffron-robed monks.
Travertine limestone tints the water a vivid milky blue, and a nearby sanctuary shelters rescued sun bears in forested enclosures.
Visitors hike from the lower pools to a thundering main drop near the city of Luang Prabang on the Mekong's tributaries.
Its name means roughly 'deer dig' in the local tongue, and the staircase of azure basins makes it the region's most photographed waterfall.
On a volcanic island arc in maritime Southeast Asia, this peak is famous for crater lakes that mysteriously change color.
It rises on the island of Flores in eastern Indonesia, within a national park reached before dawn by waiting hikers.
Three summit lakes shift between turquoise, green, red, and black as dissolved minerals and volcanic gases react over time.
Local Lio people believe the colored waters hold the souls of the dead, sorted by age and deeds into separate basins.
Sunrise viewing platforms overlook the tri-colored craters, making this one of the most surreal volcanoes in the Lesser Sunda chain.
In maritime Southeast Asia, this stratovolcano is renowned for eerie electric-blue flames that flicker across its crater at night.
It stands at the eastern tip of Java in Indonesia, a popular dawn destination from the resort island just across the strait.
The world's largest highly acidic turquoise lake fills its caldera, where miners haul baskets of bright yellow sulphur by hand.
Ignited sulphuric gases create the famous blue fire visible before sunrise, near the town of Banyuwangi and Bali's western coast.
Photographers come for the glowing flames and the sight of laborers carrying ninety-kilogram loads up from the sulphur vents below.
Deep in Southeast Asia lies what is widely regarded as the largest natural cave passage on Earth.
It hides within a karst national park in central Vietnam, near the border with Laos and the old DMZ region.
Collapsed ceilings let sunlight pour in, nurturing jungles, rivers, and clouds inside chambers tall enough to hold skyscrapers.
Discovered by a local man in 1991 and surveyed in 2009, it sits in Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng among countless other caverns.
Limited expeditions cost thousands of dollars, and its 'Hand of Dog' stalagmite and dolines make it the planet's biggest cave.
In an island nation of Southeast Asia, ancient hand-carved farming steps climb steep mountainsides like a vast green staircase.
Carved by the Ifugao people in the Cordillera highlands of northern Luzon, they are often called an eighth wonder.
Built over two thousand years ago, the green steps are watered by an ingenious irrigation system fed from rainforest above.
The nearby Batad amphitheater and Hungduan clusters form a UNESCO group in the Philippine highlands north of Manila.
Indigenous farmers still plant heirloom grain on slopes said to stretch halfway to the sky if laid end to end.
On an island in Southeast Asia, more than a thousand symmetrical mounds rise from the plains like giant brown haystacks.
They cover the interior of Bohol island in the central Philippines, a province also home to tiny wide-eyed primates.
The limestone cones turn cocoa-colored when the grass dries in summer, giving the strange formation its sweet nickname.
Viewing platforms near Carmen overlook the dome-shaped mounds, which a legend attributes to the tears of a heartbroken giant.
Nearly twelve hundred near-identical conical knolls dot the field, making this geological oddity the Visayas' signature wonder.
In Southeast Asia, a collapsed cavern roof spotlights a royal pavilion bathed in a shaft of golden morning light.
It lies within a coastal national park in Thailand's Prachuap Khiri Khan province, south of the seaside town of Hua Hin.
A reef-and-jungle hike leads to two sinkholes where sunbeams illuminate an ornate four-gabled throne hall on the grotto floor.
King Chulalongkorn visited the green pavilion, called Kuha Karuhas, built to honor a passing Siamese monarch in 1890.
Photographers time visits so light strikes the gilded sala, the iconic image of Khao Sam Roi Yot's limestone grotto.
In western Southeast Asia stand the mist-shrouded ruins of a once-mighty trading kingdom dotted with thick-walled stone temples.
These remote shrines lie in the Rakhine State of Myanmar, far less visited than the famous plain of pagodas to the east.
The fortress-like Shittaung temple holds a labyrinth of Buddha-lined passages built to withstand both invaders and earthquakes.
A former capital that traded with Portuguese, Dutch, and Bengal merchants, it once rivaled European cities in wealth and size.
Rising from foggy paddy fields, its squat sandstone stupas make this the second-greatest archaeological site in the country after Bagan.
Scattered across an upland plateau in Southeast Asia lie thousands of mysterious giant stone vessels of unknown purpose.
They sit in Xiangkhouang province of Laos, a region heavily bombed during the Indochina conflicts of the twentieth century.
Iron Age people carved the hollow megaliths from sandstone two thousand years ago, perhaps as burial urns for the dead.
Cleared of unexploded ordnance, fields near Phonsavan display the largest urns weighing several tonnes each across rolling hills.
This enigmatic prehistoric landscape of carved containers became the nation's third UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.
In Southeast Asia, a ruined hillside sanctuary predates and inspired a much more famous temple complex to its south.
It climbs a sacred mountainside in southern Laos near the town of Champasak, beside the great river that drains the region.
Khmer builders aligned its causeways, barays, and shrines toward a spring believed to feed a sacred lingam in the sanctuary.
A natural mountain peak shaped like a lingam towers above the Mekong-side ruins, sanctifying the pre-Angkorian Hindu site.
This UNESCO-listed temple, whose name means 'mountain temple,' is the oldest major Khmer monument in the country.
In Southeast Asia, clustered brick towers in a jungle valley mark the spiritual heart of a vanished Hindu civilization.
The ruins lie in central Vietnam's Quảng Nam province, inland from the lantern-lit trading town of Hội An.
The Cham people raised these red-brick sanctuaries to Shiva between the fourth and thirteenth centuries using mortarless joints still puzzling experts.
American bombing in 1969 destroyed the grandest tower, yet dozens of crumbling Champa temples survive in the bowl-shaped valley.
This UNESCO site near Đà Nẵng is the foremost relic of the Champa kingdom that once ruled the central coast.
In a highland region of maritime Southeast Asia, a people famed for elaborate death rituals carve tombs into cliffs.
The area sits in the mountains of South Sulawesi in Indonesia, reached by winding roads from the port of Makassar.
Boat-shaped houses with soaring roofs called tongkonan line villages where lavish multi-day funerals involve buffalo sacrifice.
Wooden effigies called tau-tau gaze from cliff balconies, guarding the bones of nobles buried in caves and hanging graves.
Visitors come to witness the elaborate funeral feasts of this culture, among Indonesia's most distinctive ethnic traditions.
In Southeast Asia, serene Buddha statues and lotus-bud spires rise among lily ponds at the birthplace of a kingdom.
This ruined first capital lies in north-central Thailand, north of the larger and later royal city now also in ruins.
Founded in the thirteenth century, it gave rise to the graceful walking Buddha style and an early form of the Thai script.
The seated Buddha of Wat Si Chum and the elegant Wat Mahathat anchor a ruin-field whose name means 'dawn of happiness.'
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, this cradle of the nation's first independent realm is celebrated each year with lantern-lit festivals.
On a dusty plain in Southeast Asia, thousands of brick temples and stupas stretch to the horizon in every direction.
The ancient capital sits in central Myanmar along a great river, its temples often viewed at dawn from hot-air balloons.
Built between the ninth and thirteenth centuries by a powerful Buddhist dynasty, over two thousand monuments still stand today.
The gilded Shwezigon and towering Ananda temple rise above the plain beside the Irrawaddy, near the town of Nyaung-U.
Earthquakes have toppled many spires, yet this UNESCO-listed sea of pagodas remains one of Asia's greatest archaeological wonders.
In Southeast Asia, this rugged limestone wilderness holds one of the planet's oldest karst landscapes riddled with vast caves.
It spreads across Quảng Bình province in central Vietnam, hugging the mountainous frontier shared with neighboring Laos.
Underground rivers and grottoes honeycomb the reserve, including some of the longest and largest cave systems ever surveyed.
Boat trips glide into the namesake river cavern, while explorers descend into Paradise Cave's cathedral-like stalactite halls.
This twice-inscribed UNESCO reserve, whose karst is around 400 million years old, shelters the world's biggest cave passage.
In maritime Southeast Asia, a cluster of rugged islands shelters the world's largest living lizard amid pink-sand beaches.
The reserve lies in the Lesser Sunda Islands of Indonesia, between the islands of Sumbawa and Flores.
Giant venomous monitors up to three meters long prowl the savanna hills, ambushing deer and water buffalo.
Rangers guide trekkers past the fearsome dragons on Rinca and the main island, with manta-rich reefs offshore.
A UNESCO site and one of the New7Wonders of Nature, it is named for the prehistoric reptile found nowhere else.
Perched on a cliff edge in Southeast Asia, this ancient temple commands sweeping views over plains far below.
It stands atop the Dângrêk escarpment in northern Cambodia, on a long-disputed border with Thailand.
A series of sanctuaries and stairways climbs 800 meters along the ridge, dedicated by Khmer kings to the god Shiva.
A World Court ruling in 1962 awarded the cliff-top shrine to Cambodia, sparking deadly clashes again in 2008 and 2011.
This UNESCO temple, built across centuries by the same empire behind Angkor, hugs a dramatic precipice high above the lowlands.
In Southeast Asia, a seven-tiered jungle cascade pours over emerald limestone into pools full of nibbling fish.
It lies in the Kanchanaburi province of western Thailand, not far from a notorious wartime railway bridge over a river.
The uppermost tier is said to resemble the three-headed elephant of Hindu myth that lends the cascade its name.
Hikers climb past turquoise terraces in a national park near the Burmese frontier, west of the city of Bangkok.
Each of the cascade's stepped levels has its own name, drawing swimmers to one of the country's loveliest waterfalls.
In Southeast Asia, thousands of jagged limestone islets rise from emerald seawater like dragon teeth in the mist.
This sheltered gulf indents the northeastern coast of Vietnam, a few hours by road from the capital city.
Floating fishing villages, sea caves, and hidden lagoons fill the waters, whose name means 'descending dragon' in local legend.
Junk boats cruise among karst towers near the port city of Haiphong, with sister inlets extending to the northeast.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site and New7Wonders finalist, its drowned karst seascape is the country's most iconic waterscape.
In Southeast Asia, a vast expanse of pitted rock emerges from a great river in the dry season, dubbed a 'canyon.'
It surfaces along the Mekong in Ubon Ratchathani province of eastern Thailand, near the border with Laos.
Swirling currents have drilled thousands of bowl-shaped potholes into the bedrock, exposed only when the river runs low.
Its name claims 'three thousand holes,' and the moonlike sandstone flats stretch for several kilometers along the channel.
Locals call it the country's Grand Canyon, a surreal pockmarked riverbed revealed each hot season before the monsoon floods return.
In Southeast Asia, a hillside limestone cavern is crammed with thousands of gilded Buddha images donated over centuries.
It overlooks a lake in the Shan State of Myanmar, in the cool hills east of the country's central plain.
More than eight thousand statues in every size and style fill the winding chambers, lit by candles and shafts of daylight.
A local legend tells of a prince slaying a giant spider that trapped seven princesses at the cave's mouth near the town.
Pilgrims climb covered stairways to the glittering grotto, one of the most image-packed Buddhist caverns in the nation.
In maritime Southeast Asia, smoking cones rise from a vast volcanic sea of ash beneath a towering summit.
This national park sits in East Java, Indonesia, where a Hindu minority still makes offerings into a steaming crater.
A jeep crosses the Sea of Sand at dawn to a caldera holding several volcanoes, with the country's highest peak behind.
An indigenous highland people hurl crops and livestock into the active crater during the Yadnya Kasada festival each year.
Sunrise crowds at the King Kong viewpoint frame the smoking cone against Java's highest peak, the island's most famous volcanic panorama.
On the western edge of the great southern continent, thousands of stone spires rise from a desert of yellow sand.
Within a national park north of a major western city, these limestone columns stand scattered across a windswept coastal dune field.
Formed from ancient seashell deposits hardened around plant roots and later exposed by shifting sands, some reach several metres tall.
Set in Nambung National Park near Cervantes, the eerie field of jagged pillars looks like a petrified forest or a lunar graveyard.
Visitors drive a loop among the pointed yellow towers at dawn, when long shadows make the desert resemble a field of standing tombstones.
In the remote tropical northwest of the largest southern continent, a rare tidal phenomenon turns the sea into a rushing torrent.
Hidden in the rugged Kimberley region of the country's west, seawater forces through narrow gaps between rocky ridges.
Enormous tides push water through two slim coastal gorges faster than it can pass, creating a sideways waterfall that reverses with the tide.
In Talbot Bay near the Buccaneer Archipelago, seaplanes deliver visitors who ride boats through the surging gaps between cliffs.
A naturalist once called it one of the greatest natural wonders of the world, a cascade that flows flat instead of dropping down.
Deep in the arid heart of the world's driest inhabited continent lies the country's lowest natural point.
In the dry interior of the outback nation, this vast salt pan usually appears as a blinding white crust of mineral deposits.
Only rarely, after floods drain inland from distant rains, does it fill to become the largest lake in the country.
Set in the northern part of its namesake South Australian region, its flooding triggers mass breeding of pelicans and other waterbirds.
Speed record attempts once roared across its baking salt surface, and its filling draws crowds to witness a desert transformed into an inland sea.
On the tropical northeastern coast of the southern continent, dense jungle meets a turquoise sea fringed by coral.
In the far north of the country's eastern state, this headland is where the world's oldest rainforest reaches the shore.
Here the Daintree forest tumbles down to white sand, and crocodiles, cassowaries and ancient ferns inhabit the meeting of two World Heritage areas.
A famous navigator named this promontory after his ship struck a nearby reef, calling it the spot where his troubles began.
North of Cairns and the Daintree River crossing, its name records the captain's lament that here began all his misfortunes.
Far out in the Tasman Sea east of the southern continent, a crescent of green volcanic peaks juts from the ocean.
Belonging to the eastern state of the outback nation, this tiny island limits visitor numbers to protect its fragile ecology.
Twin forested mountains tower over a sheltered lagoon edged by the world's southernmost coral reef and many endemic species.
Mount Gower and Mount Lidgbird dominate the skyline, while the rare stick insect once thought extinct survives on nearby Ball's Pyramid.
A World Heritage gem about six hundred kilometres offshore, its lagoon and cloud-forest summits made it a model of conservation.
In the red desert centre of the great southern continent, huge rounded boulders are scattered across an arid plain.
Beside the highway running through the heart of the outback nation's central territory, these granite spheres balance precariously.
Weathering split and rounded the ancient granite into enormous orbs, some seemingly stacked or perched on the verge of toppling.
Sacred to the Warumungu people who call them Karlu Karlu, the formation lies south of Tennant Creek along the Stuart Highway.
Glowing deep red at sunset, the giant ball-shaped rocks look as if dropped by a mischievous deity across the central desert.
In the dry inland of the southern continent lies a dusty basin holding some of humanity's oldest evidence outside Africa.
Within the outback nation's most populous southeastern state, this dry lakebed sits in a semi-arid World Heritage region.
Eroding sand dunes here yielded ancient cremated and buried human remains tens of thousands of years old, among the earliest known ceremonial burials.
Part of the Willandra Lakes region, its crescent-shaped clay-and-sand dunes are nicknamed the Walls of China and glow at sunset.
The remains called the Lady and the Man, dated to around forty thousand years, made this dry basin a milestone of human prehistory.
In the remote arid interior of the western part of the southern continent rises an enormous solitary rock mass.
Deep in the outback of the country's largest western state, this monolith dwarfs the more famous central icon.
Often billed as the largest rock in the world, it is actually an exposed anticline of ancient sandstone covering far more ground than its red rival.
Known to the Wajarri people as Burringurrah, it stands about eight hundred metres above the surrounding plain in a vast cattle-station landscape.
Twice the bulk of the celebrated tourist monolith near Alice Springs, this lesser-known giant sees only a trickle of determined visitors.
On a large wildlife-rich island off the southern coast of the great southern continent, weathered boulders perch above the sea.
Within a national park on the country's third-largest island, off its central-south state, these sculpted granite forms crown a dome.
Wind, rain and salt spray hollowed and shaped the orange-lichened granite over half a billion years into surreal organic curves.
Set in Flinders Chase National Park on Kangaroo Island, the cluster sits atop a granite outcrop plunging into the Southern Ocean.
Their bizarre scooped and clawed shapes, glowing in low sun, look like abstract modern sculptures balanced precariously above crashing waves.
In the iron-rich interior of the western part of the great southern continent, deep gorges slice through ancient red rock.
Within the rugged Pilbara region of the country's largest western state, narrow chasms hide hidden pools and tiered waterfalls.
Carved into rock over two billion years old, its banded iron formations form some of the planet's oldest exposed geology.
Hikers descend into gorges like Hancock and Weano to reach swimming holes such as the spiral-walled Kermit's Pool and Fern Pool.
Surrounded by vast iron-ore mining country, its plunging crimson canyons and turquoise pools sit beneath the state's second-highest peak.
In the arid heart of East Asia lies a landscape of layered sandstone painted in impossible stripes of color.
Set in the Gansu corridor of northern China, near the ancient Silk Road oasis town once guarding the Hexi passage.
Sixty million years of mineral-rich deposits and erosion created ridges striped in rust, gold, cream, and emerald hues.
Often called the Rainbow Mountains, these formations near the city of the same provincial corridor draw photographers at sunset.
A UNESCO-listed example of petrologic relief, its candy-striped hills look digitally enhanced yet are entirely natural sediment.
Carved into a desert cliff in East Asia, hundreds of grottoes preserve a thousand years of Buddhist devotion.
Near the Silk Road town in China's Gansu province where caravans crossed from the Taklamakan into the empire.
Nearly five hundred decorated chambers hold vivid murals and clay statues spanning the fourth to fourteenth centuries.
A walled-up library here yielded the world's oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, beside Dunhuang's dunes.
These Caves of the Thousand Buddhas form one of the greatest repositories of Buddhist art ever discovered.
Granite pillars wreathed in mist rise above an ancient Taoist landscape in eastern East Asia.
Located in China's Jiangxi province, this peak is a sacred mountain of the Taoist tradition.
Weathered columns bear names like the Goddess and the Python, eroded over millions of years into human-like silhouettes.
Pilgrim paths and cliff-clinging temples honor the three pure ones, deities for whom the mountain is revered.
A UNESCO natural site, its fog-shrouded spires inspired the floating peaks of countless Chinese ink paintings.
On a great muddy river of East Asia, a broad torrent narrows violently and plunges into a stone gorge.
Straddling the border of Shaanxi and Shanxi provinces in China, it churns the silt-laden Yellow River.
The water funnels from a wide bed into a channel barely thirty meters across, roaring like a giant teapot pouring.
Its name means the spout-mouth, and the ochre spray here features on the back of the fifty-yuan banknote.
The largest golden-hued cascade on Earth, its thunderous ochre torrent is a powerful symbol of the Chinese nation.
Across paddy fields in southern East Asia rise tall fortified towers blending Western and Eastern styles.
In China's Guangdong province, these multi-storey structures were built by returning overseas emigrants in the early twentieth century.
Greek columns, Baroque domes, and Islamic arches crown defensive village towers raised against bandits and floods.
Funded by Cantonese diaspora wealth from the Americas, over a thousand once dotted this watery delta countryside.
A UNESCO site, these eclectic watchtowers stand as monuments to migration, remittance, and architectural fusion in the Pearl delta.
Thousands of quartzite sandstone pillars pierce the clouds of a subtropical forest in central East Asia.
Within Hunan province in China, this area neighbors the famous Wulingyuan scenic zone of vertical spires.
Sheer columns up to several hundred meters tall stand draped in mist, draped with pines clinging to bare rock.
Named for an ancient rebel peasant leader proclaimed son of heaven, its peaks loom over Zhangjiajie's wild stone forest.
Its towering pinnacles helped inspire the floating Hallelujah Mountains of the film Avatar, drawing crowds to glass-walled cable cars.
A perfectly preserved walled merchant town survives almost intact within the heartland of East Asia.
In China's Shanxi province, this Ming-era city kept its rammed-earth ramparts and grid of grey-brick courtyards.
Here the country's first draft banks emerged, handling silver remittances across the empire from austere shop counters.
Six-kilometer battlements with seventy-two watchtowers enclose a labyrinth of timber temples and family compounds.
A UNESCO site, this banking cradle is the finest surviving example of a traditional Han Chinese county capital.
Colossal stone Buddhas sit carved into a sandstone ridge near a coal-rich frontier of East Asia.
Outside the city of Datong in China's Shanxi province, these grottoes date to the Northern Wei dynasty.
Over fifty thousand statues fill some two hundred fifty caves, the tallest seated figure rising seventeen meters high.
Carved in the fifth century, the imagery fuses Indian, Central Asian, and Chinese motifs along old caravan routes.
A UNESCO site, this is one of three great ancient Buddhist sculptural complexes hewn into the cliffs of China.
A tiered cascade tumbles through karst jungle on an international border in tropical East Asia.
In China's Guangxi region, the falls spill along the frontier shared with neighboring Vietnam.
Multiple curtains of water drop over limestone shelves into a green river where bamboo rafts drift between two nations.
Said to be the largest transnational waterfall in Asia, an old boundary marker stone stands among the spray.
Locals on both banks trade across the cataract, the only waterfall on Earth straddling these two countries' shared boundary.
A vast seated figure is carved directly from a red cliff above a river confluence in East Asia.
In China's Sichuan province, it faces sacred Mount Emei where three turbulent rivers meet.
Begun in the eighth century to calm deadly currents, its ears alone stretch seven meters and trees could grow on its shoulders.
At seventy-one meters, this Tang-dynasty colossus is the tallest pre-modern stone statue of its kind in the world.
A UNESCO site, pilgrims descend cliff-cut stairways past its serene face to stand beside feet larger than a bus.
An elegant stone arch spans a river on the northern plain of East Asia, astonishingly old yet still standing.
In China's Hebei province, this crossing dates to the Sui dynasty around the year six hundred.
Its open-spandrel design, with smaller arches piercing the haunches, was a structural breakthrough centuries ahead of Europe.
Designed by craftsman Li Chun, it is the oldest surviving open-spandrel segmental arch bridge anywhere on Earth.
Often called the Safe Crossing Bridge, this fourteen-centuries-old span endured floods, wars, and earthquakes intact.
A small island in an inland sea of East Asia reinvented itself as a sanctuary of modern art.
Set in Japan's Seto Inland Sea off the coast near Takamatsu, it blends fishing village life with avant-garde galleries.
Concrete museums by architect Tadao Ando sink into hillsides, lit by natural shafts framing works by Monet and Turrell.
A giant polka-dotted yellow pumpkin by Yayoi Kusama perches on a pier, the island's unmistakable emblem.
Centerpiece of the Setouchi art movement, this Benesse-backed isle is a global pilgrimage for contemporary installation lovers.
A narrow basalt canyon in East Asia channels a clear river between columns of ancient volcanic rock.
On the southern island of Kyushu in Japan, it lies in Miyazaki prefecture amid forested mountains.
Hexagonal cliffs formed by cooled lava frame a slender stream where visitors row boats beneath a slim waterfall.
Local legend says the sun goddess Amaterasu hid in a nearby cave, making this a cradle of Japanese creation myth.
Sacred kagura dances reenact luring the sun from her cave, performed nightly near this mist-filled mythic ravine.
Steep-roofed farmhouses cluster in a snowbound mountain valley of East Asia, built to shed heavy winter loads.
In Japan's Gifu prefecture, this remote hamlet sits among the rugged ranges of the central Honshu interior.
Thatched roofs angled like praying hands rise sixty degrees, sheltering multiple floors once used for silkworm rearing.
The gassho-zukuri style defines this village, illuminated each winter when its snow-laden roofs glow under floodlights.
A UNESCO site, its lamp-lit thatched cottages amid deep drifts are among the most photographed scenes of rural Japan.
A rain-drenched round island in East Asia shelters primeval forests of immense, moss-clad conifers.
Lying south of Kyushu in Japan's Kagoshima prefecture, it rises steeply from subtropical shores to alpine peaks.
Ancient cedars thousands of years old twist through fog and waterfalls, their gnarled roots blanketed in emerald moss.
Its mystical green woodlands helped inspire the enchanted forest of the animated film Princess Mononoke.
A UNESCO site, the venerable Jomon Sugi cedar here is reckoned among the oldest living trees in the world.
A surprising stretch of windblown desert dunes lines a northern coast of an East Asian island nation.
In Japan, these sands sweep along the Sea of Japan shore facing the Korean peninsula.
Sculpted by wind into ridges and basins over sixteen kilometers, they reach fifty meters high beside crashing surf.
Camel rides and paragliders share the slopes, and a nearby museum carves elaborate temporary statues from the sand.
The country's largest such dune field, this unexpected coastal Sahara is the pride of its namesake prefecture.
A loop of river embraces a living clan settlement preserving centuries-old aristocratic life in East Asia.
On the Korean peninsula near the city of Andong, tiled and thatched homes cluster within a tight river bend.
Yangban gentry mansions and commoner cottages survive intact, the settlement's name meaning the river that flows around.
Famous for its centuries-old masked dance dramas mocking nobles and monks, performed with grotesque carved wooden faces.
A UNESCO site, this Confucian-clan hamlet hosted a visiting British queen and embodies traditional Joseon settlement layout.
A serene granite Buddha sits within an artificial domed cave on a mountainside in East Asia.
Above the ancient capital region near Gyeongju on the Korean peninsula, it overlooks the eastern sea.
Built in the eighth century by the Silla kingdom, its hand-cut stone rotunda houses a meditating figure flanked by reliefs.
The serene image faces sunrise over the water, paired with a nearby temple as a single UNESCO listing.
A masterpiece of East Asian Buddhist art, its precisely engineered dome is a marvel of ancient Korean stonework.
Black hexagonal stone columns step down into pounding surf along a volcanic coast in East Asia.
On a subtropical island south of the Korean peninsula, these basalt pillars line the southern shore.
Formed when molten lava met the sea and cooled into geometric vertical bundles up to twenty meters tall.
Set on Jeju Island, the columnar cliffs draw crowds who watch waves explode against the angular ramparts.
A designated natural monument, this organ-pipe coastline is one of the finest basalt column formations in the region.
A walled Buddhist compound stands on a vast steppe in East Asia, ringed by over a hundred white stupas.
In central Mongolia, it rose beside the ruins of the abandoned imperial capital of the Mongol Empire.
Built in the sixteenth century using stones from nearby Karakorum, it survived purges that razed most monasteries here.
Within the Orkhon Valley, its temple roofs blend Tibetan and Chinese styles amid the grassland near old Kharkhorin.
The oldest surviving Buddhist monastery in the country, its stupa-studded wall encloses a fragile relic of the steppe faith.
Eroded red sandstone bluffs glow like embers at sunset across a great desert of East Asia.
In the Gobi of southern Mongolia, these badlands stretch beneath an immense empty sky.
Wind and time carved the ochre escarpments into ravines that turn fiery orange in the low evening light.
Here in the 1920s an American expedition unearthed the first scientifically recognized nest of fossilized dinosaur eggs.
Known by their Mongolian name Bayanzag, these crimson badlands are among the most famous dinosaur fossil sites on Earth.
Towering golden dunes rise abruptly from gravel plains and grass in a great cold desert of East Asia.
Within the Gobi of southern Mongolia, they lie below the snow-streaked Altai foothills.
Stretching over a hundred kilometers, some crests reach three hundred meters and emit a low roar when the sand slides.
Camel herders water their two-humped Bactrians at a spring-fed stream curling along the dunes' northern base.
Nicknamed the Singing Sands, these are among the tallest and longest dune fields in this landlocked steppe nation.
This protected reserve sits in the far north of a landlocked country, near a border famous for cattle ranching and red earth.
Dramatic forested hills rise abruptly from the surrounding plain, creating a striking landscape unusual for this otherwise flat region of the continent.
Archaeologists have documented pre-Columbian rock art and engravings on cliff faces scattered throughout the park's wooded valleys and caves.
The site marks where a devastating five-year regional war ended in 1870, when the besieged national leader was killed by allied troops.
A memorial commemorates Marshal Francisco Solano López, who died here, and the location lies in the Amambay department of the country.
Tucked into subtropical Atlantic forest of a landlocked nation, this reserve protects waterfalls, streams and dense greenery roughly south of the capital.
Within the wooded grounds stand the reconstructed ruins of an old iron foundry, an early industrial complex destroyed during a nineteenth-century war.
The foundry, called La Rosada, once cast cannons and munitions for the country's army before invading allied forces razed it in 1869.
Hiking trails lead past cascades, swimming pools and a restored waterwheel, blending natural beauty with preserved early industrial heritage.
It lies in the Paraguarí department, one of the oldest protected areas of its country, established in 1973.

hard.name: Valle de la Luna La Paz

clues.description: On the outskirts of one of the world's highest administrative capitals, eroded clay spires form a maze of pale jagged pinnacles and gullies.
The labyrinth of needle-like formations was carved by wind and rain stripping away soft sediment from an ancient mountain that once stood here.
Walking trails wind between towers of grey and beige earth, with the high Andean city sprawling up the slopes in the distance.
It lies in the Mallasa district of a metropolis seated in a deep canyon below the snowcapped Illimani peak.
This formation sits just south of the seat of government of a landlocked Andean country named for a liberation hero.
In the rugged highlands of an Andean nation, this remote park is celebrated for some of the continent's best-preserved Cretaceous fossil evidence.
Thousands of dinosaur footprints are pressed into tilted rock slabs, recording creatures that walked here over sixty-five million years ago.
A deep limestone canyon, the Vergel gorge, plunges hundreds of metres, while caverns like Umajalanta host stalactites and blind cave fish.
Located in the Potosí department's northern reaches, it is reached by a winding mountain road from the city of Cochabamba.
The landscape combines folded sedimentary ridges, fossil tracks and karst caves in a sparsely populated corner of the central highlands.
Perched on a forested ridge where the Andes meet the eastern lowlands, this site overlooks a transition zone of cloud forest and dry valleys.
Its centrepiece is a single enormous sandstone outcrop carved with channels, basins, niches and animal figures by pre-Columbian peoples.
Once a ceremonial centre, it was later occupied by an Andean empire and then by Spanish settlers, layering cultures across one carved rock.
Designated a World Heritage Site in 1998, it lies in the Santa Cruz department of a landlocked country in the continent's heart.
The nearby small town shares its name and sits along the old road linking the highland city of Cochabamba with eastern plains.
This stone military fort guards a coastal frontier near the Atlantic, in a small nation wedged between two much larger neighbours.
Begun by the Portuguese in 1762 and completed by the Spanish, it changed hands repeatedly during colonial rivalries over this contested borderland.
Its thick pentagonal ramparts and cannon emplacements now sit within a national park of dunes, lagoons and planted pine forest.
The structure overlooks an Atlantic coastline in the Rocha department, near the resort town of Punta del Diablo.
Today restored as a museum, it anchors a park bearing the same saint's name in the country whose capital is Montevideo.
In the gently rolling hill country of a small South American republic, a surprisingly deep ravine cuts through the grassland landscape.
The steep-sided gorge shelters a humid microclimate, allowing subtropical plants and ferns to thrive far south of their usual range.
It became the country's first protected landscape in 1986 and is a haven for nesting raptors, including vultures that give it its name.
The reserve lies in the Treinta y Tres department, amid the Cuchilla Grande range of low ridges crossing the interior.
Trails descend to a clear stream at the bottom of the cleft, a rare rugged feature in a nation known for flat pasture.
In the dry, thorny scrubland of a vast country's semi-arid interior, an ancient riverbed preserves traces of prehistoric giants.
Hundreds of fossilised footprints, left in mud over a hundred million years ago, are imprinted across exposed rock slabs along a creek.
The tracks record several species of reptiles crossing what was once a lake margin, now hardened into the bed of a seasonal river.
It lies near the town of Sousa in the state of Paraíba, in the northeastern backlands of the country known as the sertão.
This open-air paleontological park preserves one of the largest concentrations of such tracks in the largest nation on its continent.
A string of roughly forty limestone islands lies scattered along the northern shore of a vast gulf in eastern North America.
These islands shelter rare arctic-alpine plants and a major colony of comical orange-billed seabirds that nest in the cliffs each summer.
Centuries of pounding waves have carved the soft sedimentary stone into giant mushroom-shaped monoliths standing alone on the tidal flats.
The islands form a federally protected reserve off the coast of a French-speaking province, opposite the long island of Anticosti.
Reached by boat from villages along Route 138, the chain sits between the Saint Lawrence estuary and the rugged interior of the Cote-Nord.
This granite peak holds the record for the greatest purely vertical drop on the planet, an overhanging face plunging well over a thousand metres.
The mountain rises within a remote glacier-filled park on a large arctic island near the territory's main fjord-cut interior.
Climbers attempting the sheer wall must first trek for days across a treeless tundra pass linking two deep glacial valleys.
It lies inside Auyuittuq, a reserve whose Inuktitut name means the land that never melts, in a northern Canadian territory created in 1999.
The nearest community is the hamlet of Pangnirtung, the gateway settlement for hikers entering this far-northern wilderness.
A single plunge of water drops roughly one hundred and forty metres into a deep amphitheatre bowl, far taller than the famous border cataract to the east.
In deep winter the spray freezes into an enormous cone of ice that can build to over fifty metres high at the base.
The cataract sits within a volcanic plateau park renowned for its many waterfalls, fed by the Murtle River.
It lies in the interior of a western Canadian province famed for its Pacific coastline and Rocky Mountain ranges.
The protected area, accessed near the town of Clearwater off the Yellowhead Highway, is nicknamed Canada's Waterfall Park.
From a high overlook a river coils back on itself in tight loops, travelling several kilometres while advancing barely over one in a straight line.
These deeply entrenched meanders cut more than three hundred metres into ancient grey rock layers laid down some three hundred million years ago.
The site is a textbook example geologists cite to explain how a winding lowland stream became trapped as the surrounding plateau slowly rose.
It lies on the Colorado Plateau in a southwestern American state, near the small town of Mexican Hat and the borders with the Navajo Nation.
A small state park overlook north of the river offers the classic view of the snaking watercourse before it joins a larger reservoir-fed system.
Smooth rounded mounds display vivid horizontal bands of red, gold, black and tan, each stripe recording a different ancient climate era.
The colourful claystone hills are part of a fossil-rich monument preserving millions of years of plant and mammal evolution in old river floodplains.
The hues shift dramatically with moisture and light, glowing most intensely after rain or at sunset across the bare slopes.
This is one of three scattered units of a national monument along a high-desert river in a Pacific Northwest state.
Lying near the small town of Mitchell, the area is named for the John Day River that drains this remote interior region.
Thousands of slender rock spires and balanced pinnacles crowd a mountain wonderland, eroded from compressed volcanic ash deposited by a massive eruption.
The Apache once used this rugged sky-island range as a stronghold, and it bears the name of that people in the local landscape.
Cooler forested heights here form a biological island surrounded by hot desert, hosting species found nowhere else nearby.
The protected area sits in the far southeastern corner of a southwestern state, near the New Mexico line and the towns of Willcox and Bowie.
A scenic drive climbs to Massai Point, overlooking the eroded ash-flow towers nicknamed the Wonderland of Rocks.
A ring of sheer granite spires up to two thousand metres tall encircles a hanging glacial valley deep in the subarctic mountains.
Despite its forbidding name, the towers draw elite climbers from around the world to ascend a famous polished wall called the Lotus Flower Tower.
Reaching the meadow basin below the peaks usually requires a float-plane landing on a remote lake followed by a steep boulder-strewn hike.
The amphitheatre lies in a vast wilderness territory in northwestern Canada, near the Yukon border within the Ragged Range.
It sits above the Vampire Peaks region not far from the South Nahanni watershed, among the least-visited alpine areas on the continent.
A grassy volcanic crater on a remote southeastern Pacific island holds a freshwater reedy lake within its weathered tuff slopes.
Its compressed volcanic rock was the source material from which an isolated Polynesian society carved its monolithic ancestor figures.
Hundreds of unfinished statues remain embedded in the quarry walls, some still attached to the bedrock that birthed them.
Partly buried torsos dot the outer slopes, their heads protruding above the soil that accumulated over many centuries.
This quarry lies inland on a Chilean territory famous for its great stone heads, far from any other landmass.
Said to be one of the largest saltwater lagoons on Earth, it is enclosed by a double barrier reef in the southwestern Pacific.
Hundreds of low coral and volcanic islets shelter calm turquoise water rich in fish, turtles and intricate coral gardens.
Local woodcarvers are renowned for ebony and kerosene-wood carvings of sharks, dolphins and ancestral motifs sold across the region.
It stretches along the New Georgia islands, between Vangunu and the larger landmasses of the western province.
This lagoon lies within the Solomon Islands, a Melanesian nation east of Papua New Guinea.
This vast ring-shaped coral structure in the central Pacific encloses a lagoon so large a smaller island could fit inside it.
Two narrow ocean passes funnel powerful tidal currents, drawing divers to drift among sharks, dolphins and manta rays.
More than two hundred motu, low islets of coral rubble and palms, string together around the immense central body of water.
Its name in the local Polynesian tongue means immense sky, evoking the endless horizon seen from its flat shores.
Part of the Tuamotu chain, it belongs to French Polynesia, the overseas collectivity centred on Tahiti.
A triangular lagoon in the South Pacific encloses brilliant shallow water dotted with sandy uninhabited motu along its outer reef.
A single volcanic high island rises at its northern point, while coral islets fringe the rest of the encircling barrier.
One famous islet shaped like a footprint draws day-trippers across the flats by boat to wade its powdery sandbars.
It lies in the northern group of an island nation in free association with New Zealand, named for an English navigator.
The country's largest island and capital, Avarua on Rarotonga, sits roughly 220 kilometres to the southeast.
On a Pacific island regarded as a cradle of Polynesian voyaging stands a sacred ceremonial complex of stone platforms beside a lagoon.
Its open-air temple, paved with coral slabs and standing stones, was a hub for religious and political gatherings across the eastern ocean.
Voyagers from distant archipelagos carried stones from here to consecrate new temples, linking far-flung islands in a shared spiritual network.
The marae sits at the edge of a pass in the barrier reef on the island of Raiatea in the Leeward group.
This World Heritage cultural landscape lies in French Polynesia, northwest of the better-known island of Bora Bora.
A long thin crescent of coral in the southwestern Pacific shelters a lagoon often called among the finest in the region.
Its single beach of fine white sand runs unbroken for many kilometres along the western shore facing the calm inner water.
Raised limestone cliffs at the northern and southern tips contrast with the low palm-fringed central strip barely above sea level.
It forms part of the Loyalty group, an outer chain of a French overseas territory in Melanesia.
The territory's capital, Nouméa, lies on the larger mainland island Grande Terre to the southwest.
In a dry interior region of the southern continent, a long crescent of eroded sand and clay rises above a vanished lakebed.
Wind and water have sculpted the pale dunes into a wall of fluted ridges, gullies and miniature pinnacles.
These lunettes preserve some of the oldest human remains outside Africa, including ceremonial burials over forty thousand years old.
The lakes here dried up around fifteen thousand years ago, leaving fossil shorelines studied for ancient climate clues.
This eroded barrier lies in far western New South Wales, within a heritage-listed region of dry Pleistocene lake basins.
A near-perfect curve of white sand forms a half-moon cove on the eastern coast of a large southern island.
Pink-tinged granite peaks rise sharply behind the beach, their colour deepening at sunset above clear sheltered water.
A short steep walk to a saddle lookout reveals the bay's distinctive shape, named for its resemblance to a drinking vessel.
It lies within a coastal national park on a peninsula whose granite domes are known as the Hazards.
The cove sits on the Freycinet Peninsula in Tasmania, the island state south of the Australian mainland.
On a remote southern coastline, blindingly white quartz beaches meet turquoise water beneath low granite and gneiss peaks.
Kangaroos famously lounge on the squeaky sand of one bay, an unusual sight against the Southern Ocean backdrop.
Ancient rounded headlands, among the oldest rock in the region, separate a string of sheltered coves and offshore islets.
A coastal national park here faces the Recherche Archipelago, a scatter of more than a hundred granite islands.
It lies east of the town of Esperance on the southern coast of Western Australia.
On a wild, little-visited southern coast, a wave-cut rock platform reveals one of the world's most extensive fossil forests.
Petrified tree stumps and fallen logs, turned to stone around 180 million years ago, lie exposed at low tide.
Rare yellow-eyed penguins waddle ashore here at dusk, and dolphins frequent the adjacent sheltered sandy inlet.
The trees grew in a Jurassic floodplain related to ancestors of modern conifers, later entombed by volcanic sediment.
This rugged shore lies in the Catlins region of New Zealand's South Island, near the country's southern extremity.
A rocky headland on the wild western coast of a temperate island was given an unflattering name by an early European explorer.
A clifftop walkway leads to a viewing platform above a noisy colony of fur seals breeding on the rocks below.
A white lighthouse marks the point, warning ships off a coast battered by swells rolling in from the open sea.
The explorer who charted it in 1770 first called it Rocky Point before the harsher weather-inspired name stuck.
It lies near the town of Westport on the West Coast of New Zealand's South Island.
